title: Widening educational inequalities for young people attending child and adolescent mental health services: a longitudinal cohort study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: A 'mortality gap' is well-documented in individuals with severe mental illness but an 'education gap' emerges much earlier in life, with major long-term consequences. While educational attainment has improved in most high-income countries in recent decades, it is unknown whether these improvements have narrowed the education gap for young people who attend child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS).

METHODS: This nationwide, longitudinal cohort study used linked administrative data from the Secure Anonymised Information Linkage (SAIL) databank for a large cohort of individuals in Wales born between 1992 and 2003 and followed to 2019. We compared performance on the General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE) exams, taken at age 16, between young people with and without prior CAMHS contact. We divided the population into two sequential birth cohorts (1992-1997 vs 1998-2003) and tested whether the association between CAMHS contact and failure to achieve key GCSE thresholds changed over time.

RESULTS: In the total population, the proportion of young people failing to achieve the basic GCSE level one threshold fell from 6.9% in the older (1992-1997) cohort to 3.7% in the younger (1998-2003) cohort. Young people who attended CAMHS, however, were significantly more likely to fail to achieve level one GCSEs in both cohorts (aOR = 4.28, 95% CI = 4.08, 4.48). Critically, this gap widened over time for GCSE Level-1 attainment, both for CAMHS outpatients (interaction aOR = 1.30, 95% CI = 1.20, 1.40) and CAMHS inpatients (interaction aOR = 1.80, 95% CI = 1.47, 2.19).

CONCLUSIONS: Despite overall improvements in educational attainment in the general population, there is a growing gap in educational attainment between young people accessing CAMHS and their peers. The failure to attain basic qualifications may lead to lifelong socioeconomic disadvantage. Research on how to effectively address the educational needs of young people attending CAMHS is an urgent economic and public health issue.

title: Associations between Simple and Complex Executive Function skills and adaptive function in a sample of 3-year-olds enriched for variation in autism and ADHD traits
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adaptive Functioning-including communication, socialization, and daily living skills-predicts outcomes and quality of life for individuals who are autistic or have ADHD, yet its cognitive underpinnings in early development remain poorly understood. Executive Functions (EFs) are a plausible mechanism linking developmental level or IQ to Adaptive Functioning, but prior work in preschoolers has relied largely on parent-reported EF measures, which are vulnerable to shared method variance with parent-reported Adaptive Functioning. Here, we examine associations between performance-based EF and parent-reported Adaptive Functioning among 3-year-olds enriched for variation in autism and ADHD traits.

METHODS: One hundred and twenty-nine children (109 with a family history of autism and/or ADHD) completed six EF tasks, reduced through factor analysis to scores for Simple EF (pertaining to simple response inhibition, holding information in mind, and applying a rule) and Complex EF (involving complex response inhibition, shifting response in accordance with a new task set, and updating information). Adaptive Functioning was assessed using the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-Second Edition. Autism traits, ADHD traits and developmental level were measured using the SRS-2, CBCL-Preschool, and MSEL, respectively. Hierarchical regression models tested whether each EF index was positively associated with Adaptive Functioning, and whether these effects remained after controlling for developmental level, autism traits, and ADHD traits.

RESULTS: Both Simple and Complex EF were positively associated with Adaptive Functioning (β = .293, .316). While associations between Simple EF and Adaptive Functioning were accounted for by general developmental level, Complex EF showed associations with Adaptive Functioning above and beyond developmental level, autism, and ADHD traits.

CONCLUSIONS: EFs in general, and Complex EF in particular, represent a promising, developmentally-sensitive target for early support in the toddler or preschool years, which could positively impact the day-to-day functioning of children with a family history of autism/ADHD, or already showing elevated autism traits.

title: Annual Research Review: A probe into sensitive periods - how the developmental timing of adverse childhood experiences influences brain structure and function - a systematic review
abstract: It is proposed that adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) - potent predictors of mental illness - exert time-dependent effects on neurodevelopment, reflecting periods of heightened neuroplasticity and developmental sensitivity. We systematically reviewed neuroimaging studies examining the role of timing in the association of ACE exposure with brain structure and function across the lifespan. Across 43 studies spanning childhood to adulthood, findings most consistently implicate earlier onset and longer duration of adversity in alterations to limbic and paralimbic regions, including the hippocampus, amygdala, cerebellum and global brain measures. However, evidence for discrete sensitive periods is mixed and varies by brain system, outcome and analytic approach, with no consistent pattern of sensitive periods emerging across adversity types and functional neuroimaging studies remaining comparatively limited. Progress in the field is further constrained by substantial conceptual and methodological heterogeneity, including inconsistent operationalisation of sensitive periods, reliance on retrospective ACE measures and predominantly cross-sectional designs. Moving forward, we argue that advancing the field will require reconceptualising sensitive periods as probabilistic, system-specific and shaped by the nature, timing and chronicity of adversity, rather than as fixed developmental windows. Integrating longitudinal assessment of adversity and neurodevelopment with measures of the neurobiological processes underlying plasticity may help determine whether sensitive periods are better characterised by underlying neuroplasticity than chronological age alone. Improved understanding of these developmental processes may ultimately help inform the timing and targeting of preventive and therapeutic interventions for young people exposed to adversity.

title: Urbanization and the network position of loneliness in adolescent suicide risk: A four-stage analysis across 87 countries
abstract: Loneliness is a well-established correlate of adolescent suicidal ideation, yet prior cross-national studies have mainly quantified average associations with suicidal behavior. Less is known about whether loneliness occupies the same position within broader suicide-risk networks across societal contexts. Using cross-sectional data from the public World Health Organization Global School-based Student Health Survey from 87 countries (N = 439,026; 52.1% female), we examined cross-national variation in the network position and predictive role of loneliness. Stage-specific samples were 317,141 adolescents from 64 countries for network estimation, 333,940 adolescents for prediction transfer, 42 countries for feature-importance screening, 296,863 adolescents from these countries for multilevel models, and 38 countries for edge analyses. Suicidal ideation was consistently among the most central nodes, but prediction models transferred poorly across regions, with a 17.3 percentage-point loss in area under the curve. Loneliness showed the greatest cross-context variation among predictors. Across 11 macro-level indicators, national urbanization had the strongest association with loneliness's model-based importance (Spearman r = .655, p < .001 after false discovery rate correction). Individual-level models indicated a stronger association between loneliness and suicidal ideation in more urbanized countries (odds ratio = 1.096, 95% confidence interval [1.053, 1.140]), and country-level network models revealed stronger loneliness-suicidal-ideation edges where urbanization was higher (Spearman r = .639). These findings suggest that loneliness may become more tightly connected to adolescent suicide risk in more urbanized social contexts.

title: "We are given this huge responsibility": Parents' experiences of physical health risk and medical care in ARFID
abstract: Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) is associated with significant physical health complications, yet little is known about how families experience and manage these risks or access medical care. This study aimed to explore parents' experiences of physical health complications, medical risk, and healthcare in children and adolescents with ARFID. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 25 parents of children and adolescents (aged 4-17 years) with a formal diagnosis of ARFID or who met DSM-5 criteria for ARFID at study screening without a formal diagnosis. Participants were recruited across the UK using purposive sampling to capture variation in age, ARFID presentation and parent-reported weight status. Interviews were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes were developed: Living in a Body with ARFID; Parenting on the edge: responsibility, guilt, and impossible trade-offs; Seeking Help in a System with limited knowledge of ARFID; and Care in Practice. Together, these themes captured parents' experiences of ARFID-related physical health concerns as extending beyond individual symptoms, shaping children's daily lives while placing substantial responsibility on parents to manage risk and navigate variable access to ARFID-informed healthcare. Parents perceived high levels of responsibility for managing physical health risk in ARFID amid limited clinical oversight. Findings highlight the importance of clinician-led assessment of physical health concerns that extends beyond weight alone, alongside accessible ARFID-informed multidisciplinary care.

title: Beyond single risk factors: defeat and genetic variations linking cumulative interpersonal risk to suicidal ideation in Chinese adolescents
abstract: Suicide among adolescents is a major global health concern. While poor interpersonal relationships are well-established risk factors for adolescent suicide, most research has focused on isolated interpersonal domains, limiting our understanding of how cumulative interpersonal risks shape the developmental trajectories of suicidal ideation, particularly within a gene × environment framework. A total of 760 adolescents (Mage = 13.01, 54.6% girls) were assessed at baseline and followed up across three additional six-month intervals over one and a half years. Adolescents' saliva was collected at T2 for genetic extraction, and the multilocus genetic composite (MGC) was created based on the gene-by-environment interaction between SNPs and cumulative interpersonal risk for defeat via the leave-one-out machine learning approach. Findings of latent growth modeling revealed that adolescents' suicidal ideation increased over time. Cumulative interpersonal risk was indirectly associated with higher initial levels and a faster increase in suicidal ideation through defeat, particularly among adolescents with a higher MGC compared to those with a lower MGC. These findings suggest that intervention strategies should aim to reduce adolescents' exposure to interpersonal risk, alleviate feelings of defeat, and consider the genetic susceptibility.

title: Heterogeneous decision-making in ADHD: computational subtypes and their distinct prefrontal connectivity patterns
abstract: Children with ADHD exhibit decision-making deficits characterized by lower efficiency in evidence accumulation and a preference for smaller, sooner rewards in intertemporal choices. This study aimed to preliminarily explore computational subtypes of ADHD in children and to investigate differences in prefrontal functional connectivity between ADHD subtypes. A total of 94 children with ADHD and 63 typically developing children matched for sex, age, and IQ were included. All participants completed the Two Choice Impulsivity Paradigm (TCIP) and the ADHD Symptom Rating Scale, and 43 children with ADHD underwent resting-state fMRI. A hierarchical drift diffusion model was applied to analyze TCIP task performance, followed by two-step cluster analysis to identify decision-making subtypes. Differences in prefrontal functional connectivity among ADHD decision-making subtypes were then compared. The ADHD group showed fewer square selections in the TCIP (p < 0.001), lower drift rates (pBayes < 0.001), and shorter non-decision times (pBayes = 0.002). Two decision-making subtypes were identified: a decision-making deficit subtype and a decision-making normal subtype, characterized by lower and higher drift rates, respectively. The ADHD decision-making deficit subtype exhibited stronger functional connectivity between the left medial superior frontal gyrus and both the right middle frontal gyrus and the right postcentral gyrus, as well as between the right medial superior frontal gyrus and the right postcentral gyrus (all p < 0.05). The results reveal decision-making deficits and internal heterogeneity in children with ADHD during intertemporal choice, with this heterogeneity possibly associated with abnormal functional connectivity between the medial superior frontal gyrus and the middle frontal gyrus/postcentral gyrus.

title: Daring-impulsive (DI) traits versus ADHD features in adolescent girls with conduct problems
abstract: The current study examined differential associations between daring-impulsive (DI) traits and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) features in relation to conduct disorder (CD) and clinically relevant characteristics in 115 criminal justice-involved and non-criminal justice-involved girls (ages 16-17 years). Adolescents provided self-ratings of DI traits, ADHD features, externalizing and internalizing concerns, impulsivity, and academic and social outcomes. A semi-structured diagnostic interview to assess CD symptoms was also used. We estimated associations using bivariate correlations to examine the dimensional overlap and convergent and discriminant validity of DI and ADHD total, inattention, and hyperactivity-impulsivity scores. We also examined the criterion-related validity of DI scores in distinguishing adolescents with and without CD using independent samples t-tests. Finally, we tested the incremental validity of DI scores in explaining outcomes over and above ADHD scores using multiple hierarchical regression analyses. Results indicated weak to moderate associations between DI and ADHD scores (r's = 0.22-0.26). Further, DI and ADHD scores differed in relation to indices of CD symptoms (e.g., total number of CD symptoms: r's = 0.19-0.31), externalizing (e.g., proactive aggression: r's = 0.13-0.38) and internalizing concerns (e.g., anxiety: r's = -0.06-0.41), impulsivity (e.g., sensation seeking: r's = -0.03-0.40), and academic and social outcomes (e.g., number of detained friends: r's = 0.13-0.27). DI scores significantly distinguished adolescents with CD (p < .01), but ADHD scores did not. Additionally, over and above ADHD scores, DI contributed incremental variance in explaining CD, externalizing concerns, distinct domains of impulsivity, and academic and social outcomes (ΔR 2  0.04 to 0.18). These findings have important implications for understanding the usefulness of DI traits in better understanding the heterogeneity of CD among criminal and non-criminal justice-involved girls.

title: Prenatal Exposure to Wildfire PM2.5 and Risk of ASD and ADHD in Children Enrolled in Medicaid
abstract:
This cohort study investigates the association between prenatal exposure to wildfire-related fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) and risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children.

Key Points Question Is prenatal exposure to wildfire-related fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) associated with risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children? Findings In this population-based cohort study of 893 212 mother-child pairs enrolled in US Medicaid, higher prenatal wildfire PM 2.5 exposure was associated with an increase in ASD risk, whereas no meaningful association was observed for ADHD; associations for ASD were strongest with exposure to PM 2.5 during midpregnancy to late pregnancy. Meaning This study found that prenatal exposure to wildfire-related air pollution may be associated with an increased risk of ASD, highlighting the importance of reducing maternal exposure during pregnancy as wildfire activity intensifies.

Importance Wildfires are an increasing source of fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ), yet evidence on prenatal wildfire smoke exposure and long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes remains limited. Objective To examine whether prenatal exposure to wildfire-related PM 2.5 is associated with risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children. Design, Setting, and Participants This was a population-based cohort study of the US nationwide Medicaid population using Medicaid Analytic Extract (MAX) data from 2007 to 2014 with follow-up through childhood. Included were mother-child pairs with continuous enrollment and stable residential zip code during pregnancy. Exposure Weekly wildfire smoke–attributable PM 2.5 at 1-km 2 resolution, aggregated to the zip code level across pregnancy. Main Outcomes and Measures Incident ASD and ADHD identified using validated claims-based algorithms. Associations were estimated using Cox proportional-hazards models with distributed lag nonlinear models. Results A total of 893 212 mother-child pairs (mother mean [SD] age, 24.7 [5.9] years) were included in this analysis. Children entered the cohort at birth (452 218 [50.6%] male). Mean (SD) observed follow-up was 6.3 (2.4) years for children diagnosed with ASD and 7.1 (1.9) years for children diagnosed with ADHD. Among 893 212 children, 8357 were diagnosed with ASD and 22 302 with ADHD. The cumulative incidence until age 8 years was 1.9% for ASD and 10.4% for ADHD. An IQR increase in cumulative wildfire PM 2.5 exposure (0.75 µg/m 3 ) during pregnancy was associated with increased risk of ASD (hazard ratio [HR], 1.30; 95% CI, 1.07-1.59) but not ADHD (HR, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.91-1.17). Associations for ASD were strongest during midpregnancy to late gestation compared with early gestation. Results were robust to sensitivity analyses. Conclusions and Relevance Results of this cohort study show that prenatal exposure to wildfire-related PM 2.5 may be associated with increased risk of ASD but not ADHD. These findings highlight the potential neurodevelopmental impacts of wildfire smoke and underscore the need for strategies to reduce exposure during pregnancy as wildfire activity intensifies.

title: Global Burden of Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa, 1990 to 2023, With Forecasts to 2050: A Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 Analysis
abstract:
This cross-sectional study estimates the global, regional, and national prevalence and disability burden of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—and mortality attributable to anorexia nervosa—from 1990 to 2023, and to forecast prevalence to 2050.

Key Points Question What is the global burden of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa? Findings In this Global Burden of Disease 2023 analysis, an estimated 18.1 million people worldwide were living with anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa in 2023, accounting for 3.83 million disability-adjusted life-years. Burden was highest in high-income regions, the largest increases in age-standardized prevalence occurred in East Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia, and prevalent cases increased by 71% since 1990 and are forecast to rise through 2050. Meaning The burden of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa is increasing globally, highlighting the need for strengthened surveillance, earlier detection, and better integration of care into mental health systems.

Importance Eating disorders are a major cause of nonfatal mental health burden, yet global evidence on their long-term trends, geographic distribution, and future trajectories remains limited. Objective To estimate the global, regional, and national prevalence and disability burden of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—and mortality attributable to anorexia nervosa—from 1990 to 2023, and to forecast prevalence to 2050. Design, Setting, and Participants Using Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 methods, data were synthesized from systematic literature reviews, population surveys, and vital registration systems. Estimates were produced for 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023, with forecasts through 2050. These data were analyzed from October 2025 to August 2026. Exposure Anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa diagnosis. Main Outcomes and Measures Counts and age-standardized rates with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs) for anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa prevalence, years lived with disability (YLDs), and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), and anorexia nervosa mortality, reported by age, sex, and location. Results In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people (95% UI, 13.9-24.0) globally were living with anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa, of whom 12.6 million (69.4%) were female, 5.5 million were male (30.6%), and 41.2% were aged 10 to 24 years. These cases accounted for 3.83 million DALYs (95% UI, 2.23-5.69). Since 1990, the global number of prevalent cases increased by 71.0%, while age-standardized prevalence and DALY rates rose by about 21%. Females experienced substantially higher prevalence and DALY rates than males. The highest age-standardized prevalence rates were observed in high-income regions, particularly Australasia and Western Europe, whereas the largest relative increases in age-standardized prevalence occurred in East Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia. Forecasts indicate continued increases in prevalent cases through 2050. Conclusions and Relevance This GBD 2023 analysis found that anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa contribute substantially to global nonfatal health loss. These findings support the integration of eating disorders into mental health surveillance, prevention, and service planning worldwide.

Introduction Anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa are serious eating disorders characterized by substantial disturbances in eating or eating-related behavior. Anorexia nervosa is commonly characterized by restricted intake, low body weight, and fear of weight gain, whereas bulimia nervosa involves recurrent binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors and overconcern with body weight or shape. These disorders arise from both genetic and environmental risk factors, disproportionately affect adolescents and young adults, and often follow a chronic or relapsing course, with substantial medical, psychological, and social consequences. In the Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) 2010, the health burden of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa was first quantified at the global, regional, and national levels, with the most recent major update conducted in GBD 2017 following the incorporation of additional data sources. Since then, no substantial new data have been added to the estimation framework, apart from limited gray literature included in GBD 2019. Updated estimates are needed to inform evidence-based health care strategies, particularly in light of the COVID-19 pandemic, which may have affected service demand and symptom burden in some settings. While other eating disorders, such as binge eating disorder and other specified feeding or eating disorder, account for a substantial proportion of eating disorders, the absence of survey-derived disability weights for these disorders remains a barrier to quantifying their nonfatal health burden within the GBD framework. Accordingly, this analysis focuses specifically on anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa and does not represent the total burden of eating disorders. We extend previous estimates of the disease burden of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa through 2023 using updated data sources and refined methodological approaches, and we forecast future prevalence through 2050. This article was produced and conducted as part of the GBD Collaborator Network and in accordance with GBD Protocol. Methods Study Overview We estimated incidence, prevalence, and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) for anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, as well as mortality attributable to anorexia nervosa, by age and sex for 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. The GBD 2023 iteration incorporated newly identified data and methodological refinements, including changes to improve model fit in selected locations, the application of refined crosswalks for bulimia nervosa to harmonize diagnostic criteria, and adjustment for recall bias. This study follows the Guidelines for Accurate and Transparent Health Estimates Reporting ( GATHER ) statement (eMethods 1 in Supplement 1 ). Deidentified data were used and the study was approved by the University of Washington Institutional Review Board (9060), which waived the requirement for informed consent. Case Definitions and Input Data Anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa were modeled separately using DSM or International Classification of Diseases ( ICD ) case definitions. Other eating disorders were not included in the estimation because there were no available disability weights for those conditions that had been derived by disability-weight surveys. Detailed case definitions are provided in eMethods 2 in Supplement 1 . Updated systematic literature reviews were conducted to identify studies reporting the prevalence, incidence, and remission of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, as well as excess mortality associated with anorexia nervosa. Peer-reviewed literature was identified through electronic database searches of PsycINFO, Embase, and PubMed. In addition, gray literature searches and expert consultation were undertaken. Detailed search strategies for the electronic databases are provided in eMethods 2 in Supplement 1 . In total, 59 new citations were incorporated compared with GBD 2017. Vital registration data used to estimate mortality attributable to anorexia nervosa were from the GBD Cause of Death database (eMethods 3 in Supplement 1 ). Data Processing and Modeling Epidemiological data were harmonized before modeling, including age-sex splitting and meta-regression–bayesian, regularized, trimmed (MR-BRT) adjustments where required. For bulimia nervosa, crosswalks were applied to account for differences in recall periods and diagnostic criteria. DisMod-MR version 2.1 was used to estimate incidence, prevalence, and remission by age, sex, location, and year. Excess mortality was modeled for anorexia nervosa only; no excess mortality was modeled for bulimia nervosa. Mortality attributable to anorexia nervosa was estimated using the Cause of Death Ensemble Model. Fatal outcomes were not estimated for bulimia nervosa because mortality data were sparse for most countries and territories, making reliable modeling and interpretation of mortality estimates infeasible. Detailed preprocessing procedures, model assumptions, covariates, and parameter specifications are provided in eMethods 2 and 3 in Supplement 1 . DALYs DALYs were calculated as the sum of years lived with disability (YLDs) and years of life lost (YLLs). YLDs were estimated by multiplying prevalence by the corresponding disability weight, with comorbidity correction applied to account for co-occurring conditions. YLLs were calculated for anorexia nervosa by multiplying attributable deaths by the standard life expectancy at the corresponding age. Details of disability weights and comorbidity correction are provided in eMethods 2 and 4 in Supplement 1 . Forecasting Prevalence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, separately and combined, was forecast from 2024 to 2050 by sex, age, and location using a multistage forecasting framework consistent with approaches used in previous GBD forecasting analyses. Data from 1990 to 2019 were used to fit the forecasting model to avoid potential bias related to the COVID-19 pandemic. Forecast prevalence rates were multiplied by forecast population counts to obtain the number of cases. Calculating Uncertainty Uncertainty was propagated throughout the estimation process, with 95% uncertainty intervals (UI) defined as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 250 draws from the estimated posterior distributions. GBD 2023 analyses were completed using Python versions 3.8.17 and 3.10.4 (Python Software Foundation), Stata version 15.1 (Stata Corp), and R versions 3.5 and 4.2 (R Project). The statistical code used in GBD 2023 is available upon request. Results Disease Burden of Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa in 2023 In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million (95% UI, 13.9-24.0) people were living with anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa globally, corresponding to an age-standardized prevalence of 225.6 (95% UI, 173.1-301.2) per 100 000 population ( Figure 1 ) ( Table ). Females accounted for 12.6 million (69.4%) of these cases, males accounted for 5.5 million (30.6%), and 41.2% of cases occurred among young people aged 10 to 24 years. By subtype, an estimated 3.92 million (95% UI, 2.78-5.30) had anorexia nervosa and 14.2 million (95% UI, 10.1-20.2) had bulimia nervosa worldwide in 2023 (eTables 1 and 2 in Supplement 2 ). In 2023, there were an estimated 237 (95% UI, 116-373) deaths due to anorexia nervosa. Globally, these eating disorders accounted for 3.83 million DALYs (95% UI, 2.23-5.69) in 2023, corresponding to an age-standardized DALY rate of 47.8 (95% UI, 27.7-71.0) per 100 000 population ( Figure 1 ) ( Table ). Among the 2 subtypes studied, anorexia nervosa accounted for 847 000 (95% UI, 477 000-1 290 000) DALYs, whereas bulimia nervosa accounted for 2.98 million (95% UI, 1.66-4.72) DALYs (eTables 1 and 2 in Supplement 2 ). Changes in Disease Burden From 1990 to 2023 From 1990 to 2023, the number of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa cases increased by 71.0% (95% UI, 65.8%-78.0%), and the age-standardized prevalence rate increased by 20.6% (95% UI, 19.6%-21.6%) ( Figure 1 ) ( Table ). Cases increased by 57.9% (95% UI, 54.0%-62.5%) for anorexia nervosa and 75.1% (95% UI, 68.0%-83.7%) for bulimia nervosa, with corresponding increases in age-standardized prevalence of 17.0% (95% UI, 15.2%-18.5%) and 21.7% (95% UI, 20.5%-23.0%), respectively (eTables 1 and 2 in Supplement 2 ). During the same period, DALYs due to these eating disorders increased by 70.5% (95% UI, 65.1%-77.6%) and the corresponding age-standardized DALY rate increased by 20.5% (95% UI, 18.9%-21.9%) ( Figure 1 , Table ). DALYs increased by 57.4% (95% UI, 52.8%-62.7%) for anorexia nervosa and 74.6% (95% UI, 67.3%-83.9%) for bulimia nervosa, with corresponding increases in age-standardized DALY rates of 16.6% (95% UI, 13.9%-18.8%) and 21.7% (95% UI, 20.1%-23.3%), respectively (eTables 1 and 2 in Supplement 2 ). Geographical Distribution of Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa In 2023, Australasia had the highest regional age-standardized prevalence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa combined, at 946.4 (95% UI, 709.6-1260.7) per 100 000 population, whereas central sub-Saharan Africa had the lowest prevalence, at 114.8 (95% UI, 87.8-154.1) per 100 000 population. From 1990 to 2023, the largest regional increase in age-standardized prevalence occurred in East Asia (61.5%; 95% UI, 56.6%-66.2%), followed by South Asia (48.5%; 95% UI, 44.5%-52.7%) and Southeast Asia (44.2%; 95% UI, 41.1%-47.9%) ( Table ). Australasia also had the highest regional prevalence for each disorder, and East Asia had the largest increases for both anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa (eTables 1 and 2 in Supplement 2 ). At the country and territory level, age-standardized prevalence in 2023 ranged from 1026.5 (95% UI, 770.3-1370.5) per 100 000 population in Australia to 78.1 (95% UI, 59.5-106.5) in Somalia. From 1990 to 2023, the age-standardized prevalence rate increased in 156 of 204 countries and territories, with the largest increase in Equatorial Guinea (92.6%; 95% UI, 78.4%-107.5%). By contrast, 11 countries experienced declining trends, with the greatest decrease occurring in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (27.2%; 95% UI, 20.0%-35.1%) ( Figure 2 ) (eTable 3 in Supplement 2 ). Disorder-specific geographical estimates are shown in eFigures 1 and 2 in Supplement 1 and eTables 4 and 5 in Supplement 2 . The geographical pattern of age-standardized DALY rates was similar to that observed for prevalence, ranging regionally from 198.7 (95% UI, 112.8-305.6) per 100 000 population in Australasia to 24.1 (95% UI, 14.0-35.4) in central sub-Saharan Africa ( Table ). Country- and disorder-specific DALY estimates are provided in eTables 1 through 5 in Supplement 2 . Sex and Age Patterns The age-standardized prevalence of these eating disorders was higher among females than males, at 318.3 (95% UI, 246.8-416.7) per 100 000 population in females compared with 135.7 (95% UI, 101.0-186.9) per 100 000 population in males ( Table ). Similar sex differences were observed for both anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa ( Figure 3 ) (eTables 1 and 2 in Supplement 2 ). Across age groups, the prevalence of the 2 disorders combined peaked among individuals aged 20 to 24 years (487.3; 95% UI, 302.5-816.7 per 100 000 population) and subsequently declined at older ages. Peak prevalence occurred at ages 15 to 19 years for anorexia nervosa (133.8; 95% UI, 82.7-206.4 per 100 000 population) and 30 to 34 years for bulimia nervosa (388.8; 95% UI, 261.7-594.0 per 100 000 population) (eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 ). title: Effects of External Trigeminal Nerve Stimulation on Neurocognitive Functioning in Children and Adolescents With ADHD: A Phase 2b Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with atypical cognition and related autonomic nervous system regulation. Trigeminal nerve stimulation (TNS) received U.S. Food and Drug Administration clearance as neuromodulation treatment for ADHD based on findings of clinical improvements from a pilot trial that were not confirmed in the authors' larger multicenter UK trial. Effects of TNS on cognition in ADHD, however, are relatively unknown. The authors therefore tested secondary outcomes, that is, short- and longer-term effects of active versus sham TNS in youths with ADHD on a broad neurocognitive task battery, physiological indicators of autonomic nervous system regulation, and head motion.

METHODS: In the first confirmatory, multicenter, double-blind, parallel-group, phase 2b randomized sham-controlled trial, 150 youths with ADHD (ages 8-18 years) were assigned to 4 weeks of nightly active (N=75) or sham (N=75) TNS. Cognitive performance was assessed using a comprehensive battery of executive function and attention tasks (inhibition, sustained attention, time estimation, processing speed, and intrasubject response variability) at baseline, posttreatment, and 6-month follow-up. Autonomic nervous system regulation (heart rate, heart rate variability, and electrodermal activity) was measured via a wristband device and head motion with an eye tracker during rest or cognitive testing.

RESULTS: Intention-to-treat analysis showed no significant differential treatment effects between active and sham TNS on any cognitive or physiological outcomes after 4 weeks of treatment or on cognitive measures at 6-month follow-up.

CONCLUSIONS: TNS does not appear to improve neurocognitive performance, autonomic regulation, or head motion in youths with ADHD, extending negative clinical findings. The findings do not provide evidence to support TNS as a viable treatment to improve cognitive or autonomic nervous system functioning in youths with ADHD.

title: Efficacy of Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation on the Treatment of Late Life Depression: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This network meta-analysis (NMA) aimed to evaluate the comparative efficacy of non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) interventions for late-life depression (LLD), with treatment rankings provided as a secondary outcome.

METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and NMA of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing NIBS for major depressive disorder in adults aged ≥ 60 years. Comprehensive searches of PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library were performed up to June 2025. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed quality using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. A random-effects NMA was implemented using the netmeta package in R. Certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework. Primary outcomes included changes in depressive symptoms, measured by the standard mean difference (SMD). Secondary outcomes included response rates and remission rates.

RESULTS: Twenty-five RCTs involving 1344 participants and 15 NIBS modalities were included. Bilateral electroconvulsive therapy (BL-ECT; SMD = 1.13, 95% CI 0.37-1.90) and high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rTMS-10Hz-F3; SMD = 0.42, 95% CI 0.02-0.81) consistently outperformed sham across all efficacy outcomes. Both interventions formed closed loops of the network geometry, enabling formal assessment of agreement between direct and indirect evidence. Although inconsistency was detected in the symptom severity network, both interventions demonstrated consistent benefits across efficacy outcomes and retained moderate-certainty evidence.

CONCLUSION: BL-ECT and rTMS-10Hz-F3 emerged as the most consistently effective NIBS treatments for LLD, supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Other highly-ranked modalities require cautious interpretation due to sparse data.

REGISTRATION: PROSPERO (CRD42024628560).

title: Effect of Blonanserin on Neurotrophic Factors in Patients With Non-Responsive First-Episode Schizophrenia Treated With Early Risperidone Monotherapy-A Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the efficacy of Blonanserin in patients with schizophrenia who were refractory to Risperidone monotherapy and its effects on various neurotrophic factors.

METHODS: A total of 120 patients with first-episode schizophrenia who were hospitalized in our hospital from January 2022 to December 2023 and did not respond to early Risperidone monotherapy were selected as the study participants. They were randomly divided into a control group and a research group, with 60 cases in each group. The control group was treated with Clozapine, and the research group was treated with Blonanserin for 3 months. The scores of the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS), the scores of the Generic Quality of Life Inventory (GQOLI-74), the serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), the serum S100β protein, the neuron-specific enolase (NSE), and the Neuregulin-1 (NRG1) levels of the two groups were compared, and the adverse drug reactions of patients were recorded.

RESULTS: After 3 months of treatment, the PANSS scores of both groups decreased compared with those before treatment, and the PANSS scores of the research group were lower. The scores of physical function, social function, and psychological function of the two groups were higher than those before treatment, and the scores of the research group were higher than those of the control group. The differences were statistically significant (p < 0.05 for all). The serum BDNF and NRG1 levels of the two groups were higher than those before treatment, and those of the research group were higher than those of the control group. The S100β and NSE levels of the two groups were lower than those before treatment, and those of the research group were lower than those of the control group. The differences were statistically significant (p < 0.05 for all). No serious adverse reactions occurred in both groups. Most patients with adverse reactions could tolerate them or improved after symptomatic treatment.

CONCLUSION: Blonanserin can effectively relieve the symptoms of schizophrenia and improve the quality of life of first-episode schizophrenia patients who have failed to respond to Risperidone monotherapy in the early stage. Due to the short follow-up time and small sample size of this study, further prospective multicenter studies should be carried out in the future to observe the long-term treatment effect and provide more favorable reference for clinical practice.

title: Combining Cognitive Training and Brain Stimulation: A Novel Approach to Address Disordered Eating and Antipsychotic-Induced Weight Gain in People With Severe Mental Illness
abstract:
ABSTRACT Background Antipsychotic‐induced weight gain is a distressing side effect that most often occurs within the first 3–6 months of pharmacological initiation, significantly increasing cardiometabolic risk and mortality in individuals with severe mental illness. Aims To assess the feasibility of reducing food craving and binge eating using Approach Bias Modification Training (ABMT) combined with real or sham Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS). Method In this double‐blind, parallel‐group, two‐arm, sham‐controlled trial, adults with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder on stable doses of antipsychotics were randomly allocated to a total of five ABMT sessions together with either real or sham tDCS administered over 3 weeks. Assessments were made at baseline (T0), post‐treatment (T1) and at a 2‐week follow‐up (T2). Feasibility outcomes included recruitment, attendance, retention, tDCS safety, acceptability, tolerability, and blinding. Secondary outcomes were changes in food craving, binge eating, approach bias to food, body mass index, and psychological symptoms. Results Twenty‐eight participants were recruited (93% of target). Retention was high (T1 = 85.7% and T2 = 78.6%); blinding accuracy was 46.4%. Medium effect sizes favoured ‘ABMT + real tDCS’ for reducing binge eating ( d = −0.6, 95% CI −1.5, 0.3), and ‘ABMT + sham tDCS’ for reducing food cravings ( d = 0.5, 95% CI −0.4, 1.4). Within‐groups, only the ‘ABMT + real tDCS’ arm showed reduced approach bias to food and approach‐avoidance bias to food, and increased avoidance bias to food (all p < 0.05). This was followed by reduced binge eating episodes ( p < 0.05). Both groups reported frequent binge‐eating episodes (‘ABMT + tDCS’ = 43%; ‘ABMT + sham tDCS’ = 28.6%). Conclusion The initiation of antipsychotic therapy is a critical clinical window for early intervention to mitigate the long‐term metabolic and psychiatric consequences of antipsychotic‐induced weight gain. Combining ABMT + tDCS is acceptable and may help reduce binge eating in individuals on antipsychotics, with a potential synergistic effect between cognitive training and brain stimulation. A confirmatory trial is needed to assess its effectiveness and should include BED diagnosis as a stratification criterion. Trial Registration: ISRCTN Identifier: 13280178

Abbreviations ABMT approach bias modification training BIS‐11 Barratt Impulsiveness Scale BRC Biomedical Research Centre CONSORT consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials DASS‐21 depression, anxiety and stress scale dlPFC dorsolateral prefrontal cortex DSM‐5 diagnostic and statistical manual for mental disorders, Fifth edition EDE‐Q eating disorder examination questionnaire F‐AAT food approach/avoidance task FCQ‐T‐r food cravings questionnaire‐trait‐reduced FCT food challenge task fMRI functional magnetic resonance imaging IoPPN Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience ISRCTN International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number MoCA Montreal cognitive assessment NIHR National Institute for Health Research PANSS‐6 Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale RCT randomised controlled trial REC Research ethics committee rTMS repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation SLaM South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust SNAPSI Simplified Negative and Positive Symptoms Interview SPIRIT Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials SRCT stimulus response compatibility task tDCS transcranial direct current stimulation VAS visual analogue scale 1 Introduction Antipsychotic‐induced weight gain (AIWG) is a distressing treatment side effect, associated with medication discontinuation, psychiatric relapse, cardiometabolic morbidity, and with premature mortality in individuals with severe mental illness (SMI) (Brown et al. 2000 ; Ballon et al. 2014 ; Manu et al. 2015 ; Speyer et al. 2021 ). Given that rapid weight gain usually occurs within the first 3–6 months of antipsychotic therapy, the initiation of treatment provides a critical clinical window for early intervention to mitigate long‐term metabolic and psychiatric consequences (Bushe et al. 2012 ; O'Mahony et al. 2026 ). AIWG arises from alterations in central neurotransmitter systems, (including histaminergic, serotonergic, and dopaminergic pathways), as well as in peripheral hormonal signalling (Coccurello and Moles 2010 ; Kowalchuk et al. 2017 ). These result in increased appetite, reduced satiation and energy expenditure, and increased fat storage (Coccurello and Moles 2010 ; Kowalchuk et al. 2017 ), which can lead to food craving and related disordered eating behaviours, for example, binge eating, (Blouin et al. 2008 ) or to binge eating disorder (BED), overweight and obesity (Theisen et al. 2003 ; Carolan et al. 2024 ). Pharmacological treatments, including metformin and GLP‐1 receptor agonists, show moderate efficacy in preventing and managing AIWG (Carolan et al. 2024 ; Campforts et al. 2024 ; Fink‐Jensen and Correll 2025 ; Fitzgerald et al. 2022 ). However, they are associated with physical side effects (Carolan et al. 2024 ; Campforts et al. 2024 ; Fink‐Jensen and Correll 2025 ), safety concerns in the mental health population, high costs (Carolan et al. 2024 ) and weight regain after drug discontinuation (Wilding et al. 2022 ). People with SMI are reported to have higher calorie intake, particularly from energy‐dense foods, and lower energy expenditure (Manu et al. 2015 ), and adherence to dietary and lifestyle interventions is challenging and limited in this group (Manu et al. 2015 ; Fink‐Jensen and Correll 2025 ). Consequently, there is a need for strategies that target the underlying causes of AIWG, such as food cravings and binge eating, to complement lifestyle and pharmacological interventions (Alvarez‐Jiménez et al. 2010 ; Bonfioli et al. 2012 ). Cognitive training and neuromodulation techniques are relatively accessible interventions that have shown the potential to modify food‐related behaviours in people with eating disorders (Brockmeyer et al. 2015a ; Brockmeyer et al. 2019 ). Approach bias modification training (ABMT), a computer‐based form of cognitive training, aims to change implicit attention biases by training individuals to avoid a negative stimulus (e.g., high‐calorie food) and to direct their attention to a neutral or positive stimulus (e.g., non‐food objects) (Brockmeyer et al. 2015a ; Brockmeyer et al. 2019 ; Beard et al. 2012 ; Kakoschke et al. 2017 ). ABMT has been reported to lower food‐related attentional bias and approach tendencies in people who binge eat (Brockmeyer et al. 2015a ), and has been linked to reduced eating disorder symptoms in people with bulimia nervosa and BED (Brockmeyer et al. 2019 ). Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), a non‐invasive form of brain stimulation, has been shown to reduce symptoms in major depressive, anxiety and substance use disorders (Moffa et al. 2020 ; Kekic et al. 2016 ). As the regulation of eating shares neural networks with general self‐regulatory processes, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) has become a primary target for intervention (Van den Eynde et al. 2013 ; Van den Eynde et al. 2010 ). Applying tDCS to the dlPFC has been reported to modulate key eating regulation processes, including reward evaluation, attention and inhibitory control, and has been shown to reduce food cravings in healthy participants and the desire to eat in overweight and obese populations (Fregni et al. 2008 ; Goldman et al. 2011 ; Montenegro et al. 2012 ). ABMT combined with tDCS is a promising intervention strategy for its role in enhancing neuroplasticity to consolidate new learning (Barron et al. 2016 ; Heeren et al. 2015 ). By altering the balance of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters, neuromodulation is proposed to create an environment that reinforces the avoidance behaviours learned during training (Barron et al. 2016 ; Heeren et al. 2015 ). This process likely facilitates memory reconsolidation, which is essential for sustained behavioural change (Barron et al. 2016 ; Heeren et al. 2015 ). Clinical evidence from addiction research suggests a synergistic effect of the combined approach, improving long‐term regulatory control and reducing relapse (den Uyl et al. 2017 ), which in the current context, would lead to a more durable reduction in food cravings and binge eating than ABMT alone. This study investigated the feasibility of an ABMT protocol enhanced by real or sham tDCS to reduce food cravings and binge eating in individuals with SMI who were taking antipsychotic medications. Based on studies in people who experience food craving, binge eating and/or obesity (Kekic et al. 2017 ; Kekic et al. 2014 ; Jansen et al. 2013 ; Lowe et al. 2014 ; Song et al. 2018 ; Flynn et al. 2024 ; Gordon 2022 ), we hypothesised that participants in the combined ‘ABMT + real tDCS’ arm will show (a) decreased approach bias towards food stimuli, (b) reduced food craving and binge eating episodes compared to those in the ‘ABMT + sham tDCS’ arm, and compared to their baseline assessment. 2 Materials and Methods Full methodological details of the ‘Effects of Cognitive Training and Neuromodulation on Eating Responses’ (ENTER) study have been published (Grycuk et al. 2020 ). In brief, this was a parallel‐group, double‐blind, two‐arm RCT, where participants were randomly allocated to receive a total of five sessions of either ‘ABMT + real tDCS’ (treatment arm) or ‘ABMT + sham tDCS’ (control arm) within 3–4 weeks, in addition to treatment as usual (TAU). To maximise study acceptability and feasibility, waiting‐list and ABMT‐only arms were not included, balancing scientific rigour with practical limitations associated with this difficult‐to‐recruit population (Beckley et al. 2025 ). Outcomes were assessed at baseline (T0), post‐treatment (T1) and at a 2‐week follow‐up (T2). At the end of the study, participants in the control arm were offered the opportunity of receiving ‘ABMT + real tDCS’; however, none chose to do so. Procedures complied with the Helsinki Declaration of 1975 (revised, 2008) and received approval from the Oxford B Research Ethics Committee (REC reference: 19/SW/0095). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The primary aim of the study was to assess feasibility of the intervention by assessing safety, recruitment, attendance, and retention rates, and estimating treatment effect sizes and standard deviations that might inform sample size calculations for a larger scale randomised clinical trial (RCT). 2.1 Participants and Setting Eligible participants were males and females, 18–65 years old, with a current Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM‐5) (American Psychiatric Association 2013 ) diagnosis of schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, or psychosis unspecified, and on a stable dose of antipsychotic and/or antidepressant medication for at least 6 weeks before taking part in the study. Exclusion criteria included contraindications to tDCS (e.g., history of seizures, stroke, brain injury, frequent and severe headaches or dizziness, metal devices in the head), and significant co‐morbid medical or psychiatric conditions (e.g., substance dependence) needing treatment in their own right. Participants were recruited between November 2019 and February 2024 (including 18‐month COVID‐19 pandemic recruitment suspension) from inpatient and community services at the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust (SLaM), as well as through online platforms, including the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience (IoPPN) website, Call for Participants , MQ Mental Health Research website , and social media channels from the Centre for Research in Eating and Weight Disorders at King's College London (CREW‐KCL). The study was conducted at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience at KCL and at inpatient and community services at SLaM. 2.2 Sample Size, Randomisation and Blinding As a feasibility trial, this study did not require a priori sample calculation. A target sample size of 30 participants was selected, consistent with the recommended range of 24–50 participants for feasibility trials: this is sufficient to estimate effect sizes of continuous variables, which can inform sample size calculations for future large‐scale clinical trials (Lancaster et al. 2004 ; Julious 2005 ). Randomisation was conducted using the Sealed Envelope online randomisation tool (Sealed Envelope Ltd. 2019 ) by an independent researcher from KCL who was not part of the ENTER team. Participants were allocated in a 1:1 ratio to one of the two trial arms following completion of the baseline assessment. Blinding of participants and researchers to treatment allocation was ensured through the trial's parallel design. The tDCS devices incorporated a built‐in blinding feature, delivering 30 s of real stimulation (vs. 20 min for the active group) to replicate skin sensations usually reported with real stimulation. To assess blinding success, participants were asked to guess their treatment allocation in their post‐assessment session. 2.3 Intervention Participants received a total of five sessions of ABMT with either real or sham tDCS within 3–4 weeks, in addition to TAU (Figure 1 ). Each session lasted 30–40 min, inclusive of preparation time, 20 min of simultaneous tDCS and ABMT, and the administration of within‐session assessments. The cognitive training (ABMT) was an adapted version of the Food Approach/Avoidance Task (F‐AAT) (Brockmeyer et al. 2016 ; Blechert et al. 2014 ). This task employs an implicit learning paradigm, requiring participants to “push” a joystick (i.e., avoid) in response to all food pictures and “pull” the joystick (i.e., approach) in response to pictures of a non‐edible object. For more details on the task, see protocol paper (Grycuk et al. 2020 ). TDCS (real and sham) was delivered at a constant current of 2 mA (with a 10‐s fade in/out) using two 25 cm 2 surface sponge electrodes soaked in sterile saline solution (0.9% sodium chloride). Until March 2020, the neuroConn DC‐Stimulator device was utilised. Following the onset of the COVID‐19 pandemic, a self‐administered HDC Kit with MindCap by Newronika was employed (further details in ‘Changes to Protocol’ section). The stimulation site was determined using the International 10–20 system, with a bilateral montage: anode (a positively charged electrode) placed over the right dlPFC (F4 location) and the cathode (a negatively charged electrode) over the left dlPFC (F3 location) (Jasper 1958 ). In the real tDCS group, participants received continuous stimulation for 20 min, while in the sham tDCS group, stimulation was applied for 30 s before being automatically deactivated. The study followed the recommended procedures and parameters to guarantee participants' safety, and tDCS was delivered by trained researchers (Brunoni et al. 2012 ). Although tDCS is well‐tolerat

title: The Unbroken Integrative Psycho-Trauma Care Model: Health System Implementation in Wartime Ukraine
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: The ongoing war in Ukraine has generated an unprecedented burden of psychological trauma, frequently compounded by posttraumatic stress disorder, traumatic brain injury, severe physical injury, and the psychiatric consequences of captivity among former prisoners of war. In large military conflicts, civilian hospital systems are essential for delivering trauma-informed mental health care at scale while managing patients with complex, overlapping medical and psychiatric conditions under active conflict, with limited implementation guidance.

OBSERVATIONS: This Special Communication describes the implementation and clinical workflow of the Unbroken Integrative Psycho-Trauma Care Model, a multidisciplinary health system approach embedded in the Lviv First Medical Union in Western Ukraine to organize trauma-informed mental health care within a wartime civilian hospital. From February 24, 2022, through December 31, 2025, the Lviv First Medical Union treated more than 15 000 individuals for war-related injuries and cared for more than 400 former prisoners of war. During this period, 7538 unique individuals received psychiatric care through the Unbroken Model, including 4165 who received trauma-focused psychotherapy. The model was implemented through proactive psychiatric rounds across medical and surgical departments, structured triage into 4 clinical pathways, stabilization-first care sequencing, and longitudinal case management integrated with neurological, surgical, and rehabilitation services. This organization of care enabled early identification of trauma-related distress, continuity between medical and psychiatric treatment, and adaptive delivery of trauma-focused psychotherapies within a high-volume conflict setting.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: The Unbroken Model demonstrates how trauma-informed mental health care can be delivered at scale within a civilian hospital during active conflict. Its primary innovation lies in the organization of care delivery, integrating proactive outreach, triage-driven pathways, multidisciplinary coordination, and stabilization-first sequencing into a unified, scalable framework. This approach may be applicable to conflict-affected and postconflict health systems worldwide.

title: Transcriptomic Network Analysis Reveals Trauma Type- and Ancestry-Related Heterogeneity in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a debilitating psychiatric disorder that frequently co-occurs with major depressive disorder (MDD), a comorbidity that is partly attributable to shared genetic heritability and common environmental risk factors. Despite extensive efforts to identify peripheral transcriptomic biomarkers, findings have been inconsistent, potentially reflecting the substantial biological heterogeneity underlying these disorders. The primary goal of this study was to identify molecular signatures that reflect the clinical and biological heterogeneity of PTSD and MDD.

METHODS: The authors present a network analysis of blood-based transcriptomics from 466 pregnant women in South Africa, including 215 individuals with PTSD and/or MDD (mean age, 26.34 years [SD=5.77]) and 251 trauma-exposed control participants (mean age, 27.14 years [SD=5.82]). Gene expression modules associated with trauma-related phenotypes were identified, including childhood adversity, intimate partner violence, and recent life stress, as well as ancestry and depressive symptoms, highlighting multiple sources of molecular variation. To evaluate the predictive relevance of these transcriptomic features, random forest models were applied using a nested cross-validation framework with permutation testing.

RESULTS: Models achieved moderate and statistically significant performance in predicting trauma-related phenotypes (mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC], ~0.61-0.69 across models [SD=0.07-0.10]), whereas prediction of PTSD or MDD diagnosis showed near-chance performance (mean AUROC=0.52, SD=0.03).

CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that peripheral blood transcriptomic signatures are more strongly associated with trauma exposure profiles and population background than with diagnostic status. Collectively, the results support exposure-informed stratification as a complementary framework to traditional diagnostic categories for capturing biologically meaningful heterogeneity.

title: Indirect moxibustion therapy improves insomnia and associated symptoms in patients with schizophrenia
abstract:
Objective To evaluate the efficacy of low-dose dexzopiclone combined with Indirect moxibustion (IM), compared with sham Indirect moxibustion (SIM), on sleep quality (PSQI) and quality of life (SQLS) in patients with schizophrenia and comorbid insomnia. Methods This single-center randomized controlled trial ( NCT06171308 ) obtained ethics approval from Shanghai Mental Health Center (SMHC-IRB-2023-08). A total of 120 participants were randomly assigned to the IM group ( n = 60) or the SIM group ( n = 60), receiving 8 weeks of standardized intervention. Results Baseline PSQI and SQLS scores were comparable between the two groups. After 4 and 8 weeks, the IM group demonstrated significantly lower PSQI and SQLS scores than the SIM group (PSQI at week 4: 10.10 ± 1.76 vs. 13.50 ± 1.65, week 8: 10.65 ± 1.54 vs. 12.77 ± 2.05, SQLS at week 4: 28.78 ± 8.84 vs. 35.56 ± 3.38, week 8: 30.36 ± 10.63 vs. 38.07 ± 3.42). The improvement in the IM group was significantly greater than that in the SIM group in terms of change from baseline (PSQI: −3.399 [95% CI: −4.078 to −2.719] at week 4, −2.115 [95% CI: −2.795 to −1.435] at week 8, SQLS: −6.801 [95% CI: −9.104 to −4.462] at week 4, −7.732 [95% CI: −10.071 to −5.393] at week 8), with all adjusted intergroup differences being statistically significant ( P < 0.001). Conclusions Adjunctive Indirect Moxibustion led to statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in sleep quality and quality of life compared to sham procedure in this patient population over an 8-week period. These preliminary findings suggest IM is a promising adjunctive therapy. Further multicenter, long-term trials with expanded outcome indicators are required to validate its generalizability and sustained efficacy. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s13063-026-09915-w .

Highlights Indirect moxibustion significantly improved sleep quality in patients with schizophrenia and comorbid insomnia. Indirect Moxibustion effectively ameliorates quality of life in insomnia with schizophrenia. Indirect moxibustion is a promising adjunctive therapy for insomnia in patients with schizophrenia. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s13063-026-09915-w .

Introduction Schizophrenia affects approximately 1% of the global population [ 1 ]. Insomnia is a common but often overlooked comorbidity, present from prodromal to chronic stages [ 2 – 4 ]. Epidemiological evidence indicates that an estimated 25–50% of patients with schizophrenia experience clinically significant insomnia, characterized by persistent sleep difficulties and daytime functional impairment according to DSM-5 criteria [ 5 – 9 ]. Pathophysiologically, insomnia involves psychological hyperarousal, cognitive factors, and disrupted circadian and homeostatic regulation [ 10 ]. Clinically, it is categorized into short-term, chronic, and other specified subtypes. Importantly, sleep disturbance is no longer regarded as a mere secondary symptom of schizophrenia, but as an independent risk factor that exacerbates psychotic symptoms, impairs neurocognition, and deteriorates quality of life [ 11 ]. Therefore, effectively managing insomnia is essential to comprehensive schizophrenia care and reducing disease burden [ 12 ]. Despite its significance, managing insomnia in schizophrenia remains challenging and understudied. Quality of life—closely linked to prognosis [ 13 ]—is strongly influenced by sleep quality in both healthy and schizophrenia populations [ 14 ], suggesting that sleep improvement may yield broad benefits. Current pharmacotherapy relies mainly on benzodiazepine receptor agonists. Except for dexzopiclone, which is exempt from the 35-day use restriction specified by the US FDA guidelines, most hypnotic agents are only approved for short-term application. Clinicians often prescribe sedative antipsychotics to alleviate insomnia in clinically stable schizophrenia patients [ 15 ], whereas long-term hypnotic monotherapy raises risks of metabolic complications, drug reliance, and psychotic exacerbation for schizophrenia patients [ 16 – 18 ]. These concerns are particularly salient in the Chinese context. A recent real-world retrospective analysis of 33,569 valid prescriptions from 10 medical institutions in eastern China (2015–2021) found a consistent year-over-year increase in the use of benzodiazepines (BZDs) and Z-drugs (including zopiclone and dexzopiclone), with pronounced rises among elderly and female patients [ 19 ]. This rising prescription trend highlights an unmet clinical demand for low-risk auxiliary interventions for psychiatric patients with insomnia. Given these limitations of conventional pharmacotherapy, moxibustion, a core Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) therapy, has emerged as a complementary intervention [ 20 , 21 ]. It exerts therapeutic effects via thermal stimulation generated by burning mugwort, which regulates yin-yang balance and harmonizes qi and blood circulation [ 22 , 23 ]. In TCM theory, insomnia results from visceral dysfunction, qi-blood imbalance, and yin-yang disruption, often triggered by emotional stress or chronic illness. Moxibustion delivers localized thermal stimulation to specific acupoints to correct the above pathological imbalances. Indirect moxibustion (IM), a classic moxibustion technique first documented in the Zhouhou Beiji Fang compiled by Ge Hong in the Jin Dynasty, adopts a medicinal buffer between moxa materials and the skin, enabling milder, more uniform, and safer thermal delivery [ 24 ]. This enhances safety and tolerability, especially in vulnerable psychiatric populations. Nevertheless, few studies have systematically assessed the efficacy of IM—particularly as an adjunct therapy for insomnia in schizophrenia. To address this gap, we conducted a preliminary randomized controlled trial to evaluate the auxiliary efficacy of IM as an adjunct to low-dose dexzopiclone for improving sleep quality and quality of life in schizophrenia patients with comorbid insomnia. We hypothesized that IM would improve sleep quality—particularly in the subdimensions of sleep latency, efficiency, and daytime dysfunction, as measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI)—through its proposed mechanisms of regulating qi, calming the mind, and harmonizing yin and yang. We further anticipated that such sleep improvements would translate into broader psychosocial and quality-of-life benefits, assessed by the Schizophrenia Quality of Life Scale (SQLS). The primary study outcome was the between-group difference in PSQI score changes, while secondary outcomes included alterations in SQLS scores and treatment acceptability. Materials and methods Design This single-center, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06171308 ) was approved by the Ethics Committee of Shanghai Mental Health Center (SMHC-IRB-2023-08). All enrolled participants provided written informed consent prior to trial enrollment. Eligible participants were randomly assigned to the IM group (low-dose dexzopiclone + IM) or the sham indirect moxibustion (SIM) group (low-dose dexzopiclone + SIM) for an 8-week intervention. The detailed trial protocol has been previously published. The formal Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP, version 1.0) was finalized and archived prior to participant screening, in accordance with CONSORT 2025 Item 3. This SAP prospectively predefined all confirmatory intergroup comparisons and classified intragroup longitudinal pairwise comparisons as post hoc exploratory analyses. The complete SAP file is provided as supplementary material alongside this submission; full SAP text is not integrated into the main manuscript body, and qualified researchers may request a copy from the corresponding author for valid academic purposes (Fig. 1 ). Setting and participants From November 2022 to November 2023, a total of 122 inpatients with schizophrenia and comorbid insomnia were screened at the Shanghai Mental Health Center. Two patients were excluded due to early hospital discharge before randomization. The remaining 120 eligible participants were randomly allocated to the IM ( n = 60) or the SIM group ( n = 60). All participants completed the 8-week intervention and assessments, with zero dropouts and missing data. Diagnostic criteria included Western Medical Diagnostic Criteria: (1) Diagnosis of schizophrenia based on the International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision (ICD-10), with a Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) score > 60 [ 25 ]; (2) meeting the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for insomnia disorder, characterized by difficulty in sleep initiation and maintenance, early awakening, and persistent sleep disturbances occurring no less than three times per week for a minimum of 3 months [ 9 ]. TCM Syndrome Diagnostic Criteria: To ensure diagnostic consistency and reduce interpractitioner variability, the TCM diagnosis of heart-spleen deficiency type insomnia was independently determined by two licensed TCM physicians with over 5 years of clinical experience, in strict accordance with the national standard Criteria of Diagnosis and Therapeutic Effect of Diseases and Syndromes in TCM (ZY/T001.1–94) issued by the State Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine [ 26 ]. Any diagnostic disagreements were resolved by a senior TCM expert. Diagnosis required Core sleep complaint: difficulty falling asleep, frequent awakening, or dream-disturbed sleep Constitutional pattern: Primary symptoms (≥2): disturbed sleep, palpitations, mental fatigue and physical lassitude, reduced appetite Secondary symptoms (≥2): poor memory, excessive dreaming, dull or sallow complexion, postprandial abdominal distension, loose stools Tongue: pale or with a yellow, greasy coating; pulse: thready and weak; course: >6 months Disagreements were resolved by a third senior TCM expert. Inclusion criteria (1) Aged 20–60 years; (2) PSQI score > 7 with recurrent sleep difficulties (≥2 times per week) lasting for at least 1 month; (3) clinically stable disease status with consistent antipsychotic dosage for ≥1 month and no medication adjustment within 2 months prior to enrollment; (4) complete clinical laboratory data; (5) voluntary participation and signed informed consent. Exclusion criteria (1) Incomplete baseline data; (2) severe physical illness interfering with trial evaluation; (3) pregnant, breast-feeding, or having plans to conceive. Withdraw criteria (1) Occurrence of serious adverse events during the intervention; (2) voluntary withdrawal by participants; (3) disease deterioration requiring urgent clinical intervention; (4) poor adherence to trial medication and intervention protocols. Randomization and blinding This study adopted a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial. An independent statistician generated a random sequence (1–120) using Excel, with 1–60 assigned to IM and 61–120 to SIM. Allocation concealment was achieved via sealed opaque envelopes. Participants and outcome assessors were fully blinded to group assignment. Given the operational characteristics of moxibustion intervention, therapists could not be blinded, but all operators followed unified standardized operating procedures and unified explanatory scripts to minimize performance bias. Intervention Participants in both the IM and SIM groups received standardized intervention sessions twice a week for 4 consecutive weeks, with 20 min per session and a total of 8 intervention sessions [ 27 ]. All interventions were performed by licensed professional acupuncturists with no less than 2 years of clinical experience, who received unified standardized operational training before the trial. Intervention device and materials Indirect moxibustion device: The CAJ-210 Indirect Moxibustion Instrument (Zhongshan Jiaxun Medical Device Co., Ltd.) was used for all sessions, equipped with independent programmable heating units to ensure precise and stable skin surface temperature control. IM patch (Product Code: 2022112501, Zhongshan Jiaxun Medical Device Co., Ltd.): Disposable sterile patch with a 70 × 70 mm heat-resistant non-adhesive base and a central refined mugwort pancake (diameter: 30 mm, thickness: 5 mm, weight: 1.8 ± 0.1 g) (Fig. 2 A). SIM patch (Product Code: 2023020301, Zhongshan Jiaxun Medical Device Co., Ltd.): Visually identical to the active patch, but filled with inert non-thermogenic placebo materials without active medicinal ingredients and thermal effects, ensuring consistent appearance while producing no therapeutic stimulation (Fig. 2 B). Standardized treatment procedure Unified standardized procedures were implemented for all sessions: Preparation: Participants maintained a comfortable supine position, and bilateral Neiguan (PC6), Sanyinjiao (SP6), and Shenmen (HT7) acupoints were located according to standard anatomical markers (Fig. 3 ). Patch application: The assigned IM or SIM patch was removed from its sterile packaging and placed directly onto the skin over the target acupoints. Device setup and heating: The corresponding heating head of the CAJ-210 device was positioned over the patch. For the IM group: The device was activated and set to maintain a skin interface temperature between 35 and 40 °C for the duration of the 20-min session. The device’s built-in precision thermostat and temperature sensor automatically regulated the heating output to ensure the target temperature was consistently delivered and monitored. For the SIM group: The device was set up identically, and the same timer was started. However, the heating function was not activated, ensuring the patch remained at ambient temperature. Monitoring and safety: Throughout the session, the practitioner monitored the device’s readout and periodically inquired about the patient’s comfort. The pre-set temperature range was designed to elicit a comfortable warming sensation without risk of burning. No adverse events related to heat were observed. Session completion: All patches were removed after 20 min, and local skin conditions were examined and recorded. Concomitant treatment and medication control All participants received fixed low-dose dexzopiclone (1 mg, Chengdu Kanghong Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd.) every night throughout the 8-week intervention period. All antipsychotic medications and concomitant clinical treatments were maintained at a stable dosage and regimen for at least 8 weeks before randomization and during the entire trial period to eliminate confounding factors. All concomitant treatments were accurately recorded at each follow-up visit. Outcome measures Primary outcome measure The primary outcome measure employed in this study is the PSQI, a self-administered questionnaire specifically designed to quantify sleep quality and disturbances.
