title: Efficacy of Personalizing Cognitive Remediation for Schizophrenia by Targeting Impairments in Early Auditory Processing
abstract: Abstract Background and Hypotheses Early auditory processing (EAP) deficits are common but not universal in schizophrenia, are linked to impairments in higher cognitive functions and when improved are associated with downstream cognitive improvements. Assessment of baseline EAP training need provides an opportunity for cognitive remediation (CR) programs to personalize treatment and optimize impact. This confirmatory efficacy study examined the differential benefit of EAP training for those with and without baseline EAP deficits. Hypotheses were: (1) Only EAP impaired (EAP–) patients would benefit more from CR that included EAP training, (2) cognitive gains made by EAP– patients during CR that included EAP training would mediate the relationship between gains in EAP and functional capacity. Study Design 184 outpatient adults diagnosed with schizophrenia were classified as having intact (n = 91) or impaired (n = 81) EAP and randomized to CR with restorative exercise plans that either included EAP training (n = 89) or did not (n = 83). Cognitive and functional outcomes were measured post-treatment and 3 months later. Study Results Across CR treatment conditions, cognitive gain effect size was moderate. Treatment condition did not significantly impact EAP, cognitive, or functional outcomes for either EAP group at final endpoint. EAP improved significantly but modestly for EAP– patients across conditions. Cognitive gains did not mediate the relationship between EAP gains and functional capacity. Conclusions These findings support the value of CR for people with schizophrenia, demonstrate that EAP deficits are malleable, and that cognitive and functional gains can occur for EAP impaired patients, regardless of whether EAP training is provided.

title: Lithium in the Prevention of Postpartum Recurrence of Mood Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Background:  Women with bipolar disorder are at increased risk for relapse/recurrence during the postpartum period. This risk decreases with prophylactic pharmacologic treatment, compared to those who remain medication-free. Lithium use in preventing relapse has been studied extensively in individuals with bipolar disorder, though its specific use in the postpartum has not received as much attention.  Objective:  The aim of this systematic review (CRD420261357096) was to estimate risk of postpartum relapse, specifically in women with bipolar disorder who received lithium prophylactically versus those who discontinued it during pregnancy.  Study Selection:  Following PRISMA guidelines, reviewers screened 45 studies focused on women with bipolar I or II disorders from searches of PubMed, PsycINFO, and Cochrane databases conducted on April 2, 2026, that were written in English.  Data Extraction:  Two independent observers extracted data using a data extraction form created on Covidence. Random-effects meta-analysis of recurrence proportions, between-study variance, heterogeneity, and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were conducted.  Results:  Eight studies (554 women) providing information on the prophylactic effect of lithium during the postpartum period, and 2 studies evaluating the impact of lithium discontinuation on postpartum relapse, were identified. The pooled recurrence proportion was 0.21 (95% CI 0.15-0.29) in lithium-treated patients and 0.41 (95% CI 0.33-0.50) in lithium-untreated patients. The most common timing of prophylaxis initiation was during pregnancy (51.9%). Studies examining the impact of lithium discontinuation provided indirect evidence of its effectiveness in preventing postpartum recurrence.  Conclusion:  Findings from our meta-analysis suggest that lithium is effective in preventing postpartum recurrence of mood disorders; however, caution is warranted when interpreting study results because of confounding by indication and limited literature.

title: Prefrontal Cortical Changes With Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement in Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract:
Key Points Question What are the neural mechanisms through which Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE) restructures hedonic processing in individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD), and how are these changes related to clinical outcomes? Findings In this neuroimaging randomized clinical trial, compared with psychoeducational supportive therapy (PST), MORE restructured drug-biased prefrontal activity during regulation of drug vs nondrug reward as further associated with lower drug craving. Compared with PST, MORE also reduced prefrontal synchronization during a naturalistic drug-related stimulus and extended abstinence duration at follow-up. Meaning These findings suggest that MORE modulates prefrontal systems involved in reward, salience, and cognitive control, supporting its potential as a mechanistically informed adjunct to pharmacotherapy for OUD.

Importance Despite decades of clinical implementation of medications for opioid use disorder (OUD), overdose mortality rates remain high, underscoring a critical need for interventions that target the brain mechanisms underlying addiction. Objective To assess the neural mechanisms of Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE) and their associations with clinical outcomes, including craving and abstinence duration. Design, Setting, and Participants This randomized clinical trial was conducted from November 2020 to September 2024 among individuals with OUD recruited from an inpatient rehabilitation facility in New York and randomized to MORE or psychoeducational supportive therapy (PST). Data were analyzed from October 2024 to August 2026. Interventions Treatment with MORE (comprising training in mindfulness, drug cue reappraisal, and savoring positive experiences) or PST (active control condition) across 8 weekly 2-hour group sessions. Main Outcomes and Measures Outcomes included treatment-related changes in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) blood oxygen level–dependent signal (primary), abstinence length (secondary), and cue-induced craving (secondary). Results Drug cue reactivity task analyses included 59 participants (MORE, n = 24; 5 women [20.8%]; mean [SD] age, 43.6 [11.3] years; PST, n = 35; 8 women [22.9%]; mean [SD] age, 42.8 [10.0] years). Movie-watching and follow-up analyses were conducted in subsets of 37 (MORE, n = 18; PST, n = 19) and 38 participants (MORE, n = 13; PST, n = 25), respectively. Compared with PST, MORE reduced drug-biased activity in the middle frontal gyrus and other brain areas, including the precuneus, during downregulation of responses to drug cues relative to upregulation of responses to natural reward cues (even when controlling for passive cue viewing; z > 3.1; P < .05). The shift from drug to natural reward responses in the lateral and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (PFC) was associated with lower cue-induced craving exclusively in the MORE group ( z > 3.1; P < .05). Relative to PST, MORE also reduced medial PFC synchronization to naturalistic drug-related movie scenes (q = 0.019) and significantly extended abstinence duration at follow-up (approximately 4 months posttreatment; χ 2 = 6.7; P = .04; Cohen w = 0.19). Conclusions and Relevance This neuroimaging randomized clinical trial demonstrates that MORE may restructure function in PFC nodes of the reward, salience, and control networks, positioning it as a biologically grounded adjunct to pharmacotherapy for OUD. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04112186

This neuroimaging randomized clinical trial assesses the neural mechanisms of Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement and their associations with clinical outcomes, including craving and abstinence duration.

title: Instrumental Support Calls vs. Caring Contacts Texts to Prevent Suicide in Adolescents and Adults: The SPARC Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The authors sought to determine whether augmenting usual suicide care with follow-up in the form of instrumental support calls (ISC) or two-way Caring Contacts texts (CC) works best to reduce suicidal ideation and behavior (SI/SB) in adolescents and adults.

METHODS: The Suicide Prevention Among Recipients of Care (SPARC) Trial is a pragmatic comparative effectiveness randomized clinical trial stratified by age, with participants randomized in a 1:1 ratio to ISC or CC. Participants were adolescents (12-17 years, N=723) and adults (18+ years, N=797) who screened at risk for suicide in emergency departments (N=9) and primary care clinics (N=36) between May 2021 and July 2022; primary data collection was completed in August 2023. Outcomes included Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale SI/SB score at 6 months (primary) and 12 months (secondary).

RESULTS: Adolescents (N=723; mean age, 14.9 years [SD=1.6]) were mostly female (75%), White (84.1%), and non-Hispanic (84.2%). Adults (N=797; mean age, 38.3 years [SD=15.9]) were mostly female (70%), White (89.1%), and non-Hispanic (90%). At 6 months, outcomes were similar by condition among adolescents, but among adults, SI/SB scores were significantly higher among those receiving CC compared to those receiving ISC (adjusted difference in means [ADM]=0.50, 95% CI=0.12, 0.88). At 12 months, adolescents' SI/SB scores were significantly lower in the CC compared with the ISC condition (ADM=-0.64, 95% CI=-1.11, -0.18), but outcomes were similar by condition among adults.

CONCLUSIONS: The best suicide prevention follow-up care may vary by age, with adolescents benefiting most from longer-term connection-focused two-way CC and adults benefiting most from more intensive early instrumental support through ISC.

title: Hippocampal subregion volume alterations at baseline and following antidepressant treatment in youth at high risk for bipolar disorder
abstract:
Abstract Understanding hippocampal neurostructural alterations at baseline and following antidepressant treatment in high-risk youth, particularly within distinct subregions, is critical for elucidating bipolar disorder (BD) pathophysiology and treatment planning. In this prospective randomized clinical trial, 105 high-risk youth with a first-degree BD-I relative(s) and moderate to severe depression and/or anxiety disorder, along with 51 healthy controls (HCs), were recruited. All participants underwent baseline structural MRI and clinical evaluations for depression, anxiety, and adverse events. High-risk youth were then randomized to receive psychotherapy and with either escitalopram or placebo. After 4 weeks of treatment, high-risk youth underwent repeated structural MRI and clinical assessments. These clinical assessments continued biweekly over the remaining 12 weeks of treatment (up to week 16). Volumetric measurements of hippocampal subregions were analyzed at baseline and 4 weeks. Compared to HCs, high-risk youth had significant baseline volume increases in the right cornu ammonis (CA)3, bilateral CA4, bilateral granule cell and molecular layers of the dentate gyrus (GC-ML-DG), and bilateral molecular layer, but reduced volumes in the bilateral fimbria and left parasubiculum. Volume reduction in the left hippocampal tail after 4 weeks of escitalopram treatment was associated with improvements in disinhibition and impulsivity symptoms from baseline to 4 weeks, and this association remained significant from baseline to 16 weeks. CA3-4 and GC-ML-DG enlargement may reflect adaptive changes, while fimbria and parasubiculum atrophy indicate vulnerabilities in BD-risk youth. Escitalopram-related volume reduction in the left hippocampal tail may reflect neural plasticity associated with emotional symptom improvement in BD high-risk youth. Clinical trial registration information Mechanism of Antidepressant-Related Dysfunctional Arousal in High-Risk Youth; https://clinicaltrials.gov/ ; NCT02553161 .

Introduction Antidepressants are commonly prescribed to manage mood and anxiety disorders in youth, in spite of offering moderate benefits and being associated with potentially consequential psychiatric adverse events, such as treatment-emergent mania [ 1 , 2 ]. The risk for such adverse events is particularly pronounced in youth with a family history of bipolar disorder (BD), where the intersection between antidepressant use and familial risk factors may exacerbate inherent vulnerabilities toward adverse outcomes within key neurobiological systems that regulate emotion [ 3 ]. The hippocampus, critical for the regulation of emotion, cognitive functions and response to stress [ 4 , 5 ], plays a key role in understanding the pathophysiology and treatment of mood disorders, and undergoes significant plasticity with antidepressant exposure [ 6 ]. However, the specific impact of antidepressants on hippocampal structure — both in terms of efficacy and adverse events—remains inadequately explored in youth at familial risk for BD. Hippocampal volumes in BD range from being reduced or not significantly different from healthy controls (HCs) [ 7 – 9 ]. Whole volume analyses may have missed unique functional variations in hippocampal subregions, which play distinct roles in the pathophysiology of BD [ 10 , 11 ]. With advances in the resolution and accuracy of automatic hippocampal segmentations, fine-grained volume reductions have been observed in widespread hippocampal subfields such as cornu ammonis (CA)1-4, the granule cell and molecular layers of the dentate gyrus (GC-ML-DG), molecular layer, hippocampal-amygdala transition area (HATA), subiculum, and hippocampal tail in patients with BD [ 12 – 14 ]. Such patterns have also been supported by post-mortem neuropathological investigations of individuals with BD [ 15 ]. BD is among the most familial psychiatric disorders with high heritability rates; however, specific biomarkers of familial risk for BD have yet to achieve biomarker validation. Examination of anatomical variations in the hippocampus and its subregions in youth at high-risk (HR) for BD could determine whether these subregions could serve as risk factors for BD, potentially advancing predictive capabilities and preventative strategies for BD [ 16 ]. Like studies described above in BD, prior HR studies focused on total hippocampal volumes have reported inconsistent results, possibly due to volumetric averaging of its subregions. For example, in one study, increased volume in left parahippocampal/hippocampal gyrus was observed in HR youth compared to HCs [ 17 ], while another study noted trends for larger hippocampus volumes in unaffected co-twins discordant for BD compared to low-risk twins [ 16 ]. In a third study, Nery et al. reported decreased gray matter volumes in the left hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus, and thicker right hippocampus in BD unaffected first-degree relatives compared to HCs [ 18 ]. However, Hajek et al. reported comparable hippocampal volumes among unaffected relatives, affected relatives for BD, and HCs [ 19 ]. These studies underscore the significant variability of hippocampal volume differences among those at risk for BD. More fine-grain examinations of hippocampal subregions in youth at risk for BD, and in the context of symptom manifestations and treatment, may uncover subtle predispositions for BD than reported in the extant literature. Given that antidepressant exposure may be a major confound in the evaluation of bipolar risk, directly examining the effects of antidepressants on the hippocampus and its subregions provide a unique opportunity to both advance understanding of risk for developing BD and the effect of antidepressant treatment on hippocampal plasticity. Indeed, it is well known that antidepressant treatment can alter the structure of the hippocampus across species, and in specific subregions [ 20 ]. Antidepressants can both lead to adverse events or promote neurogenesis and enhance synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus, as antidepressants increases the dendritic spine density of neurons in CA pyramidal cell subfields and stimulates neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus [ 21 – 23 ], suggesting high potential for structural remodeling. Indeed, antidepressant exposure can lead to significant alterations in hippocampal subregion volumes (such as dentate gyrus) in rodent models, modulating function in areas critical for stress response and emotional regulation [ 24 , 25 ]. These insights provide a foundation for understanding how antidepressants might similarly affect the hippocampal architecture in HR youth for BD given that it is not yet unknown whether antidepressant-related hippocampal plasticity in humans is adaptive (toward improved symptoms) or linked to a risk of psychiatric adverse events. Direct evidence linking these neurobiological mechanisms to treatment outcomes and psychiatric adverse events in this vulnerable group is now needed. Youth at risk for BD are uniquely suited to examine adaptive versus maladaptive effects of antidepressants, as they may be at high risk for treatment-emergent mania compared to the general population [ 2 ]. Given these considerations, we examined hippocampal subregion volume differences compared to typically developing youth in large cohort of HR youth for BD with no prior antidepressant exposure, and then investigated early hippocampal changes from baseline to 4 weeks in HR youth randomized to escitalopram or placebo to treat symptoms of depression and anxiety. Based on the extant literature, we hypothesized that: 1) HR youth will exhibit abnormal volumes of the hippocampus and its subregions (such as CA1-4, dentate gyrus, and subiculum) compared to HC youth at baseline [ 12 – 14 ]; 2) Antidepressants will result in volumetric increases in subregions (such as CA and dentate gyrus) in HR youth who show early (within 4 weeks) improvements in depression or anxiety symptoms, and volume reductions in the other hippocampal subregions, in HR youth who develop antidepressant-related adverse events from baseline to 4 weeks; 3) Volumetric changes will correlate with changes in treatment-related efficacy or adverse events within respective treatment-responsive and adverse event subgroups over a 16-week full course of treatment. By conducting a thorough examination of the hippocampus and its subregions in the context of a clinical trial that can examine early and sustained treatment effects, our study aims to ultimately advance understanding of the earliest neurobiological underpinnings of BD risk and shed light on how antidepressant-driven changes in hippocampal structure might influence clinical outcome acutely and after a course of standard treatment. Methods Participants Youth with a first-degree relative diagnosed with bipolar I disorder ( n = 119), and age- and sex-matched HCs ( n = 55) without mood or psychotic disorders in any first or second-degree relatives, were recruited from the University of Cincinnati and Stanford University. This study followed the protocol [ 3 ] as registered on ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT02553161 , URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02553161 ) on December 1, 2015. The structural MRI analyses presented in this manuscript are reported as secondary/exploratory outcomes of the trial. The inclusion criteria the HR youth were: (1) confirmed family history of BD based on the Family History-Research Diagnostic Criteria-Modified (FH-RDC) [ 26 ], the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM (SCID) [ 27 ], and/or the Kiddie Schedule of Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (KSADS) [ 28 ]; (2) notable current depressive and/or anxiety symptoms, assessed by the Childhood Depression Rating Scale-Revised (CDRS-R) over 35 [ 29 ] and/or the Pediatric Anxiety Rating Scale (PARS) above 15 [ 30 ], (3) aged 12–17 years; and (4) no history of antidepressants. Exclusion criteria for all participants included: (1) a history of bipolar I or II disorder, (2) patients with any DSM-5 psychiatric comorbid disorders, such as autism spectrum, obsessive-compulsive, post-traumatic stress, or Tourette’s disorders, (3) intellectual disability (full scale IQ < 70), (4) drug and/or alcohol abuse or dependence. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards at both the University of Cincinnati and Stanford University (IRB ID: 2021-0102, approval date: 3/24/2021), and both participants and their legal guardians provided written assent and informed consent, respectively. All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations, including the Declaration of Helsinki. Study design All participants received Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans and assessments for psychiatric symptoms and potential adverse events at baseline. Following initial evaluations, HR youth were then randomized to receive psychotherapy plus escitalopram or psychotherapy plus placebo (2:1). The study was double-blind; participants, treating clinicians, and outcome assessors were blinded to treatment allocation. Full details of the randomization and blinding procedures are described in the trial protocol ( NCT02553161 ).Treatment adherence was closely monitored through weekly clinical follow-ups during dose titration, followed by biweekly visits through week 16, pill counts at each visit (with adherence defined as taking ≥80% of prescribed doses), participant self-report, and legal guardian interviews, consistent with our prior studies demonstrating high adherence in this population [ 31 , 32 ]. After 4 weeks of treatment, HR youth underwent follow-up MRI scans and assessments for psychiatric symptom changes and monitoring for any evolving acute adverse events or evidence of early treatment response. Then, assessments for psychiatric symptoms and adverse events were collected biweekly in the remaining 16 weeks of treatment to assess for treatment effects after a full 16 week course of treatment. Psychiatric symptoms were assessed using the clinician-rated Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) [ 33 ], the clinician-rated CDRS-R, and the clinician-rated PARS. Adverse events were rated using the clinician-rated Pediatric Adverse Events Rating Scale (PAERS) [ 34 ] and clinician-rated Treatment-Emergent Activation and Suicidality Assessment Profile (TEASAP) [ 35 ]. Specifically, from the PAERS scale, 13 items (items 1, 2, 6–11, 14, 17, 28, 29, and 36) deemed to be related to treatment-emergent mania were selected, and their clinician-rated scores were aggregated to define our primary outcome, assessing antidepressant-related adverse events. Please see Table S1 for a detailed information on these items. As a secondary outcome, the TEASAP measured adverse event severity across five dimensions: irritability, akathisia and somatic anxiety, disinhibition and impulsivity, mania, and a combined dimension of self-injury, suicidality, and harm to others. MRI acquisition The MRI scans were conducted on 3-Tesla scanners equipped with 8-channel phased-array head coils at two centers: a Phillips scanner at the University of Cincinnati and a GE scanner at Stanford University. High-resolution T1 images were acquired with similar imaging parameters across both centers, as detailed in Table S2 . Images were visually inspected by an experienced pediatric neuroradiologist to identify scans with visible cerebral abnormalities, distortions or artifacts for exclusion. Neuroimaging data preprocessing and volumetric analysis of hippocampal subregions Structural image preprocessing was performed using the open-source FreeSurfer software (version 7.0). To reduce intra-subject variability, we applied FreeSurfer’s specialized longitudinal stream [ 36 ], which involves creating a common template using all scans of a subject, and reprocessing each scan with this shared template. The longitudinal segmentation pipeline for these regions utilized a probabilistic atlas based on high-resolution ex vivo MRI data ( ~ 0.1 mm isotropic), producing an automated joint segmentation of these substructures. This longitudinal segmentation stream, increased test-retest reliability and reduced measurement noise compared to independent segmentations, offering more consistent segmentations over time [ 37 ].Two hierarchical segmentation levels were produced: (a) a broader categorization into head, body, and tail; and (b) a detailed division into parasubiculum, presubiculum, subiculum, CA1, CA3, and CA4, GC-ML-DG, molecular layer, HATA, fimbria, tail, and fissure. Finally, we extracted volumes of bilateral hippocampi and their subregions. Figure S1 presents an example of the hippocampal segmentation in a healthy participant. All segmentations were thoroughly reviewed in all three orthogonal planes, slice by slice, to ensure accuracy. Using standard ENIGMA protocols [ 38 ], any segmentations that mistakenly included non-target tissue or missed portions of the hippocampus were excluded. To address varia

title: Cancer risk among individuals with mental illness - a systematic review and meta-analysis of nordic register-based prospective studies
abstract:
Although cancer patients have a high burden of mental illness, it is less clear whether patients with mental illness experience a higher-than-expected cancer risk. This systematic review investigated the associations between a wide range of types of mental illness and subsequent cancer risk. Five electronic databases were searched for articles published from database initiation to October 24, 2024. Studies using nationwide Nordic register data to conduct a prospective analysis of the association between mental illness diagnosis and cancer incidence were included. When data from three or more countries were available for a given type of mental illness, random effects meta-analyses were performed; otherwise, narrative syntheses were conducted. A total of 7,767 non-duplicate articles were screened, of which 20 were included. Meta-analyses showed no association between schizophrenia diagnosis and overall cancer risk; however, a high level of heterogeneity was detected between studies. Individuals with schizophrenia appeared to have a higher risk of breast cancer (pooled standardized incidence ratio [SIR]: 1.28, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.08-1.52), and lower risks of rectal cancer (pooled SIR: 0.75, 95% CI: 0.59-0.95) and prostate cancer (pooled SIR: 0.53, 95% CI: 0.48-0.59), compared to individuals in the general population. A higher risk of overall cancer was observed for mood, anxiety, and stress-related disorders, as well as autism and intellectual disability, in multiple studies; however, the results differed by cancer types and sex. In summary, these findings suggest an altered risk of cancer among individuals with mental illness living in Nordic countries. Further research is needed to enable the development of targeted cancer prevention strategies to reduce mental health disparities in cancer protection.

Introduction Cancer and mental illness constitute two major contributors to the global burden of disease. In 2020, there were 19.3 million new cancer cases and ten million cases of cancer-related death worldwide [ 1 ]. Despite advances in cancer diagnosis and treatment, and the resulting continual improvements in cancer survival, over the past decades, the health burden due to cancer is still substantial. The average years of life lost due to cancer were 15.2 in 2020 and the global economic cost for cancer is estimated at as high as $25.2 trillion from 2020 to 2050 [ 2 ]. Mental illness, including psychiatric disorders (e.g., schizophrenia, mood disorders, anxiety, and stress-related disorders) and neurodevelopmental conditions (e.g., autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder [ADHD], and intellectual disability), is also one of the most common causes of morbidity today. In 2019, approximately 970 million people worldwide were reported to experience mental illness, and the global number of disability-adjusted life-years due to mental illness increased from 80.8 million in 1990 to 125.3 million in 2019 [ 3 ]. In total, mental illness was estimated to cost the world economy approximately $2.5 trillion per year in poor health and reduced productivity in 2010, a cost estimated to increase to approximately $6 trillion per year by 2030 [ 4 ]. Given their high prevalence, comorbidity of cancer and mental illness is inevitable. It is well established that cancer patients have increased risks for mental illness. We and others have, for instance, demonstrated an increased risk of mental illness during the entire survivorship of cancer patients, especially immediately following cancer diagnosis [ 5 , 6 ]. Although it is difficult to discern the exact reasons for this risk increment, severe psychological distress experienced during cancer diagnosis and treatment, in addition to cancer biology itself and side effects of cancer treatment, might play a role. Importantly, we have also demonstrated that comorbid mental illness before or after cancer diagnosis increases the risk of overall and cancer-specific mortality [ 7 , 8 ], as well as other severe adverse outcomes (e.g., sepsis) after cancer diagnosis [ 9 ]. On the other hand, conflicting findings have been observed regarding the risk of cancer among individuals with mental illness [ 10 ]. Previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses have investigated cancer incidence among individuals with schizophrenia [ 11 , 12 ], depression or anxiety [ 13 ], and anorexia nervosa [ 14 ], demonstrating high levels of heterogeneity between studies. Study results also vary by cancer type, sex, and the type of mental illness. Namely, the risk of overall cancer was shown to be slightly increased among individuals with anxiety or depression, slightly decreased among individuals with schizophrenia, and unaltered among individuals with anorexia nervosa. As a comprehensive understanding of cancer risk among individuals with mental illness is essential for effective cancer prevention strategies, we aimed to conduct an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of cancer risk among individuals with a broader range of mental illness types, including both psychiatric and neurodevelopmental conditions. Methods Search strategy and selection criteria We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of the risk of cancer after the diagnosis of mental illness, according to a protocol registered on PROSPERO prior to formal initiation of the review (identifier: CRD42024593919). Due to the extensive quantity of literature published, using varying quality of data, we subsequently restricted our review to studies using nationwide Nordic register data, to ensure minimal risk of bias. As such, studies were eligible for inclusion if they used Nordic registers to define both the exposure and outcome variables, using diagnostic codes, for the entire national population. One or more of the following types of mental illness must have been included as the exposure variable(s): schizophrenia, mood disorders (including bipolar disorder and depression), anxiety (including obsessive-compulsive disorder [OCD]) and stress-related disorders, eating disorders, and neurodevelopmental conditions (including autism, ADHD, and intellectual disability). Studies were eligible for inclusion if they used the risk of ‘any cancer’ as a combined outcome, and/or studied one or more of the following most prevalent cancer types in Europe: breast, colorectal, lung, prostate, urinary bladder, uterine, kidney, or pancreatic cancer [ 15 ]. Additionally, studies must have conducted prospective analysis of the association between the exposure (diagnosis of mental illness) and the outcome (cancer incidence) (i.e., cohort/nested case-control studies), quantified using one of the following measures of association: odds ratio (OR), hazard ratio (HR), relative risk (RR), risk ratio (RR), incidence rate ratio (IRR), standardized incidence ratio (SIR), or standardized morbidity ratio (SMR). Studies were excluded if they focused on paediatric or elderly populations, or cancer outcomes (e.g., survival or treatment) other than incidence. Studies using other designs (i.e., cross-sectional studies, case studies, case series, randomized controlled trials [RCTs], or qualitative studies), systematic reviews, conference abstracts, and studies not published in English or subsequently translated to English were also excluded. We searched five electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Scopus) on October 24, 2024, to identify eligible studies published since database initiation. Search terms were selected after reviewing keywords in known eligible literature. The full search strategies used for each database are displayed in Supplementary Table 1 . Title and abstract screening and full text review were conducted by XX and GM, with 20% of articles independently screened by FS at each stage. Any disagreement was resolved by discussion with MMB and FF. Reference lists of all relevant systematic reviews, and all included studies, were searched for additional eligible studies. Study authors were contacted if articles contained missing data for the association measures. Data analysis Data were extracted by XX, FS and MMB, using a pre-piloted data extraction sheet, and all extracted data were checked for accuracy by FF. Key study characteristics including country of study, study population, definitions of exposure and outcome variables, age, and sex were extracted. Risk of bias was assessed by MMB and FF using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklist for cohort studies [ 16 ]. This tool contains 11 questions to assess the potential risk of bias in specific study domains, each of which can be answered with ‘yes’, ‘no’, ‘unclear’, or ‘not applicable’. As certain questions did not apply to all types of study design, we calculated a total score for each study according to the number of questions for which ‘yes’ had been selected, divided by the number of applicable questions for the respective study, which was then converted into a percentage score. Based on previous literature [ 17 ], studies were classified as being at low risk of bias if they scored 70% or above, at moderate risk of bias if they scored between 50-60%, and at high risk of bias if they scored under 50%. Random effects meta-analyses were conducted when studies from at least three countries were available for the relevant exposure (i.e., mental illness type). Where multiple studies from each country were performed using the same exposure and outcome, studies were selected for meta-analyses based on the measure of association used and the date of publication. For the main meta-analyses models we included only studies that used standardized incidence ratio (SIR), as this was the association measure used in at least one study from all included countries. We also conducted a sensitivity analyses, in which the most recent study from each country was included in each meta-analysis, regardless of the measure of association used. This allowed us to ascertain whether the observed associations persisted in the most recently conducted studies. However, bias introduced by combining different estimands with different reference groups may have reduced the validity of these pooled estimates. The maximally adjusted models in each study were included in the meta-analyses. Meta-analyses were performed using STATA version 18, and heterogeneity was measured using the I² statistic. Publication bias was assessed using the Egger’s test. For exposures not eligible for meta-analysis, a narrative synthesis was conducted. Role of the funding source The funder of the study had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, or writing of the report. Results From the database searches, 7769 non-duplicate articles were identified, of which 190 full texts were reviewed for eligibility, and 20 were included in the systematic review (Fig. 1 ). Study characteristics The key characteristics of the 20 included studies are displayed in Table 1 . A total of ten studies [ 18 – 27 ] (50%) were from Sweden, eight studies [ 28 – 35 ] (40%) were from Denmark, one study [ 36 ] was from Finland, and one was a multinational Nordic study [ 37 ] using data from Sweden, Denmark, and Finland. The majority of included studies (N = 19, 95%) were cohort studies, while one was a nested case-control study. Of the 19 included cohort studies, nine compared cancer incidence in exposed vs unexposed participants, using hazard ratios (HR), relative risk (RR), incidence rate ratios (IRR) or odds ratios (OR). The ten remaining cohort studies compared cancer incidence between exposed participants and the total national population of interest, using standardized incidence ratios (SIR) or incidence rate ratios (IRR). The nested case-control study compared odds of mental illness between cases of breast cancer and controls, using OR. Age-based eligibility criteria were used in 18 (90%) of the included studies. Average follow-up time was reported in 14 studies (70%), with a mean/median ranging from 7.1 years to 16.5 years. The proportion of female participants was reported in all studies, ranging from 32% to 100%. Of the 20 included studies, 19 were classified as being at low risk of bias, and one at moderate risk of bias, according to the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies (Supplementary Table 2 ). However, seven (35%) of the included studies did not clearly describe whether participants were free of the outcome at study start. For the identification of mental illness, 11 studies (55%) used data from both inpatient and outpatient care records, eight studies (40%) used inpatient care records only, and one study used data from inpatient care and disability pension records (Supplementary Table 3 ). The model results from each study, including the covariates adjusted for, are displayed in Supplementary Tables 4 and 5 , and differed greatly between studies. Schizophrenia In total, nine studies from Denmark, Sweden, and Finland investigated the association between diagnoses of schizophrenia and subsequent cancer risk [ 18 , 20 , 24 , 26 , 29 , 30 , 33 , 34 , 36 ]. Meta-analyses of the most recent study from each country utilizing SIR showed no consistent association between countries, as the levels of heterogeneity between studies were high (I 2 : 97.4%, p < 0.001) (Fig. 2 ). Individuals with a diagnosis of schizophrenia appeared to have a higher risk of breast cancer (pooled SIR: 1.28, 95% CI: 1.10-1.50), and a lower risk of both rectal cancer (pooled SIR: 0.79, 95% CI: 0.69-0.90) and prostate cancer (pooled SIR: 0.53, 95% CI: 0.48-0.59). However, the levels of heterogeneity remained high (e.g., I²: 82% for breast cancer). Similar associations were observed in the sensitivity analyses, in which the most recent study from each country was included in each meta-analysis, regardless of the measures of association used, i.e., combining HR, SIR, IRR, and OR to calculate the pooled estimates (Supplementary Figure 1 ). Sex-stratified meta-analyses showed a difference in the association between diagnoses of schizophrenia and risk of any cancer in men, compared to women; however, none of the results from the sex-stratified meta-analyses were statistically significant, and levels of heterogeneity between studies were high (Fig. 3 ). No evidence was found for publication bias in the meta-analyses (Supplementary Table 6 ). Mood disorders Of the included studies, four studies conducted in Denmark and Sweden investigated the associations between diagnoses of mood disorders and subsequent cancer risk. One study [ 33 ] showed a slightly higher risk of any cancer among individuals with a diagnosis of any mood disorder (HR: 1.03, 95% CI: 1.02-1.05), while another study [ 19 ] observed no association between bipolar disorder and the risk of any cancer in either males or females. title: Expert guidance to inform coordinated suicide postvention responses: A Delphi study
abstract:
Background The impact of suicide is profound for affected individuals, families and communities. Suicide postvention responses, inclusive of bereavement support, have been recognised as having made a valuable contribution to suicide prevention efforts. Postvention Protocol Response Groups (PPRGs) have emerged as a central mechanism to facilitate a coordinated service system response following a suspected suicide, mobilising a range of local services to provide early intervention support to bereaved communities across a defined geographical area. There is an important role to be played by these key agencies, support services, and community groups in responding to these impacts. However, little is known about the effective implementation of PPRGs. Methods We used the Delphi method to obtain expert consensus regarding best practice implementation of PPRGs. The two-round online Delphi survey involved a panel of 30 Australian experts (comprising past or present PPRG members, postvention experts, and response beneficiaries) who rated statements in terms of their importance for PPRG implementation. Results The 126 statements endorsed by 80% or more of panel members as “essential” or “important” regarding PPRG implementation covered key aspects of stakeholder engagement, governance, practice principles, operational aspects, data surveillance, preventative capacity, sustainability, and special considerations in rural areas. Expert recommendations will serve as the foundation for the development of a PPRG implementation guide. Conclusions This study provides valuable expert guidance and practice-based evidence to inform the establishment of PPRGs in areas of need, enhance the effectiveness and sustainability of existing PPRGs, and strengthen the implementation of localised postvention responses. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-28686-2 .

Background Suicide is a major public health problem with wide ranging human and societal impacts. Globally, more than 720,000 lives are lost to suicide every year, at a rate of approximately 9 suicides per 100,000 population [ 1 ], whereas Australia counted 3,264 suicides in 2023, representing a rate of almost 12 suicides per 100,000 population [ 2 ]. Each death by suicide has wide reaching impacts for affected individuals, families and social networks, workplaces and communities. Each suicide death has been estimated to affect between 6 family members and 135 community members [ 3 , 4 ], with potential to cause significant distress among those affected. This varies in intensity and duration related to their social, psychological, and geographical proximity to the deceased. People impacted by a suicide may themselves have an elevated risk of developing mental health concerns, as well as future suicidal distress [ 5 ]. People bereaved by suicide have approximately a three-fold risk of dying by suicide compared to those non-bereaved [ 6 ]. Mainstream and social media attention following a suicide can raise the risk of further contagion of suicidal behaviour [ 7 ] through mechanisms such as social influence, affiliation, imitation, or exposure to suicide related information. This, in turn, can drive the emergence of suicide clusters, involving a greater than expected number of suicides in a specific location or linked suicides that are spread across a geographic area over a short period [ 8 ]. Suicide clusters have been estimated to account for 5.6% of youth and 2.3% of adult suicides in Australia [ 9 ] and their impact can be overwhelming for local communities, stakeholders and services [ 10 ]. Taken together, these wide-ranging suicide impacts highlight the importance of a well-coordinated postvention response to identify and provide support to those bereaved, reduce community distress, avoid duplication of response efforts, and prevent further suicide [ 8 , 11 ]. Suicide postvention has been recognised as an important component of national suicide prevention strategies [ 12 ]. However, little is known about the effective implementation of coordinated community responses [ 13 ], underscoring the need for evidence-based guidance to address varied support needs across settings. While postvention guidelines have been developed for specific settings such as schools and universities [ 14 ], there is little guidance to coordinate effective multi-sectoral and multi-agency postvention responses across an entire geographical area. Postvention as an intervention has historically been about the provision of therapeutic and psychosocial bereavement support to individuals and families impacted by a suicide. Bereavement support is acknowledged as being preventative, with the understanding that individuals bereaved by suicide are themselves at disproportionate risk [ 11 ]. The original approach to suicide postvention was based on a crisis intervention model and mainly delivered post-hoc by individuals/organisations in response to concerns about the risk of contagion and clusters. More recently, however, Postvention Protocol Response Groups (or PPRGs as they are known in Victoria), have increasingly been developed across Australia. PPRGs facilitate a coordinated service system response following a suspected suicide, mobilising local services to provide early intervention support to bereaved communities, within an agreed framework that authorises and guides collective actions. PPRGs shifted away from the crisis intervention model to a public health approach, which integrates seamlessly with contemporary suicide prevention strategies. The earliest iteration of a PPRG was established in 2012 in response to a Victorian youth suicide cluster [ 15 ]. A subsequent coronial inquiry highlighted the critical role that local organisations play in both the identification of and response to suicide, commending the coordinated ensuing response, and recommending the development of a suicide prevention and postvention response framework [ 16 ]. These early service system responses have formed the foundation of PPRGs which have matured to be key enablers of a broader and more comprehensive postvention response to people impacted by suicide. While the height of PPRG activity was originally located in Victoria during the first decade, increasing national policy and funding momentum over recent years resulted in the establishment of PPRGs in other Australian states and territories. With several PPRGs now at varying stages of operation and a growing interest in PPRGs nationally, it is essential that key insights from their establishment and implementation be harnessed, and a solid evidence base be developed to enable and guide their future implementation. To this end, we conducted a Delphi expert consensus study with the aim of developing the evidence base for best practice establishment and implementation of PPRGs and to inform the development of an implementation guide. Methods We used the Delphi method as it applies to mental health research [ 17 ], involving survey construction, expert panel selection, and survey administration over two rounds. Ethics approval for the study was granted by the Human Research Ethics Committee from The University of Melbourne (#2024-31419-60748-2). All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation. Survey construction The Delphi survey developed for this study included survey statements that were informed through a review of the scientific and grey literature on the topic. Given the relative recency of postvention protocol response groups, literature was sourced by LR, MB, and AA, using a purposive approach, drawing on the authors’ professional networks and experience in establishing PPRGs. Literature included six peer-reviewed studies [ 18 – 23 ], four existing Australian postvention protocols [ 24 – 27 ], three protocol pilot evaluations [ 15 , 28 , 29 ] and a postvention discussion paper [ 30 ]. Summaries of feedback from a workshop with suicide postvention protocol and bereavement experts held at the 2024 National Suicide Prevention Conference in Adelaide, Australia, were also used to inform survey items [ 31 ]. The first author (LR) established a high-level structure for the Delphi survey based on a review of the literature, which included sections relating to key aspects of protocol establishment, stakeholder engagement, governance, practice principles, operational aspects, data surveillance, preventative capacity, sustainability, and special considerations in rural areas. The second author (TF) reviewed the literature and workshop summaries and extracted statements that aligned with those sections and could inform best practice implementation of PPRGs. For example, the statement “Key elements needed in a postvention response activation include: Provision of emotional first aid for affected first responders” was extracted from peer-reviewed literature [ 20 ]; the statement “Factors used to identify if postvention response activation is appropriate include: The deceased was aged 10–25 years” was extracted from an existing postvention protocol [ 27 ]; and the statement “Sustainability of regional postvention protocol response groups is enhanced by: Longer term funding models” was extracted from a postvention protocol pilot evaluation [ 28 ]. Two researchers (LR & KA) reviewed all statements to ensure applicability to the topic and that each captured a distinct idea. A revised version of the survey was reviewed by AA, MB, MS, SB, LF, RH and MW, all of whom have substantive experience in establishing PPRGs. Following final revision, 129 statements were organised into four superordinate sections: (1) Establishing PPRGs (with subsections Understanding needs and context, Stakeholder engagement, Governance); (2) PPRGs in Action (with subsections Practice principles, Operational aspects, External communication, Data surveillance); (3) Preventative capacity and sustainability; and (4) Contextual considerations in rural areas. The final Delphi survey is provided in supplementary material. Expert panel selection An expert panel was formed comprising (1) PPRG members (past or present), (2) postvention experts with substantive experience in postvention protocol or bereavement responses, and (3) people with experience of suicide postvention services coordinated by PPRGs, either as service providers (e.g., first responders, health practitioners), community leaders, or people impacted by a loss to suicide more than six months ago (e.g., family, friends, colleagues, community members). The six months exclusion criterion, which has been used successfully before, was applied to avoid recruiting participants who may still be in crisis due to the bereavement [ 32 ]. Due to the particular nature of the expertise required for the study (i.e., PPRG involvement), we used purposive recruitment, with AA, MB, MS, SB, LF, RH and MW inviting members in their extensive professional networks to participate in the study via email, followed by up to two email reminders. Survey administration Online data collection occurred in March and April 2025 (Round 1 survey) and May and June 2025 (Round 2 survey) via Qualtrics (Provo, UT). Panellists were offered a $AUD25 gift voucher for their participation in each survey round. The Round 1 survey comprised (1) demographic questions including gender, location, nature of expertise, and whether the panellist identified as a person with a lived experience of suicide or suicide bereavement; (2) 129 statements to be rated in importance as key recommendations for the implementation of PPRGs; and (3) opportunity to provide feedback about existing statements or offer suggestions for additional statements. Panellists were required to rate each statement on a 5-point Likert scale as “essential”, “important”, “don’t know/ depends”, “unimportant” or “should not be included”. All panellists who completed Round 1 were invited to participate in Round 2. Preceding the Round 2 survey invitation, panellists were provided with anonymous feedback outlining how their Round 1 responses compared with the rest of the panel. Data analysis Data were analysed using Microsoft Excel, including descriptive statistics for demographic characteristics and calculation of endorsement for statements. Based on consensus thresholds used successfully in prior Delphi studies [ 33 ] and aligned with Delphi guidance [ 34 ], statements rated as “important” or “essential” by 80% or more of panellists were indicative of endorsement by the panel for inclusion in key recommendations for PPRG implementation. Statements rated by less than 70% of panellists as “important” or “essential” were excluded. Statements rated by 70-79.9% of panellists as “important” or “essential” were included in Round 2 for re-rating (or excluded after Round 2). Results Panel characteristics Table 1 outlines the demographic characteristics of panel members. The Delphi panel comprised 30 members, who were predominantly female (73%), based in Victoria (70%) and to a lesser extent in other jurisdictions, including past or present PPRG members (60%), Postvention experts (33%), and PPRG beneficiaries (7%). The majority identified as having a lived experience of suicide or suicide bereavement (76%). Twenty-one panel members (70% of Round 1 participants) completed the Round 2 survey. Key demographics of panel members in Round 1 and Round 2 were comparable and showed no substantive differences. Statements endorsed as recommendations A flowchart of the Delphi study process and extraction of recommendations from each round is presented in Fig. 1 . Round 2 comprised 16 statements, including four new items suggested by panel members as well as 12 existing items to be re-rated from Round 1. Following exclusion of 7 items (5 items in Round 1 and 2 items in Round 2; Supplementary Table S1), a total of 126 statements were endorsed (Table 2 ). All excluded items were from the PPRGs in Action section and addressed operational aspects of response activation/deactivation or data surveillance. Whereas all newly introduced items provided further clarification regarding key aspects of PPRG establishment in terms of stakeholder engagement and governance. Overall statement endorsement ratings were high across all survey sections, ranging between 40% and 100% in Round 1 and 76%-100% in Round 2. Thirteen Round 1 statements and one Round 2 statement received the maximum 100% endorsement rating. Discussion The occurrence of a death by suicide can have wide-ranging ramifications, impacting people of varying social, psychological, and geographical proximity to the deceased across multiple settings [ 35 ]. Timely and well-coordinated postvention responses are therefore essential to provide bereavement support to affected individuals and communities, and ameliorate the risk of further adverse health outcomes, including suicide contagion and future suicidal behaviour [

title: Tryptophan metabolism within the gut-brain axis in depression: mechanisms, association with heterogeneity, and therapeutic opportunities
abstract: Depression is a highly heterogeneous psychiatric disorder, characterized by substantial variability in clinical manifestations, treatment responses, and disease progression, thereby posing significant challenges to precision diagnosis and therapeutic intervention. Accumulating evidence indicates that dysregulated tryptophan metabolism, mediated through dynamic crosstalk with the gut microbiota and the gut-brain axis (GBA), plays a pivotal role in both the pathophysiology and biological heterogeneity of depression. In this review, we delineate the contributions of the three principal tryptophan metabolic pathways-the kynurenine, serotonin, and microbial indole pathways-in modulating neuroimmune signaling, neurotransmitter function, and gut-brain communication. Moreover, we synthesize current evidence demonstrating that microbiota-dependent tryptophan metabolism exhibits distinct profiles across clinical, demographic, immunometabolic, trauma-related, and genetically defined depressive phenotypes, thereby establishing its role as a unifying biological framework underlying depressive heterogeneity. We further provide a critical appraisal of emerging therapeutic strategies targeting microbiota-associated tryptophan metabolism, including pharmacological, nutritional, microbial, and traditional Chinese medicine-based interventions. Future investigations should integrate multi-omics approaches, longitudinal study designs, and mechanistic validation with artificial intelligence to elucidate causal relationships between microbiota-associated tryptophan metabolism and depressive heterogeneity, ultimately facilitating biomarker discovery and the development of precision therapeutics.

title: Evolutionary neuropharmacology of serotonergic psychedelics: a cross-species perspective on mechanisms, consciousness, and therapeutic potential
abstract: Serotonergic psychedelics have revitalized psychiatric research by producing rapid and potentially sustained clinical benefits in selected neuropsychiatric conditions. However, the mechanisms linking receptor activation to neural plasticity, altered conscious experience, and clinical improvement remain incompletely understood, while the evolutionary origins of psychedelic signaling and the translational value of animal models continue to be actively debated. In this review, we integrate evolutionary biology, molecular pharmacology, comparative neuroscience, and computational psychiatry into a unified framework for understanding psychedelic action across biological scales. Building upon predictive processing and the Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS) framework, we discuss how serotonergic psychedelics transiently reshape hierarchical inference, providing computational principles that can be experimentally investigated across species despite profound differences in neural architecture and subjective experience. Comparative analyses from invertebrates to non-human primates further suggest that conserved receptor pharmacology coexists with species-specific circuit organization, highlighting that animal models should be interpreted as complementary platforms for investigating molecular, cellular, and computational mechanisms rather than direct proxies for human hallucinatory experiences. We further discuss preclinical and emerging translational evidence suggesting that biased receptor signaling and non-hallucinogenic psychoplastogens may partially dissociate plasticity-related therapeutic actions from hallucinogenic effects, providing new opportunities for mechanism-based drug development. By integrating evolutionary biology with molecular psychiatry, this review provides a mechanistic framework linking receptor pharmacology, neural plasticity, circuit computation, and therapeutic outcomes, thereby offering new conceptual and experimental strategies for developing next-generation psychedelic therapeutics.

title: Real-world associations of antipsychotic use with clinical outcomes in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: To systematically synthesize evidence on the association between antipsychotic medication use and diverse outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia, we searched PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, and Web of Science from inception to May 1, 2026. Eligible studies were observational studies reporting associations between antipsychotic use and clinical outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed study quality. Data was synthesized using multilevel random-effects models. Outcomes were categorized into mortality (including all-cause and cause-specific), somatic disorders, and other clinical outcomes. Sixty-eight studies comprising 1,424,455 individuals were included. Among individuals with schizophrenia, antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (pooled estimate, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.54-0.77) and lower relapse risk (pooled estimate, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.12-0.99) compared with nonuse. In contrast, compared with nonuse, antipsychotic use was associated with higher risks of cancer (1.41; 95% CI, 1.17-1.69), fractures (1.35; 95% CI, 1.17-1.56), and lung infections (1.25; 95% CI, 1.04-1.51), whereas evidence for other outcomes was non-significant. Overall, the evidence base was limited, with several pooled estimates derived from a small number of studies. Subgroup analyses suggested variation by region and study design. Antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality and relapse risk, alongside increased risks for some adverse outcomes such as fractures and lung infections. These findings should be interpreted cautiously, as residual confounding and bias may influence the observed associations and preclude causal interpretation. Further studies using rigorous designs are needed to clarify outcome-specific associations.

title: Sex- and frequency-dependent acute pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic effects of smoked cannabis: a randomized controlled trial
abstract: Cannabis use is rising among women. Studies suggest females are more sensitive to the intoxicating and misuse-related effects of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). While preclinical studies point to sex-specific development of tolerance, this has not been translated to humans. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, 44 participants (22 F) smoked three cannabis strengths (0% [~0 mg] THC, 4% [~20 mg] THC, 10% [~60 mg] THC), provided blood for plasma analysis, and completed subjective mood and drug effects assessments and a self-administration task. Outcomes were analyzed by cannabis strength, sex, and use frequency ( > 4 vs. ≤4 days/week; balanced across sex). Relative to placebo, active cannabis strengths increased subjective effects and plasma THC and metabolites (ps < 0.05). Exploratory follow-up of interactions (cannabis strength*frequency p < 0.10) showed the frequent-use group exhibiting significant increases from placebo in misuse-related ratings ("Like", "Take again") and self-administering more cannabis than the occasional-use group (ps < 0.05), and this was not modified by sex. Ratings of "High", Sedation/impairment, Dysphoric arousal, and "Bad effect" were higher at active strengths for occasional-use males relative to sex- and/or frequency-matched counterparts (ps < 0.05; via exploratory follow-up for "High" and Sedation/impairment). THC and metabolites tended to be highest in frequent-use males. These findings contrast with previous evidence of greater cannabis sensitivity among females and point toward future investigation into sex-dependent exposure thresholds for tolerance development/escalation. Sex and frequency of use are both implicated in cannabis use disorder risk, and consideration of their interaction is critical in characterizing the acute effects of, and tolerance to, cannabis.

title: Adjunctive Atypical Antipsychotics in Major Depressive Disorder: A Network Meta-Analysis Perspective and Consensus Panel Discussion
abstract: Objective:  The goal of this consensus panel was to generate expert perspectives on the comparative efficacy, safety, tolerability, and clinical relevance of FDA-approved adjunctive atypical antipsychotics for adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) and inadequate response to antidepressant therapy.  Participants:  Five academic and clinical experts in psychiatry and psychopharmacology participated as panelists: Roger S. McIntyre, Andrew J. Cutler, Christoph U. Correll, Joseph F. Goldberg, and Stephen M. Stahl. The discussion was conducted as a closed expert panel.  Evidence:  The panel primarily discussed research findings from two recent network meta-analyses (NMAs) evaluating approved adjunctive atypical antipsychotics in MDD, supplemented by relevant published literature and panel expertise. The NMAs differed in study inclusion, treatment-node definitions, and analytical approaches to examine efficacy, acceptability, and safety. Panel discussion was used to contextualize the findings and address their clinical applicability and limitations.  Consensus Process:  The panel reviewed and discussed the NMA methodology, comparative efficacy and safety outcomes, effect modifiers, and implications for shared decision-making. The consensus manuscript was developed from the panel discussion and evidence review, with subsequent expert review and incorporation of relevant comments and revisions.  Conclusions:  The panel concluded that the two NMAs provide complementary and broadly concordant comparative evidence that can inform clinical decision-making. Treatment selection should integrate efficacy with tolerability, patient characteristics, preferences, and practical considerations. The panel emphasized earlier consideration of effective, FDA-approved adjunctive treatment when appropriate, while recognizing remaining relevant gaps in long-term, head-to-head, and phenotype-specific evidence. The panel did not endorse any particular agent.

title: Genotype and phenotype analyses of 689 individuals with PCDH19-clustering epilepsy
abstract: PCDH19-clustering epilepsy (PCDH19-CE) is an infantile-onset neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by clusters of seizures, typically triggered by fever. PCDH19-CE follows an unusual X-linked inheritance pattern whereby heterozygous females, and males with X-chromosome disomy or pathogenic postzygotic mosaic PCDH19 variants, are affected, while hemizygous males are spared. We aggregate published PCDH19 variants and their corresponding PCDH19-CE phenotypes to analyse phenotype-genotype correlations. Data extracted from 110 publications identified 689/735 (94%) individuals with PCDH19 variants and the typical PCDH19-CE phenotype. Three hundred seventy-three unique PCDH19 variants were identified; 195 were not recorded in ClinVar. Seizure onset prior to 12 months of age was associated with more severe intellectual disability (p < 0.001) and the presence of psychiatric morbidity (p = 0.001). There were no phenotypic differences between missense, nonsense, and frameshift variants or between individuals of different geographical backgrounds, which was assessed as a proxy for ancestry. Twenty-nine hemizygous males with constitutive PCDH19 variants did not exhibit the typical PCDH19-CE phenotype, suggesting that the identification of variants in these individuals likely results from chance or ascertainment bias. The correlation between earlier seizure onset and poorer neurodevelopmental outcomes emphasises a critical window for therapeutic intervention. The lack of phenotypic difference between variant types demonstrates that loss of PCDH19 function underpins PCDH19-CE. Moreover, the identification of PCDH19 cytoplasmic domain variants in 78 affected individuals challenges the traditional view that PCDH19-CE is caused primarily by defects in cell-cell adhesion, as variants in this domain are expected to disrupt the nuclear function(s) of PCDH19.

title: Mitochondrial complex IV disruption is a detrimental pathology conferring ssusceptibility to alzheimer's disease
abstract: Mitochondrial complex IV (CIV) is an integral part of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) and plays a pivotal role in maintaining mitochondrial function. In contrast to the long-standing recognition of its dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD), the exact role of CIV deficit in the pathogenesis of this neurodegenerative disorder remains poorly defined. In this study, by incorporating clinical resources, mouse- and human-based models of AD risk, and a genetic approach to bypass defective CIV via the ectopic expression of alternative oxidase (AOX), we examined whether CIV deficits are a pathogenic driver of or a beneficial adaptation to AD-associated pathologies. Our results showed a clinicopathological association between neuronal CIV dysfunction and pathological characteristics of AD. Further experiments linked defective CIV to the development of mitochondrial dysfunction and synaptic loss in the tested mouse- and human-based models of AD risk. In addition, a reciprocal relationship between CIV dysfunction and amyloid pathology was determined. Lastly, a proteome-wide association study (PWAS) using genetic data from large-scale AD cohorts identified that downregulation of COX11, a crucial CIV assembly factor, confers susceptibility to AD risk. Collectively, our findings suggest that CIV dysfunction is a detrimental pathology contributing to AD-associated mitochondrial and neuronal damage. The dual role of CIV dysfunction, both as a consequence of and a contributor to amyloid toxicity in AD pathogenesis, further justifies the therapeutic potential of strategies targeting CIV deficits to diversify the tools for prevention and treatment of this neurodegenerative disorder.

title: Trends in Autism Spectrum Disorder Cumulative Incidence and Incidence Density: A Systematic Review
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Claims of an "autism epidemic" imply a true increase in ASD occurrence and changing underlying risk yet largely rely on rising prevalence estimates rather than incidence. Both measures are influenced by diagnostic practices, service access, documentation, and ascertainment; prevalence is additionally affected by service-related migration. Incidence studies follow a defined population previously not identified, to examine outcomes over a specified period and study area; incidence is more likely to capture temporal changes in underlying risk. We systematically reviewed autism incidence studies across differing methodological designs.

METHODS: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we identified population-based studies reporting ASD or Autistic Disorder incidence in individuals under 18 years. Studies were classified as Category A (birth-defined cohorts with definable risk periods) or Category B (dynamic population annual incidence density). Due to heterogeneity, incidence estimates were compared narratively.

RESULTS: Twenty-seven studies met inclusion criteria (14 Category A; 13 Category B). While ASD incidence increased, patterns varied by incidence framework, diagnostic definition, risk period, and ascertainment comprehensiveness (population coverage and detection of undiagnosed cases). High-comprehensiveness birth cohort studies tended to show inconsistent patterns and lower male-to-female ratios, whereas studies with moderate or low comprehensiveness often showed consistent increases. Increases were stronger for broader ASD category.

CONCLUSIONS: ASD incidence increased in dynamic, administratively defined study populations with moderate or low ascertainment comprehensiveness. In contrast, birth-defined cohorts with fixed risk periods and high ascertainment comprehensiveness showed inconsistent patterns. Overall, the available data do not provide compelling evidence of a true increase in ASD occurrence-an "autism epidemic."

title: Exposure to antidepressant and antipsychotic medicines in pregnant women and risk of gestational diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Antidepressants and antipsychotics are commonly prescribed for psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, and severe anxiety disorders. Psychotropic medications are increasingly prescribed during pregnancy to manage severe mental illnesses. Concerns have been raised about their metabolic side effects, including the risk of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). This study aimed to systematically review and meta-analyze existing evidence on the risk of GDM development in pregnant women with prenatal exposure to two common psychotropics, antipsychotics and antidepressants.

METHODS: We conducted a systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and the Web of Science, up to June 2025, identifying observational studies reporting GDM outcomes following the use of psychotropic medicines during pregnancy. Eligible studies were reviewed, and pooled relative risks (RRs) were calculated using a random-effects model, with subgroup analyses based on medication classification.

RESULTS: Twenty-one studies were included in this review and meta-analysis. The pooled adjusted RR for GDM among women exposed to any antipsychotics and antidepressants during pregnancy was 1.43 (95% CI: 1.17,1.69), and 1.19 (95% CI: 1.10,1.27). Second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) were associated with a significantly higher risk of GDM (RR = 1.6, 95% CI: 1.23, 1.97). First-generation antipsychotics showed no statistically significant association.

CONCLUSIONS: Prenatal exposure to antipsychotics, particularly SGAs, and antidepressants is associated with an increased risk of GDM. Clinicians should consider these risks when prescribing psychotropic medications during pregnancy and ensure appropriate metabolic monitoring.

title: Associations between ADHD behavior and attachment (in)security in middle childhood: A longitudinal study
abstract: Research has consistently suggested an association between ADHD behavior and insecure attachment, yet longitudinal data in middle childhood are largely absent. In particular, the directionality of this association and the role of oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) behavior remain unclear. This longitudinal study therefore examined these links across three annual waves in a Western-European community sample. Data were available for 614 children at Wave 1 (Mage = 10.28, SD = 0.58, range 9-12; 44% boys, 54% girls), 470 at Wave 2 (Mage = 10.28, SD = 0.61, range 10-13; 44% boys, 54% girls), and 385 at Wave 3 (Mage = 12.01, SD = 0.58, range 10-14; 45% boys, 54% girls). ADHD and ODD behavior were rated by mothers using the Child Behavior Checklist; children's attachment was assessed through both explicit (questionnaires) and implicit (secure base script knowledge) measures. Random Intercept Cross‑Lagged Panel Models revealed stable small to moderate between‑child associations between ADHD behavior and attachment (in)security ( β  = -0.550 to 0.367), which largely remained significant after controlling for ODD behavior ( β  = -0.517 to 0.295). Cross‑lagged effects, reflecting prospective within-child processes, were mostly non‑significant, providing little evidence for bidirectional associations in middle childhood.

title: Adolescents' in vivo emotional responses to digital and in-person peer experiences: Differences by context and links to daily life depressive symptoms
abstract: The rise of digital media has raised questions about potential links to adolescent depression, especially among girls. This study investigated whether affective responses to daily peer interactions, and depressive symptoms, varied by context - digital media or in-person. A sample of 110 adolescents assigned female at birth, aged 12-17 ( M  = 15.30,  SD  = 1.51; 83.6% White and 96.7% non-Hispanic) and enriched for risk for depression and suicidality, participated in 30 days of ecological momentary assessments over 3 months. Participants reported their most recent "worst" and "best" peer interactions, the context of these interactions (digital media or in-person), their affective responses to these interactions, and depressive symptoms. Multilevel models revealed that greater negative affect during negative interactions was associated with higher depressive symptoms, regardless of context ( B  = 0.02,  p  < .001). In contrast, positive in-person interactions were associated with higher positive affect than digital interactions ( B  = -2.01,  p  = .02), which, in turn, was associated with lower depressive symptoms ( B  = 0.08,  p  = .01). Findings highlight the protective role of positive in-person experiences in adolescent emotional well-being, and challenge assumptions that negative digital experiences are the primary causes of depressive symptoms.

title: Intrinsic and extrinsic regulation of young children's frustration: A person-specific, dynamic approach
abstract:
Young children may draw on both intrinsic physiological systems and extrinsic caregiver support to manage frustration. While regulation is often conceptualized as feedback-control processes, there has been limited empirical evidence on how they unfold in real time. Taking a person-specific, dynamic network approach, we examined whether parasympathetic changes and maternal responsiveness serve as active regulators that effectively dampen children's regulatory demands (reflected in sympathetic arousal and challenging behaviors) on a moment-to-moment basis during a frustration challenge. Data from 139 mother-child dyads (30-60 months; 48% female; 94% White; data collected June 2017-December 2019 in central Pennsylvania, U.S.) revealed that parasympathetic responses can function as real-time regulators through both dynamic increases and decreases across children; physiological regulation was related to better effortful control (standardized coefficient β = .22). Parental regulation primarily modulated challenging behaviors and was less evident among children with greater negative affectivity and externalizing risks (βs = -.19 and -.22). Findings demonstrate how children's self-regulation emerges from heterogeneous, dynamic systems where intrinsic and extrinsic processes operate to maintain homeostasis. By linking micro-level regulation dynamics with children's emotional and behavioral characteristics, the findings further highlight the value of capturing active, unfolding regulation patterns for understanding early functioning strengths and risks.

In this study, we focused on how young children rely on their internal physiology and support from their mothers to handle a frustration challenge. By tracking physiological responses and observed behaviors for 139 mother-child pairs on a moment-to-moment basis, we found that children's internal calming systems worked in highly unique ways to help regulate their arousal and frustration-related behaviors, especially for those with better effortful self-control ability. Meanwhile, maternal responses emerged in relation to children's frustration behaviors and helped regulate these behaviors, although this appeared harder for children prone to strong negative emotions. In summary, investigating how these real-time interactions unfold moment-to-moment helps us understand how children cope with frustration and how that may relate to their emotional and behavioral characteristics.

title: Susceptibility to task-irrelevant auditory distractors in relation to visual working memory in children with and without attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
abstract:
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder associated with increased distractibility. Previous research has reported that susceptibility to task-irrelevant visual distraction is linked with visual working memory (WM) capacity in adults. Here, we examined how neural susceptibility to task-irrelevant auditory distractors related to visual WM capacity in children with and without ADHD. Across two experiments, electroencephalography (EEG) signals were recorded from 146 Chinese children aged 7-15 (63 with ADHD, 23% girls; collected in 2022-2024), during which they performed visual tasks of varying difficulty with auditory distractors. The mismatch negativity (MMN) amplitude was measured as neural susceptibility to auditory distractors, and a K-score was calculated to assess visual WM capacity. In typically developing (TD) children, those with higher visual WM capacity showed less susceptibility to auditory distractors under high audiovisual competition (r = 0.494), whereas this relation reversed under low competition (r = -0.319).
