Conversely, in children with ADHD, lower visual WM capacity predicted higher susceptibility under both high (r = 0.442) and low competition (r = 0.326). These findings indicate that susceptibility to task-irrelevant auditory distraction is related to visual WM capacity in children, but the patterns differ between typical and atypical neurodevelopment and are modulated by audiovisual competition.

This study investigated how children's sensitivity to distracting sounds was related to their visual memory capacity, and whether this relation differed between children with and without attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Brain activity was measured while children performed visual tasks under different demand levels with background sounds. In typically developing children, higher visual memory capacity was associated with reduced distraction by sounds when the visual task was more demanding, whereas the relation was reversed when visual task demand was lower. In contrast, children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder who had lower visual memory capacity showed greater auditory distraction, regardless of visual task demand. These findings suggest a close relation between auditory distraction and visual memory capacity in children, depending on both developmental deficit and task contexts.

title: Childhood exposure to interparental conflict and adolescent mental health difficulties: The mediating role of self-regulation difficulties
abstract: Interparental conflict (IPC) in early childhood is associated with mental health difficulties in adolescence. General psychological processes such as self-regulation that may underpin this relationship are important to understand during this developmental stage. The aim of the study was to investigate whether indicators of self-regulation difficulties in middle childhood, including (a) difficulties with persistence, (b) emotional reactivity, (c) behavioral disinhibition, and (d) sleeping difficulties, mediated the relationship between IPC in early childhood and mental health difficulties (anxiety and depressive symptoms; antisocial behavior) in adolescence. A second aim was to determine whether child sex moderated the associations between IPC, self-regulation difficulties, and mental health difficulties. Structural equation modeling using data from a population-based Australian sample ( N  = 9,476) supported a mediation model where higher IPC at age 4-5 years was associated with higher indications of self-regulation difficulties at age 10-11 years, which in turn predicted higher depressive symptoms, anxious symptoms, and antisocial behavior at age 14-15 years. Evidence of moderation by child sex was found. The relationship between IPC, indicators of self-regulation difficulties, and antisocial behavior was stronger for males than females, while the relationship between indicators of self-regulation difficulties and internalizing outcomes was stronger for females compared to males. These results are interpreted using perspectives on biopsychosocial development, and implications for intervention at multiple time points are discussed. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: The role of temperament and personality traits in the development of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) from late childhood through adolescence
abstract: Individual differences in temperament and personality traits may shed light on the presentation and development of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) across adolescence. The present study used multimethod, longitudinal data from a large sample of Mexican-origin youth ( N  = 674; 50% girls) to examine associations between ADHD symptoms (including combined, hyperactive-impulsive, and inattentive subtypes) and a wide range of temperament and personality traits assessed via self-, mother-, and father-reports and coded observational data. First, we found moderate 1-year rank-order stabilities of combined, hyperactive-impulsive, and inattentive ADHD symptoms (rs ranging from .27 to .51) but relatively low 8-year rank-order stability from age 10 to 17 ( r  = .19 for combined); 8-year stability was higher for boys than girls. Second, hyperactive-impulsive and inattentive symptoms were both negatively correlated with concurrent effortful control and conscientiousness and positively correlated with impulsivity, negative emotionality, and neuroticism; in addition, hyperactive-impulsive symptoms were positively associated with surgency and extraversion. Third, bivariate latent growth curve models showed that the levels and slopes of effortful control (and its facets) and negative emotionality (particularly the frustration, aggression, and depressed mood facets) were significantly related to the levels and slopes of ADHD symptom trajectories. Findings from random-intercept cross-lagged panel models showed that temperament domains and ADHD symptoms had meaningful between- and within-person associations but no significant cross-lagged associations. Associations were stronger for adolescent self-reports of temperament/personality than for mother-reports. Overall, findings highlight connections between temperament and personality traits with ADHD symptoms across adolescence. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: A systematic review of observational and report-based measures of caregiver sensitivity: A Latin American perspective
abstract:
Abstract Sensitivity is a cornerstone of early childhood mental health; however, its measurement relies heavily on tools developed in English‐speaking, high‐resource contexts. This systematic review identified observational and report‐based instruments used to assess sensitivity in caregivers of children aged 0–6 years. It evaluated the methodological robustness and usability of these instruments within Latin American contexts. Following a systematic search in Web of Science, Scopus, PsycInfo, and Redalyc, 732 eligible studies were identified. Based on a frequency‐of‐use threshold, 16 instruments (14 observational and 2 report‐based) represented across 616 papers were selected for in‐depth evaluation. Measures were coded for theoretical alignment with Ainsworth's sensitivity definition, psychometric evidence, and usability—specifically training accessibility, administration complexity, and evidence of use with diverse Latin American populations (e.g., caregivers in rural settings or with lower educational levels). Results revealed that only a minority of measures adhered explicitly to Ainsworth's original definition. Most instruments prioritized warmth and positive affect, potentially leading to cross‐cultural underdetection in contexts where responsiveness is expressed through proximity and routine‐based care. While observational tools predominated, report‐based measures showed limited validation and minimal regional use. These findings highlight the urgent need for culturally grounded validation and the development of accessible training programs for the region.

1 INTRODUCTION According to Attachment Theory, attachment refers to the affective bond that develops between an infant and their primary caregiver(s) during the first years of life and becomes organized into relatively stable patterns of security or insecurity through repeated interactions (Ainsworth, 1967 ; Bowlby, 1969 ). Secure attachment reflects the child's expectation of caregiver availability and responsiveness in contexts of stress, supporting the use of the caregiver as a secure base for exploration (Ainsworth et al., 1978 ). Key Findings Sensitivity measures often treat warmth and positive affect as central, which can miss responsive caregiving expressed through proximity and routine‐based care in some Latin American and other non‐Western contexts. Many widely used observational tools require training and materials that are not available in Spanish, limiting feasibility and standardization in Latin American low‐resource settings. Report‐based sensitivity measures are brief and potentially scalable but currently lack evidence linking them to attachment outcomes and observational convergence. Statement of relevance to infant and early childhood mental health Accurate assessment of caregiver sensitivity is essential for identifying relational risk and tailoring early caregiving interventions central to infant and early childhood mental health. This review clarifies how sensitivity is operationalized across common instruments and highlights when measures may under‐detect responsiveness in contexts where caregiving is expressed through proximity and daily routines. By integrating psychometric indicators with usability and Spanish‐language training access, the study supports practitioners and researchers in selecting measures that better fit real‐world service and research settings. A substantial body of research has documented the long‐term implications of attachment security for socioemotional development and mental health. Secure attachment has been associated with greater emotional understanding and regulation, as well as more adaptive interpersonal functioning, whereas insecure attachment is linked to long‐term elevated risks of relational difficulties, externalizing behaviors, and mental health problems (Dagan et al., 2018 ; Deneault et al., 2023 ; Obeldobel et al., 2023 ). In this context, caregiver sensitivity has consistently been identified as a robust predictor of secure attachment (Madigan et al., 2024 ). Sensitivity is defined as the caregiver's capacity to perceive, interpret, and respond appropriately to the child's signals (Ainsworth et al., 1974 ). Through ongoing reciprocal exchanges, sensitive caregiving supports trust in caregiver availability and the development of secure internal working models, providing a relational foundation for socioemotional competence and mental health across development (Thompson, 2016 ). 1.1 Assessing sensitivity Given its foundational role in early socioemotional development, attachment research has increasingly emphasized the need for reliable and context‐sensitive measures of caregiving processes, particularly sensitivity (Halty & Berástegui, 2021 ). Observational measures are often treated as the reference approach for assessing sensitivity (Lotzin et al., 2015 ), as they allow direct evaluation of caregiver‐child interaction and capture sensitive behaviors that are often intuitive and automated rather than consciously planned (Mesman, 2010 ), making them less accessible through self‐report. Ainsworth's Maternal Sensitivity Scale (AMSS; Ainsworth et al., 1974 ) is the gold standard observational measure in the study of parental sensitivity, in that it operationalizes Ainsworth's original conceptualization of sensitivity as the caregiver's prompt, appropriate, and child‐attuned responding to signals (Bretherton, 2013 ). Building on this framework, numerous observational instruments have been developed, differing in their conceptualization and operationalization of sensitivity (Mesman & Emmen, 2013 ). While some measures adhere closely to Ainsworth's original definition by focusing on contingent and contextually appropriate responses to the child's signals, others incorporate additional behavioral indicators such as warmth, verbal engagement, or structured interactional tasks (Mesman & Emmen, 2013 ). As Mesman ( 2021 ) highlighted, these operational choices reflect implicit assumptions about how sensitivity is expressed and have important implications for the cultural flexibility and comparability of observational measures. Previous systematic reviews have synthesized observational measurements of parental sensitivity. Mesman and Emmen identified eight instruments most frequently used in the literature, all developed in English and primarily validated in North American or European contexts (Mesman & Emmen, 2013 ). A more recent review by Halty and Berástegui ( 2021 ) reported similar limitations in the linguistic and cultural scope of parental responsiveness measures, conceptualized as the behavioral manifestation of sensitivity. That review also underscored the need for more systematic evaluation of sensitivity instruments using objective, comparable criteria. To date, however, the field lacks an integrative assessment that jointly considers psychometric indicators and practical usability, including training accessibility and feasibility across diverse research settings. Importantly, methodological rigor and practical usability do not necessarily converge in the assessment of sensitivity. Instruments with theoretical and empirical support often require extensive training, lengthy administration procedures, and specialized resources (Fourment et al., 2022 ), limiting their feasibility in large‐scale studies and low‐resource settings. These constraints are particularly salient in contexts such as Latin America, where access to standardized attachment measures is often restricted by financial limitations, lack of institutional infrastructure, and the high cost of training for key observational instruments, which are frequently available only in English (Mesman et al., 2016a ). Conversely, instruments designed for greater feasibility may rely on narrower or behavior‐specific operationalizations of sensitivity, which can limit comparability across studies and complicate the integration of findings within a coherent theoretical framework (Mesman & Emmen, 2013 ). 1.2 Methodological challenges in Latin America The assessment of sensitivity in Latin American research contexts presents specific methodological challenges related to the use and implementation of established measurement instruments. Cross‐national attachment research has emphasized the importance of empirically examining whether observational tools and procedures developed in Western, high‐income contexts can be validly and feasibly applied in different settings (Causadias & Posada, 2013 ). In Latin America, the use of sensitivity measures is often shaped by limited access to training, language barriers, and constrained research infrastructure, resulting in heterogeneous applications, partial adaptations, or reliance on a narrow set of available instruments (Fourment et al., 2022 ). These conditions complicate the systematic comparison of findings across studies and highlight the need to evaluate sensitivity measures not only in terms of their psychometric properties, but also in terms of their practical usability across diverse research contexts. Beyond feasibility, there are measurement‐related reasons to question the uncritical transfer of sensitivity measures developed in Western, high‐income contexts to Latin American populations. Caregiving in Latin America often involves extended family networks, shared caregiving responsibilities, higher physical proximity, and culturally specific forms of emotional expression (Causadias & Posada, 2013 ; Mesman et al., 2016a ). These caregiving features may not be fully captured by instruments grounded in dyadic, verbally oriented models of caregiver‐child interaction (Mesman et al., 2016b ). As a result, measures that foreground overt positive affect may underestimate sensitive caregiving in non‐Western rural contexts where responsiveness is often expressed nonverbally and embedded in proximity and everyday routines (Fourment et al., 2025 ), thereby reducing cross‐study comparability. Against this background, empirical research on sensitivity in Latin America remains limited. Few studies have employed established observational measures with Latin American samples (see Duhalde et al., 2020 ; Lima Ribeiro et al., 2021 ; Olhaberry et al., 2015 ), and those that have done so often rely on smaller samples than studies conducted in Western contexts (Fourment et al., 2022 ). The reliance on observational methods can be difficult to sustain in large‐scale research in the region, given the practical and institutional barriers to implementing standardized attachment methodologies in Latin America (Causadias & Posada, 2013 ). One potential strategy to address these challenges may be to use report‐based measures of sensitivity. These instruments may be more feasible for large‐scale studies and for settings where observational approaches are impractical due to the substantial demands in training, time, and resources associated with observational methods (Lotzin et al., 2015 ). However, the systematic exclusion of report‐based measures from prior reviews has left their theoretical grounding, psychometric quality, and applicability, particularly in non‐Western contexts, largely unexplored. 1.3 The present study In response to these gaps, the present study had two objectives. First, it aimed to systematically review observational and report‐based instruments used to assess sensitivity in caregivers of children aged 0–6 years, including instruments developed in English and Spanish. Second, it evaluated these instruments in terms of methodological robustness (theoretical alignment and psychometric evidence) and usability from a Latin American perspective. Usability criteria included training accessibility, administration complexity, and evidence of use with Latin American population characteristics, including caregivers with lower educational levels and those residing in rural settings. By adopting this perspective, the study extends previous reviews focused exclusively on observational methods, English‐language instruments, and North American or European contexts (Halty & Berástegui, 2021 ; Mesman & Emmen, 2013 ). To our knowledge, this is the first systematic evaluation of sensitivity measures integrating methodological indicators with usability and contextual relevance. Findings are intended to support researchers working in non‐Western and specifically Latin American contexts in selecting and prioritizing instruments for validation and use, advancing more inclusive and contextually grounded research on sensitivity. 2 METHODS 2.1 Search strategy A systematic search was conducted across four scientific databases: Web of Science (WoS), Scopus, PsycInfo, and Redalyc. The search strategy followed the PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews and meta‐analyses and aimed to identify empirical studies that used observational or report‐based measures to assess caregiver sensitivity. Prior to conducting the searches, the authors discussed and agreed upon the search terms that best captured the objectives of the review. The search keywords used in WoS, Scopus, and PsycInfo were: (“maternal sensitiv*” OR “maternal responsive*” OR “paternal sensitiv*” OR “paternal responsive*” OR “mother* sensitiv*” OR “mother* responsive*” OR “father* sensitiv*” OR “father* responsive*” OR “parent* sensitiv*” OR “parent* responsive*” OR “sensitive parenting”) AND (child* OR infan* OR toddler OR preschooler OR baby OR babies). Search terms were adapted for Redalyc to capture Spanish‐language publications. Spanish terms were combined using equivalent Boolean operators and parentheses to mirror the English strategy. The Spanish search terms were defined as: (sensibilidad materna* OR sensitividad* materna* OR responsividad* materna* OR sensibilidad* paterna* OR sensitividad* paterna* OR sensibilidad* parental* OR sensitividad* parental* OR responsividad* parental*) AND (infan* OR niñ* OR bebe* OR preescolar*). Across all databases, terms were searched within the “Topic” field or its closest equivalent (title/abstract/keywords), depending on the database. Redalyc was included to capture peer‐reviewed research published in Spanish and to mitigate known language and regional coverage biases in major international databases (Mongeon & Paul‐Hus, 2016 ). The publication time frame was restricted to studies published between December 8, 2012, and April 8, 2023. This time frame was selected to capture advances in the measurement of sensitivity following the systematic review conducted by Mesman and Emmen ( 2013 ). Records from disciplines not directly related to the focus of the study (e.g., broad behavioral and social sciences) were excluded. An updated search using the same databases and search terms was conducted on May 6, 2025. For this update, the publication period ranged from April 8, 2023, to May 6, 2025. 2.2 Selection criteria Studies were required to meet all of the following inclusion criteria: (a) empirical article; (b) published in English or

title: Higher Education Institutions: An Underused Setting for Addressing Adverse Childhood Experiences
abstract: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are potentially traumatic experiences that occur from birth through age 17 years and can undermine a child’s safety and stability ( 1 ). From various forms of abuse and neglect to other aspects that can impair a child’s well-being, ACEs are a major public health concern. In 2024, the National Survey of Children’s Health found that approximately 38% of children experienced at least 1 ACE ( 2 ). Among US adults, 64% reported at least 1 ACE, and nearly 18% have reported 4 or more ( 3 ). These experiences warrant attention because the effects may accumulate, potentially resulting in lifelong adverse health and social consequences. People exposed to ACEs are more likely to report mental illness ( 4 ), substance use ( 5 ), interpersonal violence ( 6 ), and other health-risk behaviors. The cumulative effects of ACEs may also contribute to toxic stress, disrupt healthy development, and increase vulnerability to chronic health conditions later in life ( 7 ). Because these health outcomes and potential negative effects occur across the life course, efforts to reduce exposure to ACEs are critical. Preventing ACEs requires creating safe, stable, and nurturing relationships and environments that reduce children’s exposure to adversity ( 8 ). However, opportunities to identify and respond to ACEs through screening, referral, and supportive services may not be accessible to all. These challenges warrant consideration of more opportunities to screen for ACEs and offer support beyond childhood for people with a history of ACEs. One promising approach is to focus on emerging adults. The objective of this essay is to describe how higher education institutions (HEIs) can serve as an opportune setting to address ACEs among emerging adults. Expanding the Focus on ACEs to Emerging Adulthood Policies, programs, and early interventions can decrease the prevalence of ACEs by reducing children’s exposure to adversity and strengthen relationships and environments that protect their well-being. However, some approaches implemented during childhood rely on the involvement of parents or guardians, whose engagement may not always be available or possible. Extending attention beyond childhood provides opportunities to address earlier adversity as people enter new stages of life. Emerging adulthood, generally spanning ages 18 to 29 years, is a period during which people undergo transition, including navigating their independence, exploring their identity, and embracing their career and educational choices ( 9 ). Focusing on emerging adults provides an opportunity to strengthen protective factors and, from a life course perspective, intervene before the consequences accumulate or become more pronounced ( 10 ). Access to supportive relationships, health and behavioral health services, stable housing and financial resources, and other forms of social support may help emerging adults navigate the effects of prior adversity while managing new challenges ( 11 , 12 ). In the early stages of this period, emerging adults may no longer be interacting with child- and family-serving systems through which ACE prevention and early intervention efforts are often delivered. Identifying settings that maintain sustained contact with emerging adults is therefore important for extending ACE-related support. For the millions of emerging adults who pursue postsecondary education, colleges and universities are one such setting. Strengths of HEIs in Addressing ACEs Millions of emerging adults are enrolled in colleges and universities in the US, positioning HEIs to offer ACE-related support. Some HEIs have implemented efforts to address trauma and childhood adversity, such as The Ohio State University’s Advocacy and Resources for Trauma initiative ( 13 ); however, the potential role of HEIs in addressing ACEs extends beyond individual programs or initiatives. Recognition of the opportunity for HEIs to assume a greater role in addressing trauma and adversity is growing ( 14 , 15 ). As complex institutions, HEIs engage emerging adults across multiple aspects of their lives and have many strengths that make them an ideal setting: for example, their infrastructure, resources, established systems of support, and opportunities for social support. Thus, a university-wide approach that includes student screenings, referrals, and trauma-informed interventions can be advantageous. The diverse resources, relationships, and organizational structures found at HEIs provide a strong foundation and capacity to promote student health and play a meaningful role in addressing ACEs. For this essay, we outline 2 examples of strengths, existing infrastructure and the social environment. Established infrastructure is one of the greatest strengths of HEIs. Their institutional capacity allows ACE-related efforts to be integrated into existing systems and, where feasible, coordinated across multiple areas of the institution. For example, communication platforms (eg, Canvas, social media) are routinely used to announce campus events, share resources, and connect with students. These platforms could similarly be used to disseminate key information about ACEs, increase awareness of available resources, and highlight available campus- or community-based services. HEIs also have varying levels of a health infrastructure to support student well-being, ranging from wellness and counseling centers to health clinics, pharmacies, and at some institutions, university-affiliated hospitals. Clinics and counseling centers may incorporate trauma-informed practices, identify students who may benefit from additional support, and establish referral pathways. Moreover, because HEIs are valuable sources of health care and supportive services, particularly for students who have relocated to attend college, these services and pharmacies can support continuity of care for those receiving treatment related to past trauma or adversity ( 16 ). Another strength is the social environment. Through residential life, extracurricular activities, campus events, and other opportunities for collegiate interaction, students are in an environment that can help them develop their social network and support systems. The many student organizations and groups on campus, for example, can offer a sense of belonging and community, an essential protective factor ( 17 ). Supportive relationships with faculty, advisors, and other trusted adults may also serve as a protective factor for students who have a history of trauma or abuse, potentially serving as a vital resource that fosters resilience and emotional safety ( 18 ). As students’ needs and circumstances evolve throughout their educational journey, positive interactions with others may increase their willingness to participate in ACE-related initiatives or support their healing journey. Ultimately, the social aspect of attending an HEI is a critical strength. Beyond the classroom, campuses support positive student interactions and provide opportunities for students to build meaningful relationships that can provide sources of social and emotional support for students. Proposed Solution HEIs could use a multidisciplinary approach in their existing systems to address ACEs. Having an all-hands-on deck approach can also reduce pressure on counseling offices to a more holistic system — one that includes faculty, staff, and students. We propose a comprehensive, institution-wide approach in which the university ecosystem communicates and collaborates ( Figure ). University leadership can set institutional priorities, allocate resources, champion initiatives, and promote policies that support ACE-related initiatives. Commitment from leadership can help ensure that ACE-related efforts are strategically embedded, establishing potential long-term sustainability and coordinated support. Leaders can work with all levels of the university, including divisions, administration units, departments, and offices to offer trauma and adversity awareness seminars or support faculty training to incorporate trauma-informed teaching. They can also support residence life departments in offering optional, confidential ACE screenings for all students. Routine screenings are underused despite growing recognition of the lasting effects of ACEs ( 19 ). Although some people may not be aware of the benefits of screening, ACE screening may help the university support students at increased risk for behavioral health concerns, chronic disease, academic difficulties, and other adverse outcomes. Screening may also facilitate timely referrals and connect students with services. Health services can coordinate with counseling centers and other campus services to ensure that students have a direct referral and support pathway. Moreover, student affairs offices can offer ACE-focused workshops to alleviate stigma and increase awareness about ACEs. Faculty and staff are essential partners because they often serve as the first point of contact for students experiencing academic, behavioral, or emotional difficulties. Training can help them recognize signs of distress and refer students to counseling and resources. In addition, if a student were to disclose an ACE, instructors could be trained on how to navigate the conversation without shame or assumptions. Mentorship programs are common in university communities, and establishing such a program for students who are navigating recently recognized trauma can help students. Creating peer mentorship programs in which students themselves are trauma-informed mentors can help ease the burden on strained counseling services and can also help build healthy social connections. Student organization leaders could also be trained to recognize signs of distress among the student body and create a streamlined process of communication between club board members and supportive services. Hosting campus-wide events, such as wellness walks and social gatherings, can bring students together and can help reduce toxic stress. Promoting these organizations and events requires cross-communication and collaboration so that students are aware of the available opportunities for connection and support. Institutions can further strengthen ACE identification and interventions through external partnerships with local organizations and the community. Behavioral health providers, public health agencies, community organizations, and social service agencies can expand access to specialized services that may not be available on campus. These partnerships can facilitate referrals for trauma-focused treatment, substance use services, and other forms of social support. Implications for Public Health An interdisciplinary approach that engages multiple areas of a university may encourage entire divisions of university systems to work together and offer a promising strategy to address ACEs. By leveraging existing infrastructure, services, and relationships across campus, HEIs have an opportunity to develop more coordinated approaches for ACE identification, referral, and support. If these efforts are integrated and championed across levels, from university leadership to external partners and organizations, students are likely to benefit. Such efforts can support academic success, mental health, social relationships, and resilience. Addressing ACEs should not be the responsibility of a single department or office when multiple systems in the institution can be leveraged through coordinated efforts. Additional research is needed to determine the feasibility of designing, implementing, and sustaining an interdisciplinary and university-wide initiative. Feasibility studies could identify institutional resources, barriers, and facilitators. Future research should also include short- and long-term evaluations to determine whether coordination increases ACE screening and health-seeking behavior. Leveraging the existing strengths of HEIs can be a remarkable opportunity to introduce and extend ACE-related support for emerging adults as they navigate this stage of their life course.

title: Circuit mechanisms for disentangled representations and generalization in the hippocampus
abstract: Understanding how the heterogeneous activity patterns of individual neurons give rise to coherent population dynamics and cognition is a central challenge in neuroscience. In the hippocampus, neurons are tuned to spatial location, yet their activity is also modulated by multiple external and internal variables and appears to drift randomly over time, making it difficult to link hippocampal computations to behavior. By analyzing hippocampal population dynamics in behaving mice, we reveal a structured organization underlying the diversity of single-neuron responses-the hippocampus encodes different aspects of experience as disentangled variables represented in the co-activity dynamics of cell assemblies. The temporal and contextual components of these representations are governed by local inhibitory interactions and input-driven cell-assembly dynamics, respectively. Our findings reveal the circuit basis of disentangled hippocampal representations, offering a unifying geometric principle of population coding that supports flexible memory representations and enables rapid generalization of prior knowledge to new situations.

title: Stimulus-specific recruitment of human amygdala neurons predicts episodic memory encoding success
abstract: Controlling whether an experience is encoded into long-term memory and thus later remembered is a crucial aspect of memory. Here we examined single-neuron activity in the human brain while participants formed memories for novel visual stimuli and later retrieved them with confidence ratings. Category-selective amygdala neurons exhibited elevated firing during encoding of later remembered items relative to later forgotten items. This effect was predictive of the episodic aspect of the memory, was restricted to the preferred category of each cell, emerged earlier and was stronger in the amygdala compared to the hippocampus, and did not depend on stimulus valence and arousal. Successful memory formation was accompanied by enhanced spike-field coherence between the activity of amygdala category cells and hippocampal field potentials. These findings demonstrate that stimulus-specific recruitment of the amygdala predicts memory formation and suggest category cells in the right amygdala as a target for interventions to treat disorders affecting episodic memory in humans.

title: Remak bundle size, structure, and function are regulated by the Schwann cell basal lamina
abstract: Remak bundles are groups of small-diameter unmyelinated nociceptive axons ensheathed by Schwann cells (SCs). Whereas the development and maturation of myelinating SCs have been extensively studied, the formation of Remak bundles remains poorly understood. By preventing the secretion of type IV collagen from SCs, we observe normal myelin but abnormal Remak bundles. There is a decrease in Remak bundle density, an increase in bundle size, improperly ensheathed axons, and a decrease in mechanosensitivity. While Remak bundle formation appears to be independent of integrin signaling, the loss of type IV collagen leads to a decrease in postnatal SC proliferation. Inducing the emergence of supernumerary SCs rescues Remak bundle architecture and mechanosensitivity. Taken together, our results demonstrate that SC-secreted basal lamina critically regulates Remak SC number, bundle size, and structure. Our findings provide insight into the functional role of Remak bundles and highlight their potential involvement in peripheral neuropathies and neuropathic pain.

title: Short-term outcomes, longer-term disability and relapse risk in LGI1-antibody encephalitis
abstract: Leucine-rich glioma-inactivated-1 antibody encephalitis (LGI1-Ab-E) is a common and immunotherapy-responsive form of encephalitis. However, it is not known which immunotherapy regimens improve short-term outcomes, longer-term disability and relapse risk. Further, it is not known if the widely-utilised modified Rankin Scale (mRS) accurately captures quality of life (QoL) in LGI1-Ab-E, complicating disability measurements and interpretation of immunotherapy responses. A multicentre, international, real-world comparative analysis of patients with LGI1-Ab-E. Retrospective data from patient records evaluated short-term seizure and cognitive outcomes, 1-6 year disability, and future relapse risk associations, by integrating demographics, clinical features investigations and exposures to immunotherapies and antiseizure medications (ASMs). Patient- and neurologist-rated QoL assessments were used to establish an evidence-based mRS threshold for defining clinically significant disability. Cox proportional hazard models, Anderson-Gill, and generalised linear mixed-effects models were employed. 181 patients were included, with median age at onset 63 years (range 23 - 92); 122/181 (67%) were male. Short-term outcomes, evaluated at both five and ten weeks post-treatment initiation, identified exposure to immunotherapies associated with seizure resolution (OR = 13.97, 95%CI = 6.10-32.01; p < 0.0001 and OR = 8.53, 95%CI = 4.14-17.55; p < 0.0001, respectively), notably with corticosteroids, plasma exchange and rituximab, but not ASMs, intravenous immunoglobulins or steroid sparing agents. Conversely, seizure recurrence was observed after discontinuation of oral prednisolone, but not other immunotherapies or ASMs (OR = 39.53, 95%CI = 12.70-122.20, p < 0.0001). To evaluate longer-term disability, first, mRS scores were calibrated using QoL assessments: this identified a significant increase in patient-rated disability at mRS score of 2. Hence, using mRS 0-1 as a favourable outcome, we identified worse mRS at nadir associated with greater one-year disability (OR = 2.56, 95%CI = 1.56-4.20, p = 0.0003), and each month of delayed immunotherapy associated with a 16% increased risk of disability (HR = 1.16, 95%CI = 1.06-1.35, p = 0.004). Additionally, absence of immunotherapy associated both with greater one-year disability (OR = 5.67; 95% CI 1.19-26.54, p = 0.03) and a relapsing course (OR = 7.64, 95%CI = 2.51-21.77, p = 0.0002). Both a relapsing course, observed in 38% of patients, and the number of relapses associated with step-wise worsening of disability and QoL-outcomes. Rituximab exposure was the only identified clinical factor associated with reduced future relapse risk, by 93% (HR = 0.07, 95%CI = 0.01-0.48, p = 0.002). Persistent serum LGI1-IgMs, but not LGI1-IgGs, at one-year, associated with future relapses (HR = 11.69, 95%CI = 1.58-145.80, p = 0.02). Distinctive clinical factors and select immunotherapies, particularly intravenous methylprednisolone and plasma exchange, but not ASMs, associated with favourable short-term outcomes, patient-centric longer-term disability and relapses in LGI1-Ab-E. Our findings provide evidence-based disability thresholds, highlight novel prognostic biomarkers, and pragmatically guide LGI1-Ab-E care, pending randomized clinical trials.

title: PTPRO restricts higher-order branching of terminal arbors through TrkB dephosphorylation
abstract: The structural complexity of axon collateral terminal arbors shapes synaptic connectivity. In corticospinal projections, individual axon collaterals exhibit distinct patterns of terminal arborization, ranging from sparse local branches to dense, highly complex arbors in target regions such as the pontine nuclei. How this complexity is controlled remains poorly understood. Here, using corticopontine projections in male and female mice, we show that protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) selectively restricts higher-order branching of terminal arbors in the pontine nuclei without affecting collateral number. This function requires the intracellular phosphatase domain of PTPRO but not its extracellular region. We demonstrate that PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), and that the excessive terminal arborization caused by acute PTPRO loss is rescued by TrkB depletion or phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibition. Together, these findings reveal that PTPRO-mediated TrkB dephosphorylation acts as a molecular brake on corticopontine terminal arbor elaboration. Significance Statement  How individual axons regulate terminal branching within target regions is a fundamental question in neural circuit development. This study identifies protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO), a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase that negatively regulates signaling through tyrosine phosphorylation, as a selective regulator of higher-order branching in corticopontine terminal arbors. PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a neurotrophin receptor tyrosine kinase that promotes neuronal growth and branching, thereby restricting terminal arbor complexity without affecting collateral number from the main axon. Given that terminal arbor architecture determines the synaptic territory of each cortical input, PTPRO-dependent constraint on arbor elaboration may represent a general principle by which projection-specific arbor complexity is established across long-range circuits in the central nervous system.

title: Bivalent habenula modulation of human monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways
abstract: The habenula is implicated in signaling negative reward prediction errors (RPE), yet direct evidence demonstrating its influence on downstream human brain circuits is limited. Using ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling across two negative RPE-inducing experimental tasks, we characterize habenula-directed connectivity with monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways in healthy adults (n = 47, 24 males and 23 females; n = 43, 23 males and 20 females). Negative feedback drove habenula inhibition of ventral tegmental area and dorsal raphe nucleus activity, while positive feedback had an excitatory effect. These core effects are replicated across reversal learning and perceptual decision uncertainty tasks, establishing a generalizable mechanism for behavioral adaptation. Task-specific modulatory effects emerged in pathways between the subcortical and cortical regions (ventral tegmental area→dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal raphe nucleus→medial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex→habenula), revealing context-dependent cortical elaboration of negative RPE-driven habenula signals. This provides the first evidence in humans, using model-based effective connectivity, for bivalent modulation of habenula function on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways, demonstrating how the brain integrates negative and positive signals to guide adaptive behavior. Significance Statement  The habenula - an epithalamic brain region - plays a key role in the encoding of reward and punishment. Animal studies have demonstrated the habenula to be bivalently modulated by aversive and appetitive stimuli, resulting in the bidirectional modulation of monoaminergic brain region activity. Despite this evidence, the directional impact of bivalently modulated habenula activity on its circuitry has yet to be investigated in humans. This study leverages ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling to reveal the impact of bivalent habenula modulation on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical regions across two distinct tasks. Through these methodologies, we demonstrate the habenula to have a key role in guiding adaptive behavior.

title: Chronic progressive demyelination induces a microglial state with lysosomal dysfunction
abstract: Dysfunctional immune responses impair remyelination and contribute to neurodegeneration. While immune and metabolic responses to acute myelin injury are well characterized, myeloid cell adaptations to chronic myelin damage remain poorly understood. Here we performed a comparative analysis of genetic and toxic mouse models of acute and chronic demyelination, which identified a distinct microglial state associated with chronic demyelination, characterized by sustained pro-inflammatory activation, lysosomal lipid sequestration and reduced lipid droplet formation. Transcriptomics profiling further revealed a metabolic program marked by upregulated cholesterol synthesis and diminished sterol efflux. Treatment with a desmosterol mimetic possessing 24-dehydrocholesterol reductase inhibitor activity reversed this microglial state, attenuated pro-inflammatory signaling (including C-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 4 expression), reduced myelin damage and improved motor performance in a mouse model of leukodystrophy. Our findings uncover a pro-inflammatory microglial state characterized by lysosomal dysfunction and increased myelin reactivity, highlighting a novel therapeutic target for chronic demyelinating disorders.

title: Trait-linked brainstem circuit resilience balances tau pathology-induced cellular vulnerability in Alzheimer's disease
abstract: Although tau pathology correlates with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD), some individuals exhibit resilience by maintaining cognitive function. The mechanisms enabling this protection, particularly before widespread cortical degeneration occurs, remain elusive. Here, we identify a dynamic interplay between cellular vulnerability and circuit-level resilience that shapes cognitive outcomes in AD. Tau accumulation in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (EW) impairs attention by inducing hypoexcitability in CART +  neurons via Kcnma1 upregulation, a vulnerability predictive of future decline in both 3×Tg-AD mice and AD patients. Conversely, a subset of AD mice with heightened exploratory behavior activates a compensatory medial parabrachial (mPB)-EW circuit, mediated by substance P-Tacr1 signaling, which sustains CART +  neuron function and delays cognitive deterioration. These findings reveal resilience as an active state enabled by trait-linked circuit plasticity that balances cellular vulnerability, defining multilevel targets for early intervention.

title: Glioma regulates GABAergic signaling to drive hyperactivity and tumor progression
abstract: Recent studies have identified bi-directional communication between neurons and glioma tumors as a key driver of hyperexcitability and malignant progression. Although much of this work has focused on the activity of excitatory neurons, the roles of inhibitory neurons remain poorly defined. Using in vivo screening approaches in autochthonous glioma models, we found that the loss of a γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) transporter (Slc6a1) enhanced glioma progression, promoted network hyperactivity, and influenced tonic GABA release by tumors. Mechanistically, we show that glioma tumors influence the activity of inhibitory neurons and that their subsequent stimulation suppresses tumor growth. Further screening of these phenomena identified diazepam binding inhibitor (DBI), a secreted negative allosteric modulator of GABA-A, as a link between glioma-related hyperexcitability and proliferation that functions through modulating inhibitory neuronal signaling. Collectively, our findings indicate that glioma tumors utilize multiple mechanisms to manipulate the activity of inhibitory neurons as a means to drive network hyperactivity, which ultimately facilitates malignant progression.

title: The TBK1-OTUB2-IRF3 signalling complex promotes neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration
abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway-mediated chronic inflammation drives neurodegeneration in natural aging and various neurodegenerative diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Here, we identify Otubain-2 (OTUB2) as a pivotal regulator that orchestrates the STING signalosome to amplify inflammatory responses. The function of OTUB2 in neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration was investigated through genetic deletion and pharmacological inhibition of OTUB2 in hTARDBP transgenic mice​, adeno-associated virus-mediated TDP43 overexpression mice, and aged mice. Biochemical assays were performed to dissect underlying molecular mechanisms. OTUB2 inhibited K63 ubiquitination of TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), thereby suppressing TBK1 kinase activity and promoting cell death mediated by hyperactivated receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1). Additionally, OTUB2 functioned as a scaffold facilitating assembly of the TBK1-interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) signalling complex, a prerequisite for IRF3 phosphorylation, and enhanced IRF3 dimerization by reducing its K11 ubiquitination. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of OTUB2 significantly ameliorated neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration in both ALS and aged mouse models. This study establishes OTUB2 as a critical regulator of cGAS-STING signalling and a potential therapeutic target for neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.

title: Perception of tones versus tone streams under random multi-tone masking and its representation in auditory cortex
abstract: When repeated tones are presented among random masker tones, their perceptual organization is often variable. In some trials, they cannot be segregated from the masker tones. In other trials, often with a delay, they form coherent streams, segregated from the masker tones. A strong awareness-related negativity is evoked by each segregated tone of the stream in auditory cortex. A similar negative-going response has been observed when subtle, isolated tones are detected versus missed, raising the question of whether target tones that do not form a stream under informational masking are still perceived or not. Here a paradigm is introduced to probe this question while activity in auditory cortex was recorded with magnetoencephalography. Human listeners (13 female, 8 male) were instructed to indicate when they detected an isochronous stream of tones under multi-tone masking while listening to the stimulus. Thereafter, they indicated if a cue tone, presented subsequently to each trial, was comprised in the target and masker combination. Results confirmed that target tones could still be perceived in the subset of trials where they did not form a coherent stream, but the detectability in the cued frequency report was higher for tones forming a stream. A prominent awareness-related negativity was only observed when the tones formed a stream, suggesting that this response reflects the perceptual organization of the tones into streams and beyond the pure perception of the tones themselves. We speculate that the perceptual organization into a stream further enhances the detectability of the tones comprised in the stream. Significance Statement  Tone sequences may form streams that segregate from competing aspects of the auditory scene, a phenomenon considered comparable to visual object grouping. In multi-tone masking, hearing out streams of repeated tones seemingly enhances tone detectability by a degree that makes it difficult to judge whether these tones could at all be perceived if they had not formed a coherent stream. We present a paradigm that allows for probing both, the perception of target-tone frequency and the formation of coherent streams in the same trials. Applying this setup in magnetoencephalography showed that the perceptual organization into a stream is more strongly represented in auditory cortex than the ability to correctly detect a tone frequency within a random tone masker.

title: Microglial NUS1 deficiency drives dopaminergic neurodegeneration through intercellular iron dysregulation in Parkinson's disease models
abstract: The selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta is a defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. NUS1, which encodes neurite outgrowth inhibitor-B receptor (NgBR), was recently identified as a PD risk gene. Here we show that NgBR is highly expressed in microglia, where its deficiency drives progressive PD-like motor deficits and dopaminergic neurodegeneration via the LCN2-SLC22A17 iron-transport axis in mice. NgBR deficiency in mouse and human microglia triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress and PERK-ATF4-NUPR1 signaling, which preferentially induces LCN2-mediated iron efflux over cytokine release. Subsequently, microglia-derived iron-loaded Holo-LCN2, but not iron-free Apo-LCN2, is internalized by SLC22A17, a receptor highly expressed in dopaminergic neurons, leading to iron overload and ferroptosis. Pharmacological inhibition of LCN2-SLC22A17 axis or ferroptosis alleviated dopaminergic neuron loss and PD-like symptoms caused by microglial NgBR deficiency in vitro and in vivo. Our findings identify disrupted intercellular iron homeostasis as a pathological driver of PD and highlight the LCN2-SLC22A17 axis as a potential therapeutic target.

title: The neurobiology of menopause: Implications for brain aging and Alzheimer's risk
abstract: A growing body of evidence implicates the menopausal transition as a neurobiological inflection point in women's brain aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD) vulnerability. Menopause is a midlife neuroendocrine transition characterized by a decline in sex steroid hormones and widespread systemic effects. The brain is not a passive recipient of ovarian hormones but an active endocrine-sensing organ. Menopause, however, does not act in isolation: the ovarian-brain axis is established embryonically, activated at puberty, remodeled during pregnancy and postpartum, and reconfigured during the menopausal transition, with implications for later-life brain aging. This review places menopause within a lifespan neuroendocrine framework, examining mechanisms by which the transition may influence the brain, including altered hormone signaling, bioenergetics, synaptic plasticity, neurovascular function, inflammation, and AD-related pathology. It then reviews evidence linking menopausal timing to neurobiological and AD vulnerability, discusses estrogen therapy, and considers menopause as a biologically plausible window for risk stratification and prevention.

title: KCNH1 variants associated with neurodevelopmental disorders exhibit prominent gain of function
abstract: Pathogenic variants in KCNH1, encoding the human ether-á-go-go voltage-gated potassium channel (EAG1, KV10.1), are associated with the neurodevelopmental disorders Temple-Baraitser syndrome (TBS), Zimmermann-Laband syndrome (ZLS), epileptic encephalopathy, and other undefined neurodevelopmental disorders. Investigating the functional consequences of KCNH1 variants can provide information about molecular and cellular pathophysiological mechanisms and help guide therapeutic directions. In this study, we determined the functional properties of 26 disease-associated KCNH1 variants including three recurrent and six that were previously unpublished. Findings were compared to the wildtype (WT) channel along with six rare population variants. Our approach used automated patch clamp recording of heterologously expressed KCNH1 variants in both the homozygous state (variant alone) and the clinically-relevant heterozygous state (variant co-expressed with WT channels). We also examined the impact of alternative splice isoforms on functional consequences of specific variants. We demonstrated that the majority of disease-associated KCNH1 variants exhibit features consistent with gain-of-function including hyperpolarized voltage-dependence of activation, accelerated activation kinetics, or both that promote hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential. By contrast, one unique variant discovered previously in an autism cohort had a depolarized voltage-dependence of activation and was associated with a depolarized resting potential in cells. Pharmacological testing of KCNH1 variants demonstrated differences in potency for channel block by imipramine and an investigational non-selective potassium channel blocker (LY97241) for specific variants. Collectively, our findings support gain-of-function as the most common, albeit not exclusive, molecular mechanism underlying KCNH1-related disorders and suggest opportunities for potential therapeutic drug repurposing strategies for these conditions.

title: One-shot learning of paired association navigation with biologically plausible schemas
abstract: After learning a multiple paired-association (MPA) navigation task, rodents can rapidly learn new cue-location associations after a single exposure, a phenomenon proposed to be facilitated by cognitive schemas. However, it remains unclear what schemas support this behavior and how they could be implemented in biological neural circuits. Here, we identify a set of schemas sufficient for gradual then one-shot paired-association navigation, and implement them in a fully neural agent using biologically plausible plasticity rules. The agent gradually acquires a low-dimensional spatial metric representation using a path-integration based temporal-difference error, enabling self-localization across different environments. It also contains a memory network that forms one-shot associations between sensory cues and goal locations, implemented using reward-modulated exploratory Hebbian (EH) plasticity. A third network performs vector subtraction between the agent's current and goal location to compute goal-directed actions. Supplementing these schemas with an actor-critic enables one-shot navigation past obstacles. Lastly, learning a working-memory gating mechanism using the temporal-difference error enables one-shot learning even with brief cue and distractor presentation. The model reproduces key behavioral features of rodent learning in the MPA task and generates testable predictions about the neural mechanisms underlying schema-based one-shot learning. Significance Statement  Schema-dependent learning is exemplified by better recall of a lecture when one already has a schema for understanding. A rodent navigation task showing a shift from slow to rapid learning has been proposed to reflect such schema use, yet how schemas are neurally implemented and enable faster learning is poorly understood. We clarify this gap in this computational study by describing several schemas and implement them as neural networks with biologically plausible learning rules. Composing them into an agent reproduces schema-dependent rodent learning behavior. Because schemas also shape self beliefs, clarifying their neural basis has implications for psychopathology. At the same time, understanding how biological schemas support rapid learning may inform advances in machine learning.

title: Object detection through dynamic motor-sensory convergence in freely moving rats
abstract: To detect objects in natural environments, animals must coordinate movement and sensation. This process unfolds dynamically, as perceivers actively shape sensory input through ongoing motor actions in a closed loop. In this study, we use precise tracking of behavioral kinematics to investigate the initial phase of object interaction, asking: what motor-sensory strategies support object detection during natural approach? Using high-speed videography and advanced tracking tools, we tracked whisker and head dynamics as male rats approached and contacted objects. We found that whisker-object interactions converged toward a distinct ratio between changes in whisker angle and curvature, denoted [Formula: see text] In a motor-sensory phase plane this ratio appears as a line, reflecting a regime in which small motor adjustments produce large curvature changes during contact. This motor-sensory ratio cannot stabilize during free-air whisking and thus can serve as a signature for object presence. Rats gradually converged toward this object-dependent mechanical signature across contacts, and proximity to [Formula: see text] predicted subsequent head movements and the termination of object approach. Convergence to [Formula: see text] was invariant to object shape and texture and to whisker's length. Moreover, touch-induced pumps both signaled and reinforced convergence. The results suggest that rats use successful convergence to this object-dependent motor-sensory contingency as a signature of object presence. Object detection thus emerges as a closed-loop dynamical process in which action, mechanics, and sensation jointly shape perceptual inference. Significance Statement  How does a rat know it is touching an object with its moving whiskers? We trained freely moving rats to discriminate objects while tracking whisker kinematics at high resolution. We found that the detection phase involved whisker-object interactions that converged toward a distinct ratio between changes in whisker angle and curvature. This ratio can arise mechanically only when whiskers contact an external object, making its attainment a reliable indication of object presence. During object approach, rats steered their exploratory movements to seek this motor-sensory contingency, marking the transition to focused exploration or disengagement. These findings reveal a dynamical, closed-loop mechanism for object detection in freely moving rats.

title: Internet Intervention for Functional Seizures: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract:
This randomized clinical trial investigates if a self-guided internet-based intervention reduces seizure frequency compared with standard care in adults with functional seizures.

Key Points Question Does a self-guided internet-based intervention reduce seizure frequency compared with standard care in adults with functional seizures? Findings In this 3-arm randomized clinical trial of 107 adults with functional seizures, a self-guided internet-based intervention produced significantly greater reductions in monthly seizure frequency than standard care at 6 weeks, 6 months, and 12 months after randomization, with sustained improvements in anxiety. Reductions in seizure frequency in the therapist-guided arm compared with standard care did not reach statistical significance; direct comparison between the 2 active arms was not statistically significant. Meaning Results suggest that a brief, self-guided internet-based intervention offers a scalable option for reducing seizure frequency in adults with functional seizures who cannot access specialist psychological care, with self-guided delivery showing comparable efficacy with therapist-guided delivery.

Importance Functional seizures (FS) are a common and disabling presentation in neurology clinics, but evidence-based treatments are difficult to access in Australia and in many regions globally. A brief, scalable, internet-delivered intervention could narrow this treatment gap. Objective To compare a self-guided and a therapist-guided internet-based intervention for FS, each delivered alongside standard care, with standard care alone. Design, Setting, and Participants This was a 3-arm, parallel, randomized clinical trial conducted between February 2022 and April 2024, with follow-up through to 12 months after randomization. The location was a specialist outpatient clinic in Melbourne, Australia. Included were adults (≥18 years) with a documented diagnosis of FS confirmed by video electroencephalogram monitoring and at least 4 seizures per month, excluding comorbid active epilepsy. Interventions Participants were randomized 1:1:1 to a self-guided internet-based intervention plus standard care, therapist-guided internet-based intervention plus standard care, or standard care alone. Re-PROGRAM is an internet-based intervention developed for FS, comprising 5 structured sessions integrating lifestyle factors, seizure management techniques, and elements of cognitive behavioral, acceptance and commitment, and dialectical behavior therapy. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was monthly seizure frequency at 6 weeks, 6 months, and 12 months after randomization, recorded by daily prospective seizure diary, with retrospective estimates used for incomplete records. Secondary outcomes included depression, anxiety, quality of life, psychosocial functioning, and somatic symptoms. Results Of 220 individuals screened for eligibility, 107 (mean [SD] age 36.0 [12.4] years; 89 female [83%]) were randomized. Of these participants, 96 contributed to the full analysis set (29 self-guided, 34 therapist-guided, 33 standard care). The self-guided arm produced significantly greater overall reductions in monthly seizure frequency than standard care (rate ratio [RR], 0.35; 95% CI, 0.18-0.69; Holm-Bonferroni [HB] method P = .006), with sustained between-group effects at 6 weeks (RR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.18-0.76; HB P = .02), 6 months (RR, 0.31; 95% CI, 0.12-0.78; HB P = .04), and 12 months (RR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.16-0.78; HB P = .03). The self-guided arm also showed greater improvements in anxiety than standard care at all 3 time points and in depression and mental quality of life at 1 or more time points. The therapist-guided arm showed greater improvement in anxiety at 6 months, but reductions in seizure frequency did not reach statistical significance. Direct comparison between the 2 active arms showed no significant difference in seizure reduction (RR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.33-1.36). Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness of the primary findings. No adverse events occurred in any arm. Conclusions and Relevance Results of this randomized clinical trial show that in adults with FS, a self-guided internet-based intervention reduced seizure frequency and improved anxiety relative to standard care, offering a scalable option for patients unable to access specialist psychological care. Trial Registration Identifier: ACTRN12622000262707

title: Fear conditioning research through the lens of meta-analyses: A systematic methodological review
abstract: Meta-analyses have become foundational tools for evidence synthesis and are receiving increasing attention across research disciplines, including fear conditioning - a central paradigm in affective, behavioral, and clinical neuroscience and psychology - where the number of meta-analyses has notably increased in recent years. However, substantial methodological heterogeneity among these meta-analyses complicates their interpretation and comparability. This review systematically summarizes existing meta-analyses in fear conditioning (n = 26), with particular emphasis on methodological choices and reporting standards. Our findings indicate substantial variability in reporting practices, particularly regarding review processes, applied methodological models, and the operationalization of certain variables, which may challenge reproducibility and interpretability. Most meta-analyses used aggregate data and random-effects models, while moderator analyses were frequently conducted but yielded few significant moderators. Outcome measures were frequently aggregated (e.g., skin conductance, startle responses, ratings) without a clear theoretical rationale. We discuss the implications of moderator analyses, the limited attention to temporal dynamics, and the aggregation of diverse outcome measures. We argue that the field would benefit from more precise reporting, theory-driven analytical decisions, and increased data sharing at both the primary and meta-analytic levels. Such improvements would facilitate individual participant data meta-analyses, which preserve within-study variability, enhance moderator analyses, and address challenges inherent to aggregate-level data synthesis. Establishing and expanding shared infrastructures represents a necessary step toward cumulative, reproducible, and clinically informative work in the future.

title: Effectiveness of Hippotherapy in Balance Rehabilitation for Stroke Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stroke frequently leads to balance and mobility impairments, significantly affecting patients' independence and quality of life. Hippotherapy, a therapy involving horse-based movements, has gained attention as a potential intervention for balance rehabilitation.

OBJECTIVES: This study evaluates the effectiveness of hippotherapy in improving balance and mobility in stroke patients.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following PRISMA guidelines through PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Physiotherapy Evidence Database for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing hippotherapy's effects on balance in adult stroke patients (Prospero registration number: CRD42024552688). Effect sizes were pooled using RevMan software.

RESULTS: Ten RCTs met the inclusion criteria, with seven included in the meta-analysis (n = 389 participants). Hippotherapy significantly improved balance outcomes compared to conventional exercise programs, as measured by the Berg Balance Scale (BBS) (mean difference [MD] =1.72; 95% confidence interval [CI] [1.38, 2.07], P < 0.00001) and the timed up and go (TUG) test (MD = -2.97 s; 95% CI [-4.83, -1.11], P = 0.002). Exploratory subgroup analysis showed no statistically significant difference between mechanical and real-horse hippotherapy (P = 0.64).

CONCLUSIONS: Stroke patients may benefit from hippotherapy as an effective adjunct to conventional rehabilitation. Hippotherapy significantly improves balance and functional mobility, as demonstrated by improvements in the BBS and TUG test. However, evidence regarding quality of life and psychological outcomes remains limited and inconclusive, underscoring the need for further high-quality RCTs.

title: The effect of virtual reality glasses used during chest tube removal following open-heart surgery on pain and hemodynamic parameters: a randomized controlled trial
abstract:
Background Chest tube removal (CTR) following open-heart surgery is a painful procedure that may adversely affect patients’ hemodynamic parameters. Purpose This study aimed to determine the effect of virtual reality glasses (VRG) used during chest tube removal after open-heart surgery on pain levels and hemodynamic parameters. Methods This prospective, two-arm (1:1), randomized controlled trial included 82 patients undergoing open-heart surgery. Patients in the VRG group ( n = 41) were exposed to relaxing forest-walk-themed virtual reality content starting five minutes before CTR and continuing for five minutes after the procedure. The control group ( n = 41) received routine care without any additional intervention. Pain levels were assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), and hemodynamic parameters—systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), and peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO₂)—were recorded before CTR, immediately after, and at 5, 15, and 30 min post-procedure. Results A significant group × time interaction was observed for pain ( p = 0.003). After adjustment for baseline pain and multiple comparisons, pain was significantly lower in the VRG group than in the control group immediately after CTR (adjusted mean difference [VRG − Control]: −1.26, 95% CI: −1.85 to − 0.68; adjusted p < 0.001), whereas no significant between-group differences were observed at 5, 15, or 30 min. A significant group × time interaction was also observed for SpO₂ ( p < 0.001), with significantly higher SpO₂ in the VRG group immediately after CTR (adjusted mean difference: 2.70, 95% CI: 1.88 to 3.53; adjusted p < 0.001). No significant group × time interactions were observed for SBP, DBP, HR, or RR. Conclusion VRG use during CTR was associated with lower pain immediately after the procedure and higher SpO₂ immediately after CTR. No significant effects were observed for SBP, DBP, HR, or RR. These findings suggest that VRG may be a useful non-pharmacological adjunct for short-term pain management during CTR following open-heart surgery. Further studies are needed to confirm its effects on oxygenation and other hemodynamic parameters. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT05585853 ) first submitted on October 12, 2022, and first posted on October 19, 2022. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12872-026-06778-6 .

Introduction Open-heart surgery is a major surgical procedure widely used in the treatment of cardiovascular diseases. Because this procedure requires advanced techniques, such as extensive tissue dissection and cardiopulmonary bypass, the recovery process can be prolonged and challenging [ 1 , 2 ]. Postoperatively, pain associated with incision sites, as well as pain caused by invasive chest tubes (CTs) placed to prevent complications, represents a significant clinical concern. In particular, the pain experienced during the removal of chest tubes can lead to haemodynamic instability in patients [ 1 , 3 , 4 ]. The primary purpose of using a chest tube (CT) in patients following open-heart surgery is to ensure the drainage of blood, air, and fluid accumulated in the chest cavity [ 1 , 3 , 5 ]. CTs are typically removed when drainage is less than 100 mL within the previous 24 h, the lungs are fully expanded, and no air leak is present [ 2 , 3 ]. Although CTs help reduce the risk of complications and accelerate postoperative recovery, their adhesion to surrounding tissues after placement can cause acute and severe pain. Consequently, the routine removal of CTs is a painful procedure that may trigger significant stress responses in patients [ 2 , 3 , 6 , 7 ]. In individuals with high cardiovascular sensitivity, such as those who have undergone cardiac surgery, pain can initiate a neuroendocrine response that negatively affects haemodynamic parameters, including heart rate (HR), systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and respiratory rate (RR) [ 8 ]. Therefore, effective pain management prior to chest tube removal (CTR) following cardiac surgery is of critical importance for enhancing patient comfort and reducing the risk of complications [ 4 , 8 , 9 ]. During CTR, mediators such as bradykinin, kinins, and histamine are released as part of the inflammatory response, lowering the pain transmission threshold. This process can lead to peripheral sensitization and hyperalgesia, resulting in increased pain sensitivity beyond normal tolerance and a heightened perception of pain [ 7 , 10 , 11 ]. In addition to the direct effects of pain, sympathetic nervous system activity increases, leading to elevations in HR, SBP, DBP, and RR, while peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO₂) may decrease [ 1 , 8 , 9 ]. Furthermore, patients’ fear of experiencing pain prior to the procedure can exacerbate pain levels through nociceptive responses mediated by the limbic system. Therefore, identifying effective strategies to manage pain associated with CTR during the postoperative period is essential for reducing cardiac workload and improving long-term outcomes [ 3 , 10 , 12 ]. Non-pharmacological methods are increasingly used for pain management during CTR following cardiac surgery [ 1 , 8 ], including virtual reality glasses (VRG) [ 1 , 2 , 9 , 13 ]. VRG provides an interactive audiovisual environment that may reduce pain perception through distraction [ 1 , 5 ]. Several individual studies have reported reductions in pain associated with VRG use [ 5 , 9 , 13 , 14 ]; however, the overall evidence remains inconsistent. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Micheluzzi et al. found no statistically significant effect of VR on pain compared with standard care [ 15 ]. Previous studies have reported lower pain levels during and after CTR with VRG use [ 1 , 2 ], while another study reported differences in SBP, DBP, HR, and RR following CTR [ 9 ]. Although previous studies have investigated the effects of VRG on pain during CTR following open-heart surgery [ 1 , 2 , 9 ], evidence regarding its effects on pain and physiological parameters assessed at multiple time points remains limited. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the effect of VRG used during CTR following open-heart surgery on pain and physiological parameters. We hypothesized that, compared with routine care, VRG use during CTR would reduce pain intensity and favorably affect physiological parameters, including systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and SpO₂. Method Aim and study design This prospective, parallel-group, two-arm (1:1) randomized controlled trial aimed to evaluate the effect of virtual reality glasses (VRG) applied during chest tube removal (CTR) following open-heart surgery on postoperative pain and hemodynamic parameters (SBP, DBP, HR, RR, and SpO₂). This randomized controlled trial was reported in accordance with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) guidelines [ 16 ]. The study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT05585853 ) and completed without protocol modifications. The study protocol was prospectively registered with ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT05585853 ) in 2022. The ethical approval process took longer than initially anticipated and was completed in July 2023. Following ethical approval, initiation of participant recruitment was delayed due to clinical scheduling considerations and the availability of eligible patients undergoing open-heart surgery. Participant recruitment therefore commenced in January 2025. No protocol modifications were made during the study. The CONSORT flow diagram is presented in Fig. 1 . Primary and secondary objectives The primary objective of this study was to determine the effect of VRG use during chest tube removal on pain intensity in patients undergoing open-heart surgery. The secondary objective was to determine the effect of VRG use on physiological parameters, including systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), and peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO₂). Research hypotheses H₁ There is a difference between the VRG group and the control group in terms of pain levels experienced during CTR. H 2 There is a difference between the VRG group and the control group in terms of hemodynamic parameters (SBP, DBP, HR, RR, SpO₂) during CTR. Population and sampling The study sample consisted of 82 patients undergoing open-heart surgery who were hospitalized in the Cardiovascular Surgery Intensive Care Unit of a university hospital in Mersin, Turkey, between January 1, 2025, and August 26, 2025. An a priori power analysis was conducted to determine the required sample size. The study by Guo et al. (2015) was used as a reference [ 17 ]. In that study, the mean Visual Analog Scale (VAS) score following VRG was 2.63 ± 1.27 in the intervention group and 7.64 ± 3.41 in the control group, corresponding to a large standardized effect. To avoid basing the sample-size calculation on this very large observed effect, a more conservative effect size of Cohen’s d = 0.80 was used in the present study [ 18 ]. With a two-sided significance level of 0.05 and 90% statistical power, the minimum required sample size was calculated as 68 participants (34 per group) [ 19 ].
