To allow for potential participant loss and to increase the robustness of the study, the minimum sample size was increased by approximately 20% (68 × 1.20 = 81.6), resulting in a target sample size of 82 participants (41 per group). Sample-size calculations were performed using G*Power software [ 20 ]. Inclusion criteria The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age ≥ 18 years; (2) undergoing elective open-heart surgery; (3) being scheduled for chest tube removal on the second postoperative day; (4) being hemodynamically stable; (5) being alert and cooperative and having sufficient cognitive capacity to understand and follow the study and VRG instructions; (6) being able to communicate in Turkish; (7) having no previous experience of chest tube removal; and (8) providing written informed consent to participate in the study. Exclusion criteria The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) hemodynamic instability; (2) a visual impairment that prevented adequate viewing of or engagement with the VR content; (3) sensitivity, injury, or trauma that prevented the appropriate use of the VRG; and (4) unwillingness to participate in or continue the study. During the study, 87 patients underwent open-heart surgery. Of these, 3 patients declined participation and 2 had an unstable hemodynamic status. Therefore, 5 patients were excluded, and 82 patients were included in the study (Fig. 1 ). Randomization Block randomization was used to allocate the 82 patients to two groups in a 1:1 ratio. The randomization sequence was computer-generated by an independent statistician who was not involved in participant recruitment, intervention delivery, or data collection. Before participant recruitment, a random draw was used to designate Group A as the control group and Group B as the VRG group. Group assignments were placed in sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes and kept by the coordinating investigator (G.A.U.). After admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) following open-heart surgery, patients were assessed for eligibility by the researcher (F.E.Ö.). After eligibility was confirmed and written informed consent was obtained, the next sequentially numbered envelope was used to determine group allocation. Thus, the allocation sequence remained concealed until participant enrollment and assignment. The VRG intervention was administered by a single researcher (F.E.Ö.) according to a standardized protocol. The study included patients undergoing open-heart surgery who were scheduled for CTR on the second postoperative day, were able to speak and understand Turkish, had stable hemodynamic parameters, were aged ≥ 18 years, were alert and cooperative, had undergone elective surgery, had no prior CT experience, had no sensitivity or trauma in the VRG application area, and voluntarily agreed to participate. During the study, 87 patients underwent open-heart surgery. Of these, patients who declined participation ( n = 3), had unstable hemodynamic status ( n = 2), or did not meet the inclusion criteria were excluded. A total of 5 patients were excluded (Fig. 1 ). Blinding Due to the nature of the intervention, participants and the researcher who administered the VRG intervention and collected the outcome data (F.E.Ö.) could not be blinded to group allocation. After completion of data collection, the dataset was coded using group labels (A and B) by an independent researcher (T.Ç.Y.). Statistical analyses were subsequently performed by an independent statistician who was blinded to the identity of the treatment groups. Data collection tools The “Demographic Information Form,” “Visual Analog Scale,” and “Hemodynamic Parameters Monitoring Form” were used for data collection. Descriptive characteristics form The Descriptive Characteristics Form was developed in line with the study aims and hypotheses, based on relevant literature [ 8 , 13 , 21 , 22 ]. It consists of six items assessing patients’ sociodemographic characteristics (age, gender, marital status, educational level) and surgical characteristics (diagnosis and type of surgery). Visual analog scale (VAS) The VAS is a reliable and widely used tool consisting of a 10-cm line with endpoints labeled “no pain” (0 cm) and “maximum pain” (10 cm). Participants mark a point on the line corresponding to their pain level, which is then measured in centimeters to obtain a numerical value [ 23 , 24 ]. Hemodynamic parameters monitoring form This form records SBP, DBP, HR, RR, and SpO₂ values in both groups at the following time points: 5 min before CTR, immediately after CTR, and at 5, 15, and 30 min after CTR. Data collection As part of routine postoperative care, all patients received tramadol (100 mg) by intravenous infusion. The infusion was initiated approximately 30 min before awakening and continued at a rate of 5 mg/h until discharge from the intensive care unit. No additional analgesic medication was administered specifically for chest tube removal in either group. To standardize the procedure and minimize operator-related variability, all chest tubes were removed by the same physician using the same routine clinical procedure. Before CTR, all patients completed the “Descriptive Characteristics Form,” VAS, and the Hemodynamic Parameters Monitoring Form. Five minutes before CTR, patients in the VRG group were fitted with a virtual reality device (VR Box Virtual Reality Headset 3D VR Glasses V2.0, 2020 model) connected to an Android smartphone (Lenovo P2a42) while in the semi-Fowler position. title: Music-Based Intervention in Postoperative Lung Transplant Care: A Feasibility Study
abstract: Music-based interventions may support recovery in medical and surgical settings; however, their implementation during the immediate postoperative period following lung transplantation remains understudied. This single-center randomized feasibility study examined whether a structured music-based intervention delivered by board-certified music therapists could be implemented at clinically meaningful postoperative recovery milestones and explored preliminary trends in pain, anxiety, medication use, sleep, and length of stay. Twenty-nine adult lung transplant recipients (experimental n = 17, control n = 12) were enrolled between September 2021 and September 2023. Participants in the intervention group received music-based intervention sessions during spontaneous awakening trials, 24-48 hr following extubation, and within 72 hr of transfer from the intensive care unit to a step-down unit. Intervention components included patient-preferred live music, music-assisted relaxation, and optional receptive or active music engagement tailored to patient status. Intervention delivery was feasible across all three postoperative milestones, although challenges related to recruitment, retention, sleep measurement, and intervention standardization were identified. Exploratory analyses suggested lower observed pain scores and lower median acetaminophen use in the intervention group compared to standard care; however, no outcomes reached statistical significance. Anxiety outcomes did not differ between groups, and sleep measurement using consumer-grade wearable devices was not feasible. These findings support the feasibility of music-based interventions during postoperative lung transplant recovery and provide guidance for the design of future adequately powered trials using refined outcome measures, milestone-based intervention delivery, and improved implementation strategies.

title: Predictors and clinical outcomes of pretreatment length in an outpatient Veterans Affairs dialectical behavior therapy program
abstract:
Objective: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) pre-treatment is a standard component of DBT designed to prepare patients for treatment, identify treatment goals, and build commitment. Examination of DBT pre-treatment is of particular importance in naturalistic clinical settings, where clinical resources are limited, such as Veterans Affairs Medical Centers (VAMC), where DBT has become more widespread. Methods: Eligible veterans ( n = 89) were enrolled in an outpatient DBT program at a midwestern VAMC. Thirteen potential predictors (spanning demographic, healthcare utilization, and clinical factors) of DBT pre-treatment length, operationalized as pre-treatment duration and number of pre-treatment sessions, were examined. Partial least squares regression was used to identify latent components. The relationship between pre-treatment length and treatment outcomes was also examined. Results: A significant one-component solution explained 29.10% of the variance in pre-treatment duration. Borderline personality disorder symptoms, past suicide attempts, past inpatient days, and past psychiatric ER admissions were positively associated with pre-treatment duration. A significant one-component solution, consisting of the same predictors, with the exception of past suicide attempts, and the addition of race, sex, and psychiatric comorbidity, explained 18.10% of the variance in number of pre-treatment sessions. Neither pre-treatment duration nor number of pre-treatment sessions was related to treatment attendance, completion, or symptom severity. Conclusions: Indicators of clinical severity and complexity predict number of days and sessions spent in DBT pre-treatment. Non-White race, male sex, and psychiatric comorbidity predict greater number of DBT pre-treatment sessions. Deviation from the standard four session pre-treatment approach may be needed for some veterans.

Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is a multicomponent treatment originally designed for individuals at high risk for suicide ( Linehan et al., 1991 ) as well as individuals with borderline personality disorder (BPD; Linehan, 1993 ). Since the introduction of DBT, it has been widely implemented across various treatment settings (e.g., DeCou et al., 2019 ; Kliem et al., 2010 ). Despite the widespread dissemination, portions of the treatment protocol remain understudied. Known collectively as “full model”, or “comprehensive” DBT, the multi-modal treatment consists of individual therapy, skills group, phone coaching, and therapist consultation team ( Linehan, 1993 ). Before beginning comprehensive treatment, patients enter a pre-treatment period designed to prepare patients for DBT and assess the appropriateness of the DBT modality. Despite pre-treatment constituting a formal and necessary component of DBT, little empirical research has been conducted examining the DBT pre-treatment period. The pre-treatment stage of DBT was first outlined in Linehan’s treatment manual ( Linehan, 1993 ) where she described “contracting strategies” for beginning DBT. There are five central goals of DBT pre-treatment: 1) identifying treatment goals; 2) determining if DBT is an appropriate treatment modality; 3) assessing suicidal behavior and nonsuicidal self-harm; 4) establishing and building commitment for treatment/reducing life-threatening behaviors; and 5) cultivating a strong therapeutic rapport ( Coyle et al., 2019 ). More succinctly, the aim of pre-treatment is to elicit the patient’s agreement to the specified treatment plan and treatment targets as well as optimize the patient’s commitment to this plan ( Swenson, 2016 ). Thus, pre-treatment builds the foundation for comprehensive treatment. Elucidating factors related to length of pre-treatment would provide clinicians with a framework for clinical decisions about if and when to extend pre-treatment. Additionally, understanding how length of pre-treatment impacts treatment outcomes would provide clinicians with important information regarding potential consequences of brief or prolonged pre-treatment. Furthermore, while pre-treatment is an essential and unique component of DBT, the term “pre-treatment” can be interpreted, from a resource management or administrative perspective, as indicating a patient is not yet receiving needed treatment. Critically, this perception can negatively impact access-to-care metrics which can cause downstream consequences for the degree to which the pre-treatment period is recognized and prioritized from an institutional standpoint. Thus, empirical research supporting the necessity of this component and elucidating empirically backed guidelines for the ideal duration of pre-treatment, informed by patient characteristics, is sorely needed. A specified portion of treatment focused on assessing life-threatening behaviors and building rapport is of critical importance given DBT targets individuals with complex presentations and high-risk behaviors (e.g., McCauley et al., 2018 ; DeCou et al., 2019 ). Additionally, pre-treatment provides clinicians with dedicated time to obtain and strengthen commitment utilizing commitment strategies which are a central component of DBT ( Linehan, 1993 ; Koerner, 2011 ). To our knowledge, there is no empirical research specifically examining the pre-treatment stage. However, broader DBT research can provide some insight into DBT’s effectiveness at achieving the chief goals of pre-treatment. For example, in a study comparing DBT to community treatment, DBT therapists reported achieving alignment in treatment goals earlier in treatment as well as greater treatment alliance ( Bedics et al., 2015 ). These findings suggest that the pre-treatment stage may provide a strong foundation for facilitating rapport early on in treatment—compared to other modalities without this specific treatment period. The recommended length of DBT pre-treatment is approximately 4 weekly sessions ( Swenson, 2016 ). However, it is currently unknown if there is an optimal dose of pre-treatment. While sufficient time in pre-treatment is likely advantageous, as it provides ample time to complete pre-treatment goals, it is possible that prolonged pre-treatment may have negative ramifications. For example, extending pre-treatment for individuals who are reluctant or avoidant to begin skills group may unintentionally reinforce avoidance by allowing the patient to continue in their preferred treatment modality (i.e., individual therapy only). Similarly, prolonged pre-treatment delays the start of comprehensive DBT treatment, which can be iatrogenic to patients who warrant the full model treatment, as well as tax provider resources. For naturalist treatment settings, particularly community-based settings, such as Veterans Health Administration, conserving provider resources needed to be able to meet the mental health treatment needs of a large population is vital. Given the high rates of suicidal behaviors among veteran populations (Veteran Affairs Report, 2024), DBT has become more widespread in these clinical settings. Currently, empirical evidence to inform pre-treatment clinical decision making within DBT programs in VA settings is lacking. To address this, the sample for the current study is drawn from a naturalistic DBT program in a Veteran Health Administration setting. Importantly, DBT has been implemented in numerous veteran samples (e.g., Goodman et al., 2016 ; Koons et al., 2001 ). Evidence suggests DBT reduces future mental health service utilization, including reducing the number and length of hospitalizations, among veterans ( Meyers et al., 2014 ). Thus, the tradeoff between longer pre-treatment, and thus longer overall treatment, may be worth the up-front time and resources—if effective DBT reduces future resource utilization. In sum, additional research is needed to determine the optimal length of DBT pre-treatment, however, it is likely that optimal length is person-dependent and some common factors may influence pre-treatment length. Although there is no existing literature examining predictors of DBT pre-treatment length, specifically, broader treatment/adherence literature can provide insight into what factors may influence pre-treatment length. For example, it is well-established that a myriad of demographic factors (i.e., age, sex, education level) impact treatment adherence and dropout ( Cavicchioli et al., 2021 ; Landes et al., 2016 ; Perroud et al., 2010 ; Kröger et al., 2013 ; Cawood et al., 2025 ). Additionally, there is empirical evidence suggesting psychological comorbidity ( Cavicchioli et al., 2021 ; Rüsch et al., 2008 ; Kröger et al., 2013 ; Wnuk et al., 2013 ; i Farrés et al., 2018 ) and greater affective difficulties ( Cavicchioli et al., 2021 ; Landes et al., 2016 ; Doyle et al., 2023 ) are related to greater likelihood of DBT treatment dropout. Similarly, extant research suggests history of suicide attempts is related to treatment dropout in DBT; however, the direction of this relationship is unclear ( Rüsch et al., 2008 ; Wnuk et al., 2013 ). In addition to these factors, as clinical complexity has the potential to impact pre-treatment length, we considered relevant variables representing clinical complexity for veteran populations, such as military sexual trauma (MST) and service connection. History of sexual trauma is common among patients in DBT programs ( Harned et al., 2010 ), and veterans report high rates of MST, with a prevalence of over 40% among females ( Nichter et al., 2022 ). While explicit treatment of trauma-related symptoms typically occurs in later stages of DBT, after targeting life-threatening and therapy-interfering behaviors ( Linehan, 1993 ), the existence of MST may still influence pre-treatment length through avenues such as contributing to heightened emotion dysregulation or impacting time spent to build rapport. In addition to MST, another measure of clinical complexity among veterans engaged in VA Healthcare Systems is a service connection rating, which rates the percentage of disability a veteran has due to their military service, wherein a higher rating indicates more severe impairment due to their diagnoses. These percentages are based on clinical interview by independent licensed clinicians assessing level of impairment. For our study, we looked at service connection rating broadly, as well as for mental health conditions specifically, as higher degree of impairment may impact pre-treatment length wherein more severely impaired veterans may require more time to identify goals, build rapport, and/or safety plan. Taken together, while predictors of DBT pre-treatment length have not been previously examined, it is reasonable to hypothesize, based on the broader treatment literature, that several demographic and clinical factors play a role in the length of DBT pre-treatment. Given the lack of empirical research examining DBT pre-treatment, many questions remain unanswered. Namely, are certain factors related to length of DBT pre-treatment? And does length of DBT pre-treatment impact treatment outcomes such as symptom change and likelihood of completing DBT? The current study aimed to address these questions. First, we aimed to examine potential predictors of length of pre-treatment. Length of pre-treatment was quantified using two different metrics: 1) duration of pre-treatment, in days; and 2) number of pre-treatment sessions. Regarding predictors, we examined age, sex assigned at birth, race, education, service connection, mental health service connection, history of MST, BPD symptoms, BPD diagnosis, number of psychiatric diagnoses, history of suicide attempt, number of inpatient days, and psychiatric emergency room visits as potential predictors of length of pre-treatment. Given the exploratory nature of this work, we choose to include a wide range of potential predictors with theoretical and/or empirical support suggesting their potential impact on length of pre-treatment. While there is limited extant literature to base specific hypotheses on, we broadly hypothesized that indicators of greater clinical severity (i.e., greater BPD symptoms, BPD diagnosis, higher comorbidity, history of military sexual trauma) as well as risk-related variables (i.e., significant history of suicide attempt, greater inpatient days, more psychiatric emergency room visits) would be related to longer pre-treatment. We did not make specific hypotheses regarding the potential direction of the relationship between demographic variables and length of DBT pre-treatment. Second, to explore the potential impact of pre-treatment length, we examined the relationship between DBT pre-treatment length and treatment outcomes, specifically: 1) treatment completion; 2) treatment attendance; and 3) change in BPD symptoms. Methods Participants Participants were eligible veterans at a midwestern Veterans Affair Healthcare System enrolled in an outpatient DBT program between July 2007 and October 2016. Participants were deemed eligible if: 1) they exhibited clinically significant BPD symptoms based on a structured clinical screener and 2) they had a recent suicide attempt, recent nonsuicidal self-injury, and/or recent psychiatric hospitalization (recent was defined as ≤ 1 year). When the DBT program was first initiated some veterans were enrolled in individual and group therapy concurrently. However, as the program progressed, fidelity to the comprehensive DBT model was prioritized, and veterans did not begin group therapy until completing pre-treatment. Individuals were excluded if they started DBT skills group before or concurrently with individual therapy as this indicated they did not complete a pre-treatment period. Of the 145 veterans who presented to the DBT program for evaluation, 115 were eligible and enrolled into treatment (see Cawood et al., 2025 for information on full sample). One hundred and eight of these veterans participated in pre-treatment and had available pre-treatment data. Nineteen individuals were missing data on at least one predictor variable, resulting in a final sample size of 89 participants. Procedures Study measures were collected as part of program evaluation for a comprehensive DBT program. Veterans who were referred to the DBT program were screened using the McLean Screening Instrument (MSI-BPD; Zanarini et al., 2003 ) to determine their eligibility. Eligible veterans were then assigned to an individual therapist to begin pre-treatment. After completing pre-treatment veterans entered comprehensive DBT treatment (i.e., weekly individual therapy, weekly DBT skills group, as needed phone coaching (within VA business hours), and DBT consultation team for providers) for a period of at least 6 months—that could be extended to a year. Of note, while careful efforts were taken to maximize fidelity to the DBT model, some deviations, based on system concerns and access to care, were deemed necessary. title: Predicting Depression Risk in Early Intervention in Psychosis Services: A Machine Learning Study Utilising Electronic Health Records and Natural Language Processing
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Depression is prevalent in early psychosis and associated with poorer functional outcomes and suicide risk. Early identification of depression risk is critical to inform targeted interventions. This study aimed to develop models to predict depression risk using electronic health records (EHRs) from patients accepted into South London and Maudsley (SLaM) Early Intervention in Psychosis Services.

METHODS: EHRs from 3,559 patients were analysed using a nested cross-validated machine learning framework. Structured sociodemographic, medication, and 66 natural language processing (NLP)-derived clinical note variables were used to train support vector regressors (SVRs) and classifiers (SVCs) to predict future changes in depressive symptoms, antidepressant prescriptions (AD0-6m) and treatment escalation for depression (TE0-6m). Model performance was generalised in out-of-cross-validation samples and across SLaM boroughs. Clustering analyses were also conducted to identify depressive symptom trajectories.

RESULTS: SVRs accurately predicted changes in depressive symptom scores over the first year following referral, with R² ranging 58.5%-72.1%. SVCs predicted AD0-6m with a balanced accuracy (BAC) of 65.6% and TE0-6m with a BAC of 68.0%. Patients with deteriorating trajectories were most likely to receive antidepressants, had higher antipsychotic treatment attempts and a psychotic-affective mixed presentation of symptoms. Model performance remained robust across clusters, and poor-prognosis clusters were captured in the +TE0-6m outcome.

CONCLUSION: This study provides an initial demonstration that predictive modelling of clinically documented depressive outcomes in EIP services is feasible using routinely collected EHR data. The findings address a major unmet clinical need and mark a critical step toward integrating depression risk prediction into psychiatric practice.

title: Take no risk!-Persistent avoidance after interoceptive fear conditioning
abstract: Maladaptive fear and avoidance of interoceptive threat are central to many anxiety and somatic disorders, often persisting even after exposure therapy and thereby contributing to relapse. While fear conditioning paradigms have mostly focused on avoidance in response to external threats (e.g., electric shocks), less is known about avoidance in response to interoceptive threat. Therefore, the present study investigated fear acquisition of interoceptive threat and subsequent avoidance behavior. Healthy participants (n = 35) underwent a differential fear conditioning paradigm in which one cue (CS+) predicted restricted breathing (US), whereas another (CS-) signaled safety. In the subsequent avoidance phase, participants were informed that they could prevent the US by pressing a button. During the consecutive response prevention phase, the avoidance option was no longer available. Finally, an avoidance test assessed the persistence of avoidance after extinction. No US was delivered during avoidance and response prevention phases. Results suggests that participants successfully learned to discriminate between CS+ and CS-, as reflected in US expectancy, fear ratings, startle eyeblink response and skin conductance responses. Although participants consistently reported greater fear of the CS + than the CS-, differential responding in psychophysiological measures was no longer observed following the introduction of the avoidance option. Participants demonstrated high levels of avoidance to CS+ and CS-, with avoidance persisting even after extinction with response prevention. The findings indicate a "better-safe-than-sorry" strategy despite awareness of threat contingencies. The generalization and persistence of avoidance may contribute to the development and maintenance of anxiety and somatic disorders.

title: An mHealth Stress Management Intervention for Latino Millennial Caregivers: Pilot Feasibility Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
Abstract Background Latino millennial caregivers comprise over one-quarter of millennial family caregivers in the United States. Latino millennial family caregivers face unique challenges due to cultural, structural, and economic burdens that may increase stress and stress-related health effects. These caregivers also report time limitations due to their multiple roles. Technology may be a way to deliver an accessible and flexible intervention to support stress management and emotional regulation in this population. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary outcomes of a culturally tailored mobile health (mHealth) intervention to support stress management and emotional regulation for Latino millennial caregivers. Methods Participants (N=30) were recruited nationally in the United States using a recruitment agency and were randomized to the intervention or waitlist control groups. The 4-week fully automated intervention included daily mindfulness exercises and journaling prompts delivered via a custom mHealth platform. The waitlist control group received a written handout with mindfulness, journaling, and support information. Feasibility data, including recruitment and retention rates and intervention adherence, and postintervention acceptability surveys were collected. Study outcome measures were collected electronically at baseline and 2, 4, and 6 weeks. Primary outcomes included caregiver burden and perceived stress, and secondary outcomes included well-being, informational support, and emotional support. Feasibility and acceptability data were analyzed descriptively alongside study outcome measure data from participants who completed week 6 data collection (n=21). No efficacy testing was conducted. Results Enrollment was completed in 12 weeks (N=30), with a 70% (21/30) retention. Participants showed differential adherence, with 60% (6/10) completing a daily journal activity and 30% (3/10) completing a daily mindfulness activity. Adherence patterns were reflected in the acceptability findings, with journaling being preferred over mindfulness. Preliminary outcomes showed varying patterns between the intervention and control groups, with the intervention group showing decreased median burden levels from before (median 20, IQR 15-27.25) to after the intervention (median 15, IQR 10.50-28.75) but increased median stress levels from 19.50 (IQR 12-26.75) to 21 (IQR 8.75-22.75), while the control group burden and stress levels remained the same before and after the intervention. Positive affect and well-being and informational support increased for both groups. Median emotional support levels increased from 15 (IQR 12-20) before the intervention to 16 (IQR 13-19) after the intervention for the control group and decreased from 14.5 (IQR 11.5-17.75) to 14 (IQR 12-17.25) for the intervention group. Conclusions Findings demonstrate areas for further intervention iteration to address both adherence and acceptability issues with the mindfulness component of the intervention. Intervention implementation also needs to be addressed, including participant retention rates. Our team will use lessons learned alongside feedback from Latino millennial caregivers to address these issues.

Introduction Family caregivers of family members, neighbors, and friends with chronic illnesses and disabilities are the economic and care backbone of our health care system [ 1 , 2 ]. Millennial family caregivers are those born between 1981 and 1996 and comprise 25% of caregivers in the United States [ 3 ]. Millennial family caregivers have unique needs specific to their generational experiences and development stage [ 4 - 7 ]. Broadly, the millennial generation has experienced significant economic setbacks, including two global recessions and the COVID-19 pandemic [ 7 ]. These economic challenges have contributed to delayed important developmental milestones for millennial caregivers, such as educational progression, career development, home ownership, and retirement savings [ 8 ]. Millennials are also more diverse than previous generations across gender identity, sexual orientation, race, and ethnicity, and in the United States, there continue to be inequities in social and health outcomes among minoritized groups [ 6 , 9 ]. In addition to family caregiving, which is stressful, millennial family caregivers navigate complex economic, developmental, and social issues that impact their caregiving experiences [ 10 ]. Approximately 27% of millennial caregivers identify as Latino [ 4 ]. For the Latino millennial caregiver population, there are significant socioeconomic and health care barriers in the United States due to immigration policies and historic and current practices that reinforce bias and segregation [ 11 , 12 ]. There continue to be issues in the health care system with language access and lack of cultural alignment between social and health care resources and Latino family-centered cultural expectations [ 11 , 13 - 15 ]. Many within this group experience poverty and limited career prospects, which add to the stress of caregiving [ 16 , 17 ]. Additionally, Latino caregivers contribute a higher percentage of their income toward caregiving expenses compared to their non-Latino peers despite often holding lower-income jobs than their White, non-Hispanic counterparts [ 3 ]. These financial burdens, combined with the physical and emotional toll of caregiving, expose them to a higher risk of adverse health outcomes [ 17 , 18 ]. Finally, among Latino millennial caregivers, there are additional layers of stress due to cultural expectations such as familismo (loyalty to family) and gendered expectations ( marianismo and machismo) that may impact how the caregiving role is experienced regardless of gender [ 11 , 13 , 19 ]. Family caregivers experience acute and chronic stress that can contribute to a wide range of adverse health effects, including mental health issues, compromised quality of life, and elevated mortality [ 20 ]. Myruski et al [ 21 ] introduced the dynamic fit model as an approach to understanding acute and chronic stress. They propose that there are in-the-moment responses to high acute stress and sustained responses to lower-level chronic stress. They posit that well-being is best achieved when coping strategies are aligned with the type of stress. Mindfulness is a stress management and emotional regulation tool that emphasizes being in the moment, and it can be deployed readily without the need for specific tools or change in location [ 22 ]. Mindfulness techniques such as mindful breathing, meditation, and guided reflection exercises can induce emotional regulation, leading to a decrease in stress and depressive symptoms [ 23 ]. Through practice, mindfulness can be an orientation to life events that can facilitate stress management and emotional regulation in the moment [ 22 ]. To address sustained stress and deliberative coping, narrative interventions (ie, expressive writing, journaling, and gratitude journal) promote the ability to communicate life experiences, whether positive or negative, and have been linked to enhanced stress management and well-being and lower depression in family caregivers and other populations [ 24 - 27 ]. For family caregivers who are juggling multiple responsibilities such as work and family, the accessibility of interventions is of utmost concern. In our prior work with millennial caregivers, both overall millennial caregivers and Latino millennial caregivers noted the demands on their time [ 8 , 16 , 28 ]. Digital health interventions, especially mobile health (mHealth) interventions, present promising solutions by offering scalable, accessible, and flexible support tailored to caregivers’ needs [ 29 - 31 ]. mHealth interventions have been found to be effective in providing support, enhancing communication, and increasing self-efficacy among caregivers [ 32 ]. Given the unique challenges faced by Latino millennial caregivers, it is crucial to develop interventions that are culturally sensitive and directly address their specific needs [ 16 ]. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary outcomes of a stress management and emotional regulation mHealth intervention for Latino millennial caregivers. Findings from this study will be used to inform further intervention iteration. Methods Study Design A 6-week pilot feasibility and acceptability study (4 weeks of active intervention—baseline to 4 weeks) was conducted to test an mHealth-delivered intervention focused on stress management and emotional regulation for Latino millennial family caregivers using an attention, waitlist control approach. Our goal was to ensure that all participants were eventually granted access to the intervention. The protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework retrospectively to align with publishing standards (digital object identifier 10.17605/OSF.IO/B62NH). Prospective registration was not sought due to the pilot nature of our study. We followed the CONSORT-EHEALTH (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials of Electronic and Mobile Health Applications and Online Telehealth) guidelines and have included a checklist ( Checklist 1 ). During consent, participants were told about the study activities they might engage in, but they were not specifically identified as intervention or control activities. After consent procedures, participants were randomized to the treatment or control group using a computer-based random number generator. Participants were blinded to their group assignment, but the study team was not. Participants were assigned a study ID number and given a link to the REDCap (Vanderbilt University) baseline survey, which included demographics and measures for caregiver burden, perceived stress, well-being, and perceived social support ( Table 1 ). Surveys were collected at baseline (pretest) and at 2, 4, and 6 weeks (posttest) for the intervention and control groups. The control group was administered further surveys at weeks 8, 10, and 12. All participants received US $15 for every survey completed. Findings from the baseline and 6-week time points were collected to understand trends in study outcomes, while the 2- and 4-week surveys were collected to determine the feasibility of interim data collection. Participants in the intervention group received information about UpLode app access, which was the platform used to deliver the intervention. Participants in the control group were given an informational packet about stress management, mindfulness, and support resources at the start of pilot-testing, and then they received access to the app-based intervention after the 6-week data collection time point. All study information and procedures were available in English and Spanish in verbal and written forms, including written study materials. Surveys were translated into Spanish by a bilingual study team member and/or a certified Spanish translation service. Study meetings and email contact with Spanish-speaking participants also took place with a bilingual study team member. Intervention This intervention was iteratively designed with feedback from millennial caregivers broadly and Latino millennial caregivers specifically and was guided by 2 frameworks: the stress process model and the dynamic fit model [ 21 , 33 - 35 ]. The stress process model explains how ongoing caregiving demands, especially when combined with limited resources, can lead to emotional distress and health outcomes such as anxiety and depression over time [ 35 ]. It highlights how resources and support can buffer the effects of stressors, including family caregiving. On the basis of caregiver feedback and this model, a resource list and support tools were included in the intervention design [ 33 ]. The dynamic fit model emphasizes that stress management and emotional regulation strategies are more effective when they match the demands of the stressful situation [ 21 ]. The intervention design includes mindfulness as an in-the-moment strategy and journaling as a sustained strategy to manage stress and emotional regulation (see Table 2 for more details). In alignment with the dynamic fit model, stress and caregiver burden were our primary study outcomes. Our fully automated intervention was developed using iterative refinement based on feedback from a broad millennial family caregiver population followed by feedback from Latino millennial caregivers, and then it was tested for usability in both English and Spanish [ 33 , 34 ]. Through interviews with Latino millennial caregivers, the need for practical social support was highlighted, including education, more tailored support resources by geography and culture, and ways to connect with other family caregivers. Additional suggestions included having more mindfulness options and flexibility with journaling content, including an emotions checklist [ 34 ]. By incorporating mindfulness, journaling, and practical support strategies, this intervention sought to address the diverse needs of caregivers ( Table 2 ). Study participants received instructions to complete 1 mindfulness activity per day and respond to the 3 journaling prompts daily. The mindfulness instructions were a protocol deviation. We originally planned for participants to complete at least 6 minutes of mindfulness, but through feedback from Latino millennial caregivers, we adjusted this to mindfulness activities of varying lengths. Participants were also given information on communicating with the app developer if they were having functionality issues with the app. Pilot-testing of the intervention took place concurrently in the non-Latino and Latino populations, and the results from the non-Latino study are reported elsewhere. The trial architecture and instrument battery were shared across both study populations [ 36 ]. Study findings from the non-Latino group revealed slightly higher ratings for mindfulness on its use for stress. There were lower study retention rates in the intervention group. Regarding preliminary study outcomes, the intervention group did not experience significant improvement in burden and stress but did experience statistically significant improvements in positive affect and well-being, informational support, and emotional support [ 36 ]. Sample and Setting Participants were self-identified family caregivers (including family members, friends, and neighbors) of individuals with chronic illnesses or disabilities who were recruited nationally in the United States from August 1 to October 31, 2023. Recruitment took place with support from Trialfacts, a research recruitment company. Trialfacts assisted the research team with the development of advertising materials consistent with the goals of the study and approved by the research team and the institutional review board prior to distribution. title: A randomised feasibility trial of VR-enhanced cue exposure therapy versus neutral VR exposure for cocaine use disorder, with wearable monitoring and JITA-EMA: Feasibility randomised controlled trial protocol
abstract:
Background Cocaine use disorder (CUD) is associated with high rates of relapse, with craving and cue reactivity playing important roles in ongoing use. Cue Exposure Therapy (CET) aims to reduce conditioned responses to drug-related cues through extinction learning, but traditional approaches may be limited by poor ecological validity. Virtual reality-enhanced Cue Exposure Therapy (VR-CET) offers a potentially more immersive and realistic method of delivering cue exposure. Concurrently, advances in wearable physiological monitoring and just-in-time adaptive ecological momentary assessment (JITA-EMA) enable the real-time assessment of craving in everyday life. Objective To assess the feasibility of recruitment, consent, randomisation, blinding, intervention delivery and retention over 8 weeks post-randomisation. Method This is a two-arm, parallel-group, randomised feasibility trial conducted in UK community drug treatment services. Sixty adults receiving treatment will be randomised (1:1) to either VR-CET or an active VR-Relaxation control condition. Both arms will receive six VR sessions over four weeks, alongside continuous physiological monitoring using a wearable device and smartphone-based JITA-EMA for eight weeks. Feasibility outcomes will include recruitment, retention, intervention adherence, wearable wear time, EMA completion, acceptability, and safety. Clinical outcomes will include cocaine use measured by Timeline Follow-Back, cue reactivity assessed through subjective and physiological measures, and participant-confirmed craving episodes captured via wearable-triggered JITA-EMA. Qualitative interviews with participants and service providers will explore intervention acceptability and implementation facilitators, barriers and suggestions. Results Planned start date is July 2026, and enrolment is due to end in April 2027. Data analysis is estimated to be completed by the end of spring 2027. Conclusions To our knowledge, this is the first feasibility RCT of VR-CET for CUD within UK drug treatment services. Results from this trial will help assess the feasibility of integrating VR-CET, continuous physiological monitoring, and real-time craving JITA within CUD treatment. This can be used to inform the design of a future definitive trial and contribute to the development of personalised, technology-enabled approaches to relapse prevention and substance treatment. Trial registration: ISRCTN21409750, https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN21409750 .

Introduction Current treatment for powder or crack cocaine use primarily relies on psychosocial interventions, including cognitive behavioural approaches [ 1 , 2 ]. However, relapse remains common, with craving playing a central role [ 3 ]. A major clinical challenge is that craving is transient, strongly context-dependent, and often triggered by cues and emotional states encountered in everyday life [ 4 ]. Craving is both a recognised diagnostic criterion in DSM-5 and ICD-11 and a predictor of relapse. Despite its clinical importance, most evidence is derived from laboratory or clinic-based assessments, limiting understanding of how craving occurs in naturalistic settings [ 5 ]. Just-in-time adaptive ecological momentary assessment (JITA-EMA), combined with wearable physiological monitoring, offers an opportunity to capture craving and cue reactivity in real time and everyday environments. By prompting assessments during periods of elevated risk, JITA-EMA can increase the likelihood of recording clinically relevant events [ 6 ]. Wearable devices can continuously measure physiological signals associated with cocaine use and craving-related arousal, including heart rate, electrodermal activity, skin temperature, and movement [ 7 – 9 ]. Studies have also demonstrated physiological responses during cocaine cue exposure, supporting the potential value of these measures as markers of cue reactivity [ 10 – 14 ]. Virtual reality-enhanced Cue Exposure Therapy (VR-CET) uses immersive environments to simulate substance-related cues and high-risk situations within a controlled setting [ 15 , 16 ]. The approach is grounded in classical conditioning theory [ 17 ], whereby repeated pairings of cocaine use with environmental stimuli result in conditioned responses such as craving and physiological arousal. Cue Exposure Therapy (CET) seeks to weaken these associations through repeated exposure to cues without drug reinforcement, promoting extinction learning and reducing conditioned responses [ 18 ]. VR may enhance CET by providing realistic, repeatable exposure to complex scenarios that are difficult to recreate safely in clinical settings. It also enables the rehearsal of coping strategies without access to cocaine [ 19 ] and can be tailored to individual triggers across multiple environments or contexts, potentially improving generalisation of treatment effects [ 20 , 21 ]. Two linked studies conducted by this research team informed the development of the present study (Ref: 24/NW/0342 and 25/ES/0061). These studies demonstrated the feasibility of combining continuous wearable monitoring with smartphone-based EMA among people receiving treatment for cocaine use disorder and provided evidence that physiological changes associated with craving can be detected in everyday life ( in preparation ). The previous VR study further refined the VR-CET cocaine scenarios, in addition to the literature review [ 22 ] and ongoing patient and public involvement (PPI). Building on this work, the current feasibility RCT will integrate VR-CET, wearable monitoring, and JITA-EMA to evaluate feasibility, acceptability, safety, and deliverability, while generating preliminary estimates of effects on cue reactivity and cocaine use outcomes to inform a future definitive trial. The study is guided by an explicit programme theory proposing that repeated VR-CET without reinforcement will reduce cue-elicited craving and physiological reactivity through extinction learning. In parallel, wearable-triggered JITA-EMA will facilitate near-real-time identification and assessment of high-risk craving states, providing a foundation for future JITAI to support craving, relapse and recovery. Objectives and hypotheses The primary objective is to assess the feasibility of recruitment, consent, randomisation, blinding, intervention delivery and retention over 8 weeks post-randomisation. The secondary feasibility objectives are: To assess acceptability and adherence/data completeness for: (i) VR-enhanced CET and VR Relaxation sessions, (ii) wearable wear-time, and (iii) EMA completion. To obtain variance estimates of key outcomes for future sample size calculations. To assess the safety and tolerability of VR-enhanced CET and remote monitoring procedures (including adverse events, distress management, and cybersickness). To assess the feasibility and performance of the wearable-triggered JITA-EMA approach, including trigger frequency, response rates, and the proportion of triggers associated with participant-confirmed craving/high-risk states. To assess the feasibility and acceptability of implementation in routine services and identify barriers, facilitators, and potential solutions from the perspective of service providers and participants. The clinical objectives are: Cocaine use: measured at baseline and 8-week follow-up using Timeline Follow ack (TLFB) 28. Key derived endpoints will include frequency of use, cocaine-free days, and time to first use. Cue reactivity: change from baseline to week 4 (end of treatment), operationalised as (i) subjective craving (e.g., Cocaine Experience Questionnaire (CEQ-S)) and (ii) physiological indices from EmbracePlus in response to a standardised static cue reactivity test. Craving episodes over 8 weeks post randomisation : frequency of participant-confirmed craving episodes captured via wearable-triggered JITA-EMA prompts, with episode severity rated on a visual analogue scale (VAS). This study uses a feasibility RCT trial design, randomising participants into the VR-CET or VR-Relaxation arm (1:1) to investigate this. Methods Trial design Multi-centre, individually randomised, two-arm feasibility trial with 1:1 allocation to VR-CET or VR Relaxation control arm, a 4-week intervention period (six sessions), and 8-week follow-up post-randomisation. This study has an additional service provider qualitative component. Staff working in the participating services will be invited to complete one semi-structured interview to explore service providers’ views of the intervention and implementation in routine services. A Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) advisory board has contributed to the study design and procedures, providing input into the acceptability and feasibility of the intervention, participant-facing materials, recruitment and retention strategies, and study procedures to ensure they are appropriate and relevant to the target population. Participants, eligibility and settings Six addiction clinics across two regions in England are participating sites: South London and Maudsley (SLaM) NHS drug services, NHS Humber, Waythrough, and CGL services in London and Hull. Individuals will be able to participate if they are attending one of the participating services and meet the following criteria: 1) Treatment-seeking patients for cocaine SUD, and 2) Able and willing to provide informed consent. Individual’s will be excluded if they meet any of the exclusion criteria: 1) Evidence of severe mental illness or cognitive impairment, 2) Impaired vision or hearing that cannot be corrected (i.e., with contact lenses, glasses or hearing aid), 3) Physical inability to wear a wrist device, both arms having tattoo sleeves (as the device requires contact to ink free skin), 4) Current participation in similar research study. Service providers: Staff at participating sites will be invited to complete a semi-structured interview to assess the feasibility and acceptability of implementing VR-CET in routine drug and alcohol services and to inform future scale-up. Inclusion criteria: 1) Health care professional working in a drug outpatient or inpatient setting in one of the participating drug services, 2) Over 18 years old, 3) Willing to provide informed consent to participate. Ethical approval This study was approved by the Chelsea REC (Ref: 25/ES/0061). All participants will provide written informed consent after reviewing consent documents with research staff. Participants will be given a unique study ID that will be used to identify their data throughout the study. Only trained research staff have access to the key that matches the participant with their ID. The key is password-protected and stored on a secure server at King’s College London (KCL). Intervention arms Both arms will complete six VR sessions over four weeks, wear the physiological monitor and complete daily JITA ( Fig 1 ). The VR-CET arm will experience scenes created to elicit cocaine craving. The VR-Relaxation arm will experience scenes created to induce relaxation. The VR-Relaxation arm provides a credible control condition matched for session number, staff contact, equipment, and study procedures, allowing assessment of the feasibility and acceptability of VR-CET beyond the non-specific effects of VR participation. VR-CET Across the six sessions, participants will complete four VR scenarios per session (24 total exposures in total). Participants will be exposed to eight pre-specified Environment × Cue combinations ( Table 1 ). The cocaine cues designed are: Purchasing from a dealer and consuming cocaine, and observing others talk about and then use cocaine. These occur in different environments: Flat, Car, Pub, Public toilet, House party, Bathroom, Stairwell, Alleyway. After the cocaine scenarios have been completed, the researcher will guide the participant through a relaxing or distracting activity designed to de-escalate cocaine cue-elicited arousal. Participants will remain with the researcher until their self-reported craving returns to their pre-VR level. Craving will be monitored at regular intervals before participants leave the study premises. Participants will also be given a coping with craving handout to take away with them. VR-Relaxation Across the six sessions, participants will complete repeated exposure to a fixed set of VR scenarios using the commercially available Liminal application [ 23 ]. The relaxation and meditation activities were chosen because they are non-drug-related, low risk, suitable for repeated use, and have a clear rationale for participants as calming or stress-management activities. They also avoid exposing participants in the control group to cocaine cues while still providing an engaging and credible VR experience. Liminal immerses users in calming virtual environments (e.g., beaches, forests, or meditation spaces) and includes guided breathing and mindfulness exercises with soothing audio-visual content. Eight pre-specified Liminal environments will be used across the six sessions, with each session comprising four scenario exposures, matching the structure and intensity of the VR-CET arm ( Fig 2 ). The equipment used is the Meta Quest 3 headset and controllers. VR delivery All VR sessions, research meetings and questionnaires will be delivered by a trained member of the research team. The research team have prior experience of delivering VR-CET from the previous linked study (IRAS: 357025, REC: 25/ES/0061). Prior to data collection, the team will undertake refresher training on the delivery of the VR-CET and VR relaxation procedure. Session standard operating procedures (SOPs) and distress management protocols have been developed and are in place. Distress procedures include monitoring during exposure, the option to pause/terminate the session at any time, post-session debriefing, and signposting/escalation in line with local clinical pathways. Procedure Below in Figures 3 and 4 , a flow chart visualises the study procedure. Participants will be recruited from the participating sites and approached either by the researcher or service staff. Staff will be aware of the study and inclusion criteria and have Participant Information Sheets (PIS) to provide. The research team will then speak to the individual directly, answer any questions and arrange a meeting if the individual meets the inclusion criteria and is willing to participate. The researcher will also attend group meetings at each service and be able to talk to service users directly and provide PIS. Randomisation will occur in the first meeting after informed consent has been provided. The participant will be enrolled as part of the VR-CET or VR-Relaxation arm. Apart from VR content (cocaine cue exposure versus relaxation, and interview only for VR-CET arm), study procedures and meetings follow the same design.
