title: Management of shift work disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine systematic review, meta-analysis, and GRADE assessment
abstract:
Introduction The purpose of this systematic review is to provide supporting evidence for a clinical practice guideline on the treatment of adults with shift work disorder (SWD). Methods The American Academy of Sleep Medicine commissioned a task force of six experts in sleep and circadian medicine. A systematic review was conducted to identify randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and treatment trials in which treatments for the symptoms of excessive sleepiness and/or sleep disturbance/insomnia in adults with SWD, and for circadian adaptation to shift work schedules was tested. Evidence from controlled laboratory trials of simulated shift work and of field-based trials of shift workers with and without a diagnosis of SWD was included. Statistical analyses were performed to determine the significance of critical and important outcomes and clinically meaningful thresholds were set to determine the clinical relevance of treatments on the outcomes examined, where possible. Finally, the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) process was used to assess the evidence for making recommendations. Results The literature search resulted in 3,045 articles; 118 studies provided data suitable for statistical analyses. The task force provided a detailed summary of the evidence along with the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, and resource use considerations. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s44470-026-00076-w .

Introduction This systematic review is intended to provide supporting evidence for a clinical practice guideline on the treatment of shift work disorder (SWD), and update the evidence review conducted for the previously published American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) guidelines. Primary critical outcomes examined include excessive sleepiness/alertness, accident risk, sleep quality, and cognitive performance/work performance. Secondary important outcomes examined include circadian alignment, quality of life, mental health, sleep outcomes other than quality (sleep latency, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, wakefulness after sleep onset), as well as disease severity. Background In our current society, shift work is a common phenomenon, whether out of necessity in fields such as healthcare, transportation, and public safety, or for economic reasons in manufacturing and consumer businesses. Shift work can be defined broadly as being required to regularly work during times when an individual would normally be sleeping. Shift work schedules can range from requirements to work fixed early morning, evening or overnight shifts or can consist of a schedule of rotating, split or irregular shifts. Based on those definitions, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, approximately 16% of the US work force is engaged in shift work with some occupations having more than 33% engaged in shift work [ 1 ]. As a result of working on a shift work schedule, individuals can develop symptoms of insomnia from attempting to sleep when due to their circadian biology they would normally be awake and/or symptoms of excessive sleepiness from working during times they would normally be sleeping. To be diagnosed with shift work disorder (SWD), an individual must have clinically meaningful symptoms associated with working a shift work schedule that have been present for at least 3 months. It is important to note that not all individuals who engage in shift work develop symptoms of SWD. A recent meta-analysis determined the overall prevalence of SWD among shift workers to be ~ 26.5%, but with a range of 2.3% to 84% depending on the study [ 2 ]. Not all individuals with SWD will experience the same constellation of symptoms. As such, the International Classification of Sleep Disorders [ 3 ] has proposed three distinct phenotypes of SWD: 1) insomnia 2) sleepy and 3) mixed. When determining the appropriate treatments for a patient with SWD, it is important to evaluate which symptoms a patient is experiencing, as not all treatments recommended will be appropriate for all patients. In addition to symptoms of insomnia and sleepiness, leading to impairment in cognitive and work performance and safety, there are also health consequences associated with shift work and SWD, stemming primarily from a combination of insufficient sleep (i.e., < 7 h per 24 h day [ 3 ]) and circadian misalignment (e.g., wakefulness, food intake, and activity occurring when the endogenous circadian system is promoting sleep and sleep occurring when the endogenous circadian system is promoting wakefulness [ 4 , 5 ]). Whether from difficulty sleeping, or from competing demands of nighttime work and daytime familial or social responsibilities, shift workers experience an average weekly reduction in total sleep time of 10 h or more. Even when on a fixed shift schedule, individuals engaged in shift work often do not align their circadian system with the shift work schedule [ 6 ], with alignment being a near impossible goal while on rotating shifts. As a result, shift workers may be in a state of circadian misalignment with the environment (wakefulness occurring during the solar night and sleep occurring during the solar day), as well as in a state of internal circadian misalignment between components of the internal circadian system, resulting in symptoms that extend beyond difficulties with sleep and alertness. The daily production of melatonin occurs with a circadian rhythm and represents the timing of the brain’s endogenous master circadian clock located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus. For a day worker, melatonin levels typically increase in the evening before bedtime, representing the beginning of the biological night, and levels typically decrease in the morning after waketime [ 7 ], representing the beginning of the biological day. Exposure to light at night can acutely reduce melatonin levels as well as shift the timing of the circadian rhythm of melatonin [ 8 , 9 ]. The melatonin rhythm in some night shift workers remains similarly timed to that of day workers (i.e., high levels at night), whereas in others the melatonin rhythm is shifted/timed earlier or later [ 5 ]. In humans, the rise of melatonin levels is a circadian signal to prepare for sleep and associated functions that occur preferentially during the biological night. High melatonin levels are incompatible with behaviors associated with shift work schedules such as wakefulness, food intake, and being physically active. The endogenous circadian system also includes local clocks in brain and body tissues outside of the SCN [ 10 – 15 ]. These local clocks are important components of the internal circadian system that time cellular and tissue physiology to prepare the body for time-of-day relevant behaviors and environmental exposures (e.g., metabolic tissues are prepared for nutrient intake, cardiovascular and neuromuscular systems are prepared for physical activity, the immune system is prepared for exposure to pathogens). Shift work is associated with an increased risk for adverse health outcomes, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, hypertension, obesity, gastrointestinal disease, depression, negative reproductive outcomes, and cancer [ 16 – 23 ]. For example, findings from several large cohort studies have demonstrated that exposure to shift work is associated with increased risk for the development of cancer, leading to the International Agency for Research on Cancer to declare it a probable carcinogen in 2007. These adverse health effects are thought to be due to a combination of the impact of sleep disruption, circadian misalignment, and internal circadian desynchrony (i.e., misalignment among internal circadian clocks). Patients with SWD often have a higher medical burden than shift workers without SWD [ 24 – 28 ]. Based on the available evidence, the current treatment guidelines focus primarily on the impact of treatments on the more acute outcomes of excessive sleepiness/alertness, accident risk, sleep quality, and cognitive performance/work performance. Future studies are needed to address the impact of interventions for shift work and SWD on well-being and the long-term health consequences of shift work exposure. Methodology Expert task force The AASM commissioned a task force (TF) of sleep and circadian medicine researchers and clinicians with expertise in circadian rhythm disorders and shift work, and the treatment of SWD, along with guideline methodologists. The TF was required to disclose all potential conflicts of interest (COI), per the AASM’s COI policy, prior to being appointed to the TF and throughout the research and writing of these documents. In accordance with the AASM’s conflicts of interest policy, TF members with a Level 1 conflict were not allowed to participate. TF members with a Level 2 conflict were required to recuse themselves from any related discussion or writing responsibilities. All relevant conflicts of interest are listed in the Disclosures section. Patient, intervention, comparison, and outcomes (PICO) questions PICO questions were developed by the TF based on a review of the existing AASM practice parameters on the clinical evaluation and treatment of circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders and a review of systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and guidelines published since 2007. The AASM Board of Directors approved the final list of questions presented in Table 1 before the literature searches were performed. Through consensus, the TF then developed a list of patient-oriented, clinically relevant outcomes to determine the efficacy of the interventions. Input on interventions, outcomes, and adverse events from interest holders (formerly known as stakeholders, e.g., patients, caregivers, and health care providers) was collected using electronic surveys. The TF rated the relative importance of each outcome to determine which outcomes were critical versus important for decision-making. A summary of these outcomes by PICO is presented in Table 2 . The TF set a clinically meaningful threshold (CMT) for outcome measures to determine whether the mean differences between treatment and control or the mean differences between before and after treatment were clinically meaningful. The CMT was defined as the minimum level of improvement in the outcome of interest that would be considered clinically important to clinicians and patients. CMTs were determined based on a TF literature review of commonly used thresholds. When no clearly established threshold values were available, the TF used their clinical judgment and experience to establish a CMT based on consensus; yet CMTs were not determined for all outcomes as some outcomes were not used clinically and/or were not used widely in research. A summary of the CMTs for the clinical outcome measures is presented in Table 2 . Literature searches, evidence review and data extraction The TF performed an extensive review of the scientific literature using PubMed, Web of Science, and PsycINFO databases (see Fig. 1 ) to retrieve articles that addressed the PICO questions. Articles that met inclusion criteria but did not report outcomes of interest were rejected from the final evidence base. The key terms, search limits, and inclusion/exclusion criteria specified by the TF are detailed in the supplemental material. The initial literature search was performed in January 2021. Subsequent literature searches were conducted in April 2023, July 2024, and August 2025 to identify studies published since the initial search, updating the body of evidence for the review. These searches identified a total of 3,045 articles. Lastly, the TF reviewed previously published guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses to spot check for references that may have been missed during the prior searches. The TF set inclusion and exclusion criteria, which are presented in the supplemental material. All studies were reviewed based on inclusion/exclusion criteria by two TF members. Any discrepancies between the reviewers were discussed and resolved by the two reviewers or a third TF member. A total of 118 studies were determined to be suitable for meta-analysis and/or grading. Statistical and meta-analysis and interpretation of clinical meaningfulness Meta-analysis was performed on outcomes of interest, when possible, for each PICO question (see Table 1 ). Comparisons of interventions to controls and/or assessment of efficacy before and after treatment of shift work disorder were performed. The analyses were performed using Review Manager 5.3 software by pooling data across studies for each outcome measure. Data was separated into three separate groups based on the patient population/participants studied. The first group included individuals with a formal diagnosis of SWD. The second group included studies with participants who were shift workers without a formal diagnosis of SWD. The final group included healthy participants who did not participate in shift work and were most often studied in a lab simulated shift work setting. Both the second and third groups were judged to provide indirect evidence as these individuals lacked the long-term symptoms seen in SWD. The evidence was further divided into lab and field sub-groupings based on the setting in which the SWD or shift work participants were observed. Clinical meaningfulness of treatments was determined by critical or important outcomes crossing the predetermined CMTs. Outcomes that did not meet the CMT are described by the magnitude and direction of change. As noted, reasons for not establishing CMTs for outcomes included the test not being used clinically and/or not being used widely in research. Further, for some outcomes used in research where there was no agreed upon threshold for clinical meaningfulness, the TF did not want to establish clinical cutoffs that could not be justified by current scientific evidence. Outcomes without a CMT are described by the magnitude and direction of change. Post-treatment data from each arm were used for meta-analysis of Randomized Control Trials (RCTs) when change values were not reported and baseline values between the two study groups were statistically similar. Pre-and post-treatment data were used for meta-analyses of observational studies. The pooled results for each continuous outcome measure were usually expressed as the mean difference between the intervention and control for RCTs or pre-treatment versus post-treatment for observational studies; however, for some outcomes where individual component scales were pooled, a standardized mean difference (SMD) or effect size was determined. The pooled results for dichotomous outcome measures were expressed as the risk ratio or risk difference between the intervention and comparator or pre- versus posttreatment.

title: The effectiveness of addiction prevention training based on dialectical behavior therapy on family friendship and loneliness in adolescent boys
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The ever-evolving addiction poses a serious threat to the younger generation today. Addiction mostly threatens individuals with mental vulnerabilities and poor interpersonal relationships—both within the family and among peers. Thus, having an effective communication skill serves as a critical component in addiction prevention programs. This study aims to investigate the effectiveness of the dialectical behavior therapy (DBT)-based addiction program on adolescents, focusing on its impact on family connectedness and feelings of loneliness. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This semi-experimental study employed a pretest–posttest–follow-up design with two experimental and control groups. The study population consists male adolescents aged 12–18 in Isfahan during 2024. Forty male adolescents were selected through a purposive sampling, considering the inclusion and exclusion criteria. The selected participants were then randomly assigned to the experimental or control groups. All participants were assessed three times during the three stages of the study, using the Family Connectedness Questionnaire and the UCLA Loneliness Scale. The control group was placed on a waiting list, while the experimental group received ten 90-min sessions of the DBT-based addiction prevention training. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation, as well as the repeated-measures analysis of variance. RESULTS: The results indicated that the intervention significantly improved both family connectedness and reduced feelings of loneliness ( P < 0.05). CONCLUSION: Based on the findings, the DBT-based addiction prevention program has been shown to be an effective intervention for enhancing the dependent variables of the present study.

Introduction Adolescence is a critical stage for the onset of substance use.[ 1 ] Substance dependence is a major psychological and social challenge that can easily undermine the foundations of individual, family, and societal well-being.[ 2 ] The growing prevalence of drug use among adolescents poses a significant threat to both individual health and public safety, often leading to a range of negative consequences, such as wasted national resources, reduced workforce productivity, increased corruption, rising crime rates, and widespread violence.[ 3 ] The increasing tendency of adolescents to substance use is particularly concerning since a large number of users are adolescents who begin using drugs at a very early age and continue such behaviors later in their adulthood.[ 4 ] However, establishing a healthy and positive family connectedness is considered a key factor in addiction prevention among adolescents, offering a potential for positive change.[ 5 ] Those adolescents who grow up in a warm, healthy, and supportive family environments are more likely to feel and experience emotional security, affection, a sense of responsibility, and commitment to the family members.[ 6 ] It should be noted that “family connectedness” refers to the emotional bonding, sacrifice, dedication of time, and physical and psychological resources to the family, as well as striving for the success of both the family and its members.[ 7 ] In contrast, adolescents who are raised in toxic and dysfunctional families and those whose emotional needs are not entirely met, lack a supportive family, which leads to a deep sense of loneliness as a result of not being able to establish a healthy family connectedness appropriately. Loneliness itself can result in anxiety, depression, a feeling of rejection, hypervigilance, intrusive thoughts, paranoia, social isolation, gloominess, and a lack of life purpose. Moreover, it is often associated with behavioral disorders, such as overeating, suicidal tendencies, alcohol abuse, and drug addiction.[ 8 ] Studies indicate that adolescents are more likely to participate in social, friendly, and interpersonal activities when they are accepted and liked by their peers.[ 9 ] According to the biopsychosocial model, emotional dysregulation—arising from an interaction between biological predispositions and invalidating environmental conditions—can set the stage for maladaptive behaviors such as substance use and self-harm.[ 10 ] These behaviors, although temporarily relieving, are ultimately maladaptive strategies for managing emotional distress.[ 11 ] Therefore, DBT can be beneficial for those adolescents from dysfunctional families and poor interpersonal relationships. DBT is a form of cognitive-behavioral therapy that manages extreme impulsive behaviors or emotional dysregulation. This therapy equips individuals to regulate their emotions without losing control or any self-destructive behaviors. DBT is particularly effective for individuals who experience intense emotional pain and try to avoid it or choose to escape the pain.[ 12 ] In addition to employing standard cognitive-behavioral skills, including cognitive restructuring and crisis management, DBT targets maladaptive behaviors such as aggression and impulsivity through the cultivation of dialectical thinking ability, acceptance, emotional regulation, distress tolerance skills, and improving interpersonal relationships.[ 13 ] In general, the primary focus of DBT is the acquisition, application, and generalization of adaptive coping skills, with the ultimate goal of helping individuals break free from destructive cycles and achieve a more balanced and healthy life.[ 14 ] Numerous studies have confirmed the effectiveness of DBT in addressing various psychological variables: aggression and anxiety,[ 15 ] emotion regulation and depressive symptoms,[ 16 ] psychological capital and academic buoyancy,[ 17 ] psychological coherence,[ 18 ] psychological stress,[ 19 ] and self-injurious behaviors.[ 20 ] This investigation aimed to address a significant gap in the existing studies, since no published work has specifically examined the effectiveness of a DBT-based addiction prevention program on adolescents’ family connectedness and loneliness. To fill this gap, we employed a mixed-methods approach. The initial qualitative phase is focused on developing and validating a specialized DBT-based prevention package tailored for adolescents. This intervention is designed to target both internal and external risk factors linked to addiction prevention and includes four core strategies: acceptance, emotion regulation, mindfulness, and communication skills. It is important to note that experts who specialize in the field of addiction psychotherapy validated the devised training package. The present article reports on the quantitative phase, which evaluates the effectiveness of the package on key psychological variables associated with addiction. The findings of these studies can not only contribute to the development of DBT and enrich the literature review on addiction prevention. They also provide practical tools for counselors and therapists working with adolescents. Therefore, this research provided an answer to the following question: Does the devised training program (package) effectively impact family connectedness and the feeling of loneliness among adolescents? Study design and setting This semi-experimental study consisted of pretest, posttest, and follow-up stages with two control and experimental groups. Study participants and sampling The study population also included adolescents aged 12–16 in Isfahan during 2024. Forty participants who met the inclusion criteria were selected using the continence sampling method. Then, they were all divided into two control and experimental groups, with 20 individuals in each group. The inclusion criteria are as follows: willingness to participate in the study; no severe physical problems, no severe mental disorders, and no concurrent psychological or psychiatric treatment. The exclusion criteria for the study included missing more than two sessions, irregular attendance at training, and lack of cooperation between the adolescents and the researcher. Data collection tools and techniques The following instruments were used to measure the variables of the study: Family connectedness scale: We employed the Family Connectedness Questionnaire to assess the variable of family connectedness.[ 7 ] The content validity of this scale was confirmed through a review by experts in family studies. The scale includes 13 items, and its face validity was assessed and approved by a panel of 10 adolescents. The items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale, where 1 means “strongly disagree” and 5 means “strongly agree.” This scale consists of two subscales: attachment to family and detachment from family.[ 7 ] The internal consistency reliability of the scale was originally reported as 0.94. In the current study, the internal consistency for both subscales was reevaluated and found to be above 0.85. UCLA Loneliness Scale: The UCLA Loneliness Scale is a 20-item questionnaire developed by Russell et al .[ 21 ] It is rated on a 4-point Likert scale, where 1 indicates “never” and 4 means “always.” The developers assessed the scale and reported its psychometric properties to be reliable and valid. It has been effectively used among various high-risk populations prone to loneliness, such as teenage mothers, homeless adolescents, and low-income immigrants, indicating good discriminant validity,[ 21 ] and the original Cronbach’s alpha was reported at 0.94. Moreover, the present study reassessed the reliability of this scale, yielding a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.88. Procedure First, the necessary approvals were obtained from the university, along with the research ethics code. Following that, we received the required permissions from the Department of Education, as well as coordinating with relevant officials to conduct the study. After the official procedures, one secondary school was randomly selected. Forty male adolescents who met the inclusion criteria were selected and then randomly assigned into two groups of control and experimental, each consisting of 20 individuals. Both groups completed the family connectedness and the UCLA loneliness scales during the pretest. Subsequently, the experimental group received the DBT-based addiction prevention training package, delivered by the researcher, throughout ten 90-min sessions twice a week. On the other hand, the control group received no intervention, placing them on a waiting list. At the end of the training program, both groups again completed the same questionnaires as part of the posttest. Eventually, 45 days after the intervention, a follow-up session was conducted in which both groups completed the questionnaires for the third time. It is important to note that the researcher conducted the intervention sessions based on a structured protocol developed for the study. The protocol included clearly defined content and objectives for each session and was implemented under the supervision of the supervising professor. The contents of the sessions are presented in Table 1 in detail. Ethical consideration The present study received approval from the ethics committee under the ethics code of IR.IAU.KHUISF.REC.1403.033. Results The researchers employed the repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to provide an answer to the following research question: “Does the devised training package effectively impact family connectedness-attachment and detachment-and the feeling of loneliness among adolescents?” Table 2 also presents the results of the Shapiro–Wilk test of normality, Levene’s test for homogeneity of variance across groups, testing equality of covariance matrices using Box’s M test, and Mauchly’s test of sphericity regarding the variables of family connectedness (attachment and detachment), and loneliness. As shown in Table 2 , all three variables—attachment, detachment, and loneliness—demonstrated a normal distribution ( P > 0.05), equality of error variances ( P > 0.01 and P > 0.05), and equality of the variance–covariance matrix ( P > 0.05). Moreover, Mauchly’s test was significant, indicating that the sphericity assumption was violated. Accordingly, the final ANOVA results were corrected using Greenhouse–Geisser estimates. Table 3 presents the means and standard deviations of family connectedness and loneliness across the pretest, posttest, and follow-up stages for the experimental and control groups. As illustrated in Table 3 , the DBT-based addiction prevention group showed significant changes in family connectedness and loneliness in the posttest and follow-up stages compared to the control group. The results of the repeated measures ANOVA for these variables are presented in Table 4 . Because the sphericity assumption was violated [ Table 2 ], the Greenhouse–Geisser correction was applied to adjust the results [ Table 3 ]. (1) Family connectedness—attachment: Both the main effects of time ( F = 127.76, df = 1.53, and P < 0.0.1) and the group × time interaction ( F = 166.96, df = 1.53, and P < 0.01) were statistically significant in the within-subject effects. This indicates a significant difference over time and in the interaction between time and group (experimental and control) in terms of attachment to the family. Notably, the eta squared for time was 0.77, with a statistical power of 1, while the eta squared for the interaction was 0.78, also with a power of 1. These results revealed that 77% and 78% of the variance in attachment to family is explained by the independent variable—the implementation of dialectical behavior therapy (DBT)-based addiction prevention training—with full statistical power (100%). Moreover, the between-group effect was significant ( F = 166.94, df = 1, and P < 0.01), with eta squared of 0.81 and statistical power of one, indicating that 81% of the variance in attachment to family between the DBT group and the control group is attributable to the intervention. (2) Family connectedness—detachment: In the within-subject effects, both the main effect of time ( F = 138.79, df = 1.53, and P < 0.01) and the interaction time × group ( F = 131.45, df = 1.53, and P < 0.01) were significant. This indicates a meaningful difference over time and in the interaction between time and group regarding family detachment. The effect size, measured by eta squared for time, is 0.78, with a power of 1. The effect size for the interaction is also 0.78, with a power of 1. Therefore, 78% of the variance in detachment from family can be explained by the intervention, which is supported by 100% statistical power. Additionally, the between-group effect was significant ( F = 117.26, df = 1, and P < 0.001), with an eta squared value of 0.75 and a power of 1. This indicates a strong impact of the DBT-based intervention in reducing family detachment. title: Evaluating large language models versus human therapists in generating interventions for patients with depression in psychodynamic psychotherapy
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Recent advances in artificial intelligence, especially the rise of large language models (LLMs), hold great promise for transforming mental health care, but their growing integration also raises pressing questions about their ability to deliver meaningful therapeutic interventions. This study compared the capabilities of LLMs to those of human therapists in producing context-sensitive psychotherapy responses within 16-session supportive-expressive psychodynamic psychotherapy for patients with depression. Specifically, it compared LLM and human therapists on (a) the frequency and typicality of their intervention choice and (b) the quality and general helpfulness of their interventions.

METHOD: We developed an LLM-based framework composed of four specialized LLM agents, each representing a different therapeutic dimension, and a Judge-LLM that selects the most appropriate intervention for a given context. A sample of 300 therapy session segments, each containing both human- and LLM-generated responses, served as the evaluation data set. Expert clinical judges assessed interventions for typicality and quality.

RESULTS: LLMs and human therapists relied on broadly similar intervention types. However, the contextual choice of when to use a specific type differed. Human interventions were rated as generally more helpful. Specifically, humans produced higher quality meaning-making interventions, while no differences were found for supportive, directive, or exploratory interventions.

CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that under the specific locally deployed multiagent configuration tested, LLMs can generate a range of context-sensitive therapeutic responses but showed limitations in producing high-quality meaning-making interventions. These findings highlight both the promise and the current boundaries of such systems as supervised therapeutic adjuncts. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: Job Coaching and Smartphone-Based Cognitive Behavioral Techniques for Returning to Work and Coping With Unemployment (DRIVEN): Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
Abstract Background Unemployment has economic consequences and is associated with emotional distress and impairment. Joblessness is often associated with depression, leading to a vicious cycle of reduced drive to seek work, deepening financial stress, and worsening depression. Few scalable interventions exist that integrate job-search strategies with cognitive behavioral techniques. Objective The study aimed to determine the efficacy of a Distress-Informed Return-to-Work Intervention (DRIVEN). The primary hypothesis was that DRIVEN would be more efficacious than the control condition in improving job-search behavior. Secondary analyses examined job attainment, depression, and positive affect. Methods A randomized controlled trial was conducted from August 2023 to September 2024. Assessments were at baseline, weeks 1 through 6, and 8 and 16 weeks postintervention. Participants were a nationwide sample of unemployed job seekers aged 18 years or older who had never earned more than US $100,000 in a year. Participants received either (1) DRIVEN, which included 6 weeks of cognitive behavioral exercises in a mobile app combined with three 1-hour coaching sessions over videoconference or (2) emailed articles containing job-search advice. Primary outcome measures were subscales of a modified Job Search Behavior Scale (preparatory and active job search). Secondary outcomes included job attainment and mental health outcomes. Results Participants were a nationwide sample (N=126; mean age 33.6, SD 6.6 y), including 62 (49.2%) females. During the acute treatment phase, mixed-effects linear models showed that for DRIVEN, preparatory job-search behavior increased by an estimated 0.053 (95% CI 0.031-0.076) units per day from baseline, which was a larger effect than in the control condition (0.011, 95% CI −0.011 to 0.033 units per day; P =.008). Active job-search behavior increased by 0.061 (95% CI 0.038-0.084) units per day from baseline, which was significantly larger than in the control group (point estimate: 0.025, 95% CI 0.001-0.047; P =.03). Depression decreased more in the DRIVEN group vs control (DRIVEN point estimate=−0.214, 95% CI −0.255 to −0.172 vs control group point estimate=−0.122, 95% CI −0.163 to −0.081; P =.002), and participants were more likely to get a job in the DRIVEN group (68.3% vs 50.8%; P =.046). Self-report outcomes did not significantly differ during the follow-up periods. Conclusions DRIVEN was superior to emailed job-search advice for the primary outcome (job-search behavior) and secondary outcomes (job attainment, depression, and positive affect). This intervention may be beneficial for distressed unemployed individuals seeking work.

Introduction Employment is a social determinant of health that can affect an individual’s economic status, social connection, and access to health care, especially in the United States, where health insurance is often obtained through an individual’s employer [ 1 - 3 ]. As of May 2026, the US Department of Labor reported that approximately 4.3% of the population (over 7 million individuals) were unemployed [ 4 ], which not only creates costs to the government to cover unemployment insurance but also leaves these individuals without income, social connections, and a sense of meaning and purpose [ 2 ]. As such, it is unsurprising that unemployment has been associated with both symptoms of depression and major depressive disorder [ 5 ]. Joblessness also can lead to a vicious cycle of reduced drive to seek work, deepening financial stress, and worsening depression [ 6 - 8 ]. Thus, there is an urgent need for scalable programs that can both treat emotional distress—such as depression and anxiety—as well as teach effective job-search strategies. In fact, previous meta-analyses of job-search interventions have found they can reduce depression, but few studies have assessed mental health outcomes more broadly [ 9 ]. For these reasons, we created a smartphone app–delivered intervention for job seekers (Distress-Informed Return-to-Work Intervention [DRIVEN]) that (1) integrates job-search strategies with cognitive and behavioral techniques to address emotional distress and diminished motivation and (2) includes brief videoconference meetings with a job coach to support motivation, review intervention techniques, and discuss job-search strategies. In this way, DRIVEN combines the strong evidence for cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for depression [ 10 ] with practical support and coaching specific for a job search. This research builds upon existing evidence that cognitive behavioral skills may aid job seekers. For example, in a sample of 75 job seekers, cognitive behavioral skills predicted job-search self-efficacy, even after covarying for depression [ 11 ]. In addition, Della-Posta and Drummond [ 12 ] found unemployed job seekers (n=39) experienced less distress and were more likely to find work when receiving a combination of cognitive behavioral techniques and job-search support vs standard job-search support alone. In another study, unemployed individuals completed either a 7-week CBT (n=94) or control program (n=89) that both emphasized social support. After the program, the CBT group reported better mental health outcomes and more participants found full-time employment [ 13 ]. The purpose of this research was to build upon previous studies to determine whether DRIVEN—which was designed to be brief, mostly self-guided, and smartphone-based—could help unemployed job seekers attain jobs and improve mental health. Our primary hypothesis was that the DRIVEN intervention would lead to more job-search behavior at a postintervention assessment point and follow-ups at 8 and 16 weeks, relative to a control condition designed to reflect usual job-search behavior (ie, weekly emails containing articles and recommendations for job seekers). Secondary outcome measures included self-report measures of depression, positive affect, and job attainment. Methods Overview This study was a 2-arm, parallel-assignment randomized controlled trial (RCT). Job-search behaviors and other outcomes were captured at baseline, during each of the 6 weeks of the intervention, and again at the 8- and 16-week postintervention follow-ups. Additional details about the study design, study protocol, and statistical analysis plan can be found in our protocol study [ 14 ]. The study was funded by the National Institute of Mental Health; the sponsor had no role in the design, conduct, analysis, or reporting of the trial. Throughout the study, an advisory board was maintained, comprising community members and experts in human resources, business, clinical psychology, and community engagement. A Data Safety Monitoring Board comprising a clinical psychologist with expertise in digital interventions and 2 statisticians was maintained; it met midway through the trial and approved continuation based on its review of data and procedures. The first participant was enrolled on August 7, 2023. The study was retrospectively registered with ClinicalTrials.gov on August 30, 2023, and the registration was publicly visible on September 7, 2023. Ethical Considerations Data were stored in REDCap, which allowed data to be exported for analysis without identifying information, such as names and addresses [ 15 ]. Access to the REDCap database was available only to approved study team members, and data files used for analysis were kept on secure computers. Participants received compensation for the completion of study assessments of up to US $350 (US $50 for the baseline assessment; US $20 for each of the first 3 weeks of questionnaires; US $30, US $40, and US $50 for the fourth, fifth, and sixth weeks of questionnaires, respectively; and US $60 for each of the 2 follow-ups). Compensation was not provided for time spent on the intervention procedures in either of the 2 groups. Advarra served as the Ethics Review Board (Pro00062697) and approved the study; all participants provided written informed consent. Randomization A randomization list, stratified by gender, was created by JWG using the blockrand package for R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing) [ 16 ], which used randomly varying block sizes and then equally allocated participants to groups within the block (ie, the study used a 1:1 allocation ratio). Block sizes were 2, 4, 6, and 8. A seed was set for reproducibility. The randomization list was uploaded by a study coordinator to REDCap [ 15 ] and then used for sequential participants, within gender. After randomization, participants were onboarded by study coordinators (who had access to the randomization in REDCap) to their respective arms of the study. Participants were told in the consent form “You will be randomized to one of two approaches that are designed to give you the tools to help you (a) cope with the stress of being unemployed and having to search for work and (b) navigate your job search most effectively.” Thus, participants did not receive information about which group was the DRIVEN group vs the control group. Participants Overview Participants were English-speaking, unemployed adult job seekers aged 18 years or older who had never received an annual salary of more than US $100,000; detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria are shown in Table S1 in Multimedia Appendix 1 . Setting and Eligibility Using online advertisements on Craigslist, 126 participants were recruited from 7 US metropolitan areas, selected for their geographic diversity (New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston, Jacksonville, Philadelphia, and Phoenix). The sample size (N=126) was determined by our a priori power analyses; the study protocol specified a maximum of 150 participants to account for the possibility of overrecruitment. Recruitment took place from August 2023 to September 2024. Eligible participants were 18 to 65 years of age, currently unemployed (defined as working <8 h/wk), actively searching for work, previously employed full-time (≥35 h/wk) for at least 1 year prior to unemployment, had a highest individual salary of US $100,000 or less, owned an iPhone (Apple Inc) or Android (Google LLC) smartphone, were able to provide informed consent, had a minimum depression score according to the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Depression 8a scale (T-score of 45, which is within 0.5 SD of the mean of the US general population but above the floor of the questionnaire), and were able to communicate in English (verbal and written). Exclusion criteria included current (at the time of enrollment) moderate or severe alcohol/substance use disorders, suicidal planning and/or active suicidal ideation, current manic or psychotic symptoms, or being a full-time/part-time student. Research coordinators were available to both groups in case adverse events needed to be reported. Sample Size Justification Using the pwr.r.test() function in R [ 17 ], we estimated that 100 participants (50 per group) would yield 93% power for a between-group delta of 0.7 standardized units, assuming a 2-sided test; the sample size was inflated to 126 to account for a possible dropout rate of 20%. Intervention Procedures Table 1 summarizes the content of the DRIVEN intervention as well as that of the control group. DRIVEN The DRIVEN intervention was designed to combine skills derived from CBT —thinking flexibly (ie, cognitive reappraisal) and taking action (ie, behavioral activation)—applied to unemployment-related distress and job searching (eg, coping with rejection after a job interview). Software development was led by KA, who met with the research team to outline the mobile app, built necessary features for DRIVEN (eg, sequential exercises, videos, and a resource list), and integrated changes based on pilot testing. The intervention was 6 weeks long, with weekly, self-paced activities delivered through participants’ iPhones or Android smartphones. Activities included instructional and/or motivational videos, activities related to self-monitoring (eg, a weekly mood self-assessment), and self-guided cognitive reappraisal activities. A coaching manual was created by the authors, and each participant received three 1-hour sessions with a job coach via videoconference. Coaching was oriented toward providing individualized guidance to the participants on topics including job searching, networking, resume review, cover letters, reviewing homework during the intervention, and interview preparation. The app’s information was delivered in a fixed sequence so that all participants had a consistent experience. Screenshots of representative activities are presented in Multimedia Appendix 1 . Control Group The control group received weekly emails with information about job searching. It was designed to be an “active” control group with helpful articles that a person might find useful, rather than an “inert” control group. Table 1 summarizes the contents of the emails, which were intended to reinforce “job seeking as usual” by providing helpful and supportive advice, without using principles of CBT. Study Measures Job-Search Behaviors Job-search behaviors were measured using a variant of the Job Search Behavior Scale proposed by Blau [ 18 ]. Adaptations to the questionnaire used updated wording to reflect modern job-search practices (referencing “job postings” rather than “classified ads in a newspaper”). The questionnaire assessed the number of times participants engaged in 10 different job-search activities and divided into 2 subscales: preparatory job-search behaviors (5 items; eg, preparing/revising resume and speaking with previous employers about possible job leads) and active job-search behaviors (5 items; eg, going on a job interview and sending out applications). Items are scored on a 1 to 5 scale from “0 times” to “6 or more times,” and subscales are scored by summing the items. During the intervention period (baseline through week 6), participants reported weekly on job-search behaviors. At the 2 follow-up periods (8 and 16 weeks postintervention), participants were asked to report on job-search behaviors over the past 2 months. PROMIS Emotional Distress-Depression—Short Form 8a This PROMIS Depression 8a short form contains 8 items rated using a 5-option rating scale from “Never” to “Always,” rated over the past 7 days. The PROMIS depression item bank showed a high degree of convergent validity with other depression questionnaires (Pearson correlation coefficient r of 0.86 for the Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression scale and 0.81 for the Patient Health Questionnaire-9) and a reliability coefficient of 0.92 [ 19 ]. The PROMIS depression scales are also responsive to changes in clinical status [ 20 ] and have been extensively used in RCTs.
