title: A Behavior Change Technique-Based Text Messaging Intervention for Obesity Among Employed Adult Men Younger Than 40 Years: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
Abstract Background In Japan, employed men younger than 40 years are not eligible for specific health guidance, and evidence regarding obesity interventions targeting this population is limited. Furthermore, due to the shortage of human resources in occupational health settings, a need has arisen for simple and implementable support methods. Support via SMS text message is expected to be a low-cost and scalable method for health guidance; however, its effectiveness in this target population has not been sufficiently evaluated. Objective This pilot randomized controlled trial aimed to assessed the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary effectiveness of an SMS text messaging intervention among employed men younger than 40 years with obesity (BMI ≥25 kg/m²). Methods An unblinded randomized controlled trial was conducted with 35 participants (intervention group, n=17; control group, n=18). The intervention group received one-way SMS text messaging based on behavior change techniques targeting diet and physical activity, delivered 3 times per week for 12 weeks (36 messages total). The control group received a pamphlet and a self-monitoring record sheet at baseline. The primary outcome was the proportion achieving ≥3% weight loss. Secondary outcomes included BMI, waist circumference, and psychological and behavioral measures. Feasibility and acceptability were also assessed. Results The proportion achieving ≥3% weight loss was 23.5% (4/17) in the intervention group and 5.6% (1/18) in the control group ( P =.18; odds ratio 5.23). Waist circumference significantly decreased in the intervention group compared to baseline ( t 16 =2.71, P=. 02), whereas no significant between-group differences were observed in weight, BMI, or psychological measures. The SMS delivery rate was 95.5%, with a total cost of JP¥ 15,264 over 12 weeks. The follow-up rate was 100%, and the ratings for satisfaction, utilization, and willingness to recommend were 3.5, 2.8, and 3.0 out of 5, respectively. Conclusions The findings support the feasibility and acceptability of an SMS text messaging intervention for health guidance among employed men younger than 40 years with obesity, although evidence of its effectiveness remains preliminary. Further research with larger samples is needed to evaluate its effectiveness and optimize the intervention.

Introduction Obesity is a major global health issue, with projections suggesting that by 2035, approximately 50% of the world’s population will be overweight or obese [ 1 ]. In Japan, given the risks of obesity-related health problems, a BMI of 25 kg/m² or higher is classified as obesity [ 2 ]. This differs from the World Health Organization classification, which defines obesity in adults as a BMI of 30 kg/m² or higher [ 3 ]. Obesity in men is characterized by its onset in young adulthood. According to the 2024 National Health and Nutrition Survey conducted by the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare, the prevalence of obesity (BMI ≥25 kg/m²) among Japanese adults was 25.3%; among men aged 20‐29 and 30‐39 years, the rates were 21.0% and 34.3%, respectively [ 4 ]. These findings suggest that intervention from young adulthood through early middle age is crucial. Factors contributing to obesity in this age group include work-related stress, irregular eating habits, and physical inactivity [ 5 ]. In individuals with obesity, the accumulation of visceral fat increases the risk of metabolic disorders and atherosclerotic diseases; however, weight loss achieved through lifestyle modifications can improve blood glucose levels, lipid levels, and blood pressure [ 2 ]. Therefore, interventions supporting lifestyle changes are crucial for the prevention and management of obesity. In Japan, specific health checkups and specific health guidance are conducted for individuals aged 40 years and older, and certain improvements have been reported [ 6 , 7 ]. Some reports also indicate that improvements in cardiovascular risk factors other than obesity have been limited [ 8 ]. On the other hand, health management support for employed men younger than 40 years, who are not eligible for specific health checkups, is primarily left to voluntary corporate initiatives; however, due to a shortage of occupational health professionals, many workplaces have difficulty providing sufficient support [ 9 ]. Evidence for obesity interventions targeting employed men younger than 40 years is also scarce. To the best of our knowledge, obesity intervention studies targeting young employed men are limited to a single report combining website use with face-to-face support [ 10 ]. Against this backdrop, there is a need to develop simple and feasible intervention methods for this population. In recent years, the spread of information and communication technology has led to the expansion of lifestyle improvement support using mobile health (mHealth). In obesity interventions, support using text messages has been reported to offer implementation advantages over app-based interventions, such as lower dropout rates and higher reach and open rates [ 11 , 12 ]. Although the effectiveness of SMS text messaging–based obesity interventions in adults has been demonstrated [ 13 ], the same review identified a lack of sufficient analysis of the sex-specific effects of SMS text messaging interventions as a key challenge. Men are significantly underrepresented in obesity intervention studies [ 14 , 15 ]; to the best of our knowledge, no randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have evaluated SMS text messaging as the primary intervention method for employed men younger than 40 years. Behavior change techniques (BCTs) constitute an internationally standardized framework based on intervention components common to numerous existing health behavior theories [ 16 , 17 ]. BCTs have been incorporated into text message interventions for various health issues and applied to improve physical activity and dietary habits [ 18 - 21 ]. The Game of Stones Trials is an example of a text message intervention designed to explicitly incorporate BCTs and target individuals with obesity. In this trial, narrative-style text messages incorporating BCTs were developed and evaluated in a multiarm parallel-group randomized controlled trial involving men with obesity aged 18 years or older with a BMI of 30 kg/m² or higher [ 22 ]. However, this study targeted the general adult male population, and findings on employed men younger than 40 years are limited. Therefore, this pilot randomized controlled trial aimed to assess the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary effectiveness of an SMS text messaging intervention among employed men younger than 40 years with obesity. Methods Overview This pilot randomized controlled trial was conducted to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary effectiveness of an SMS text messaging intervention focused on lifestyle self-management for weight management among employed men younger than 40 years. To strengthen the theoretical basis of the intervention, this study incorporated internationally standardized BCTs into an SMS intervention in Japan. Participants were randomly assigned to the intervention or control group. Owing to the nature of the intervention, neither the participants nor the principal investigator could be blinded to group allocation. Population The inclusion criteria were as follows: male workers aged 18‐39 years with a BMI of ≥25 kg/m², possession of a smartphone or mobile phone and ability to use SMS text messaging services and access the internet, ability to read and write Japanese and understand the study content, and participation in workplace health checkups. The exclusion criteria were as follows: work involving night shifts and current medical treatment for a pre-existing condition that prevents participation in healthy eating or physical activity for weight management. Workers engaged in night-shift work were excluded to reduce heterogeneity related to work schedules and associated differences in lifestyle patterns, such as eating and sleeping patterns, in this pilot study. Recruitment and Procedure Occupational physicians and occupational health nurses recruited participants from their workplaces using written or email invitations and workplace postings, as appropriate to each workplace. The participating workplaces were identified through the professional networks of the principal investigator and a coinvestigator. The researchers did not directly recruit employees. The recruitment period extended from December 2024 to April 2025 because the planned number of participants was not reached within the initial recruitment period. Participants who met the inclusion criteria received a QR code on the study website and provided informed consent. After obtaining consent, the occupational health nurses measured the participants’ weights and waist circumferences at the participating workplaces. Body weight was measured using a TANITA BC-315 body composition scale (Tanita Corporation). Waist circumference was measured using a seca 201 ergonomic circumference measuring tape (seca GmbH & Co KG). Height data for the BMI calculations were obtained from workplace health examination records. The participants completed a questionnaire, including demographic characteristics, using Google Forms. Follow-up assessments were completed in August 2025. Randomization Participants were randomly assigned to the intervention or control group in a 1:1 ratio using permuted block randomization with a block size of 2. Participants from the same workplace could be assigned to either the intervention or control group. Randomization was implemented using a Microsoft Excel–based tool incorporating the RAND function, which was prepared and provided by a statistician who was not involved in participant recruitment. After informed consent had been obtained and participant enrollment was completed, the principal investigator entered each participant into the randomization tool, which generated the group assignment. Thus, group allocation remained unknown until after participant enrollment. Owing to the nature of the intervention, neither the participants nor the principal investigator could be blinded to group allocation. However, the occupational health nurses who performed the outcome measurements were not informed of participants’ group allocation. The principal investigator conducted the statistical analyses and was aware of group allocation. Interventions Intervention Group At the start of the study, participants were given the March 2023 versions of the “Lifestyle Habits Review Notebook for Healthy Body Building (Men’s Edition)” and the “Lifestyle Improvement Record Sheet,” developed by the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare [ 23 ], to help them review and monitor their lifestyle habits. The pamphlet contained information on obesity and metabolic syndrome, physical activity and dietary habits, strategies for increasing physical activity and modifying dietary habits, weight-loss goal setting, and self-monitoring. The record sheet included fields for recording body weight, step count, two lifestyle improvement goals and their achievement, weekly satisfaction with their efforts, and comments. Over a 12-week period, health guidance on the self-management of lifestyle habits for weight management was provided via SMS text messaging 3 times per week. The technical platform used for sending text messages was the SMS messaging service provided by CM.com Japan Co Ltd. The intervention consisted of one-way SMS text messaging, and the participants were not asked to reply. Text messages were created by the principal investigator and the coinvestigator. The content of the messages addressed lifestyle behaviors and related factors relevant to weight management, including diet, alcohol consumption, physical activity, sleep, psychosocial and socioeconomic factors, and self-monitoring. These lifestyle domains were based on the 2022 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Obesity [ 2 ] and the Standard Health Checkup and Health Guidance Program (FY 2024 Edition) [ 24 ] (Table S1 in Multimedia Appendix 1 ). The intervention was not designed to prescribe a specific reduction in energy intake or increase in energy expenditure to achieve a predetermined energy deficit. To support behavior change within these lifestyle domains, 10 BCTs commonly identified across all 6 review articles included in our previously published narrative review [ 25 ] were used as the basis for the intervention design (Table S2 in Multimedia Appendix 1 ). During message development, the principal investigator primarily selected the BCT(s) to be incorporated into each message, and their appropriateness was reviewed with a coinvestigator. Neither researcher had completed formal BCT coding training. Independent BCT coding and formal assessment of interrater agreement were not conducted. Based on these lifestyle domains and BCTs, short messages and quiz-style messages were developed. The message content remained unchanged during the intervention. Multimedia Appendix 2 presents all text messages delivered during the intervention, together with the corresponding lifestyle domain(s) and BCT(s) for each message. URLs of web pages were included to provide additional explanations as needed. Messages were delivered 3 times per week (Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays) between 12:00 PM and 1:00 PM. During the development of the text messages, we solicited feedback on the draft messages from 5 research collaborators who were occupational health nurses and 4 men in their 20s and revised the text based on their input. The occupational health nurses reviewed the messages for accuracy, readability, and tone. As part of the formative evaluation, all text messages were sent to 4 men in their 20s to assess the clarity and readability of the messages, identify wording that they considered inappropriate or unclear, evaluate the appropriateness of the sending times, and ensure that there were no issues with transmission or reception. Additionally, to ensure the stable implementation of the intervention, a system was established in advance, whereby researchers could send messages directly from their research smartphones in the event of delivery problems. Control Group At the start of the study, participants were provided with the same pamphlet and record sheet as those provided to the intervention group. No additional text messages were sent during the intervention. Outcome Primary Outcome The effectiveness of the intervention was assessed based on the weight loss achievement rate from baseline to the 3-month follow-up assessment. Weight loss achievement was defined as a reduction of 3% or more of baseline body weight. The 2022 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Obesity recommend a reduction of at least 3% of current body weight as the initial weight-loss target and evaluation of treatment outcomes over 3‐6

title: Crisis Interventions for Children and Adolescents with Depression and Suicidality: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To review the evidence on crisis services for children and adolescents experiencing acute psychopathological crises, particularly severe depression, suicidal ideation, self-harm, and suicidal behaviour, and to examine their effectiveness in reducing symptoms, improving family functioning, and preventing hospitalisation.

RECENT FINDINGS: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO. Searches of PubMed, Web of Science, PsycInfo, and ClinicalTrials.gov identified 15 eligible studies evaluating 15 crisis interventions. Four interventions targeted suicidal ideation and self-harm through brief, structured approaches, demonstrating reductions in suicidal thoughts, suicide attempts, and emergency department visits. Seven family-focused interventions (evaluated in eight studies) improved communication, family cohesion, and reduced hospitalisation rates. Three interventions aimed to stabilise crises and facilitate linkage with community services, improving continuity of care and decreasing emergency service utilisation. One residential intervention (evaluated in two studies) showed mixed findings, with some behavioural improvements but limited effects on internalising symptoms. Current evidence suggests that crisis services might be a promising alternative to hospitalisation for children and adolescents experiencing acute mental health crises. These interventions provide intensive support within the young person's natural environment, promote family involvement, and were associated with reductions in suicidal ideation, depressive symptoms, emergency visits, and hospital admissions. Despite promising findings, the evidence base remains limited, largely observational and heterogeneous, and causal conclusions cannot be drawn. Future research should directly compare different crisis service models and include long-term follow-up to determine the most effective approaches and their sustainability over time.

title: Electroacupuncture Combined with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia Alleviates Insomnia-Anxiety Comorbidity in Gynecological Cancer Patients Undergoing Chemotherapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
Simple Summary Insomnia and anxiety often occur together in gynecological cancer patients receiving chemotherapy. These symptoms reduce quality of life and can interfere with treatment. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) helps many patients, but responses vary. This randomized trial tested whether adding electroacupuncture (EA) to CBT-I could improve outcomes. Seventy-six patients received either EA plus CBT-I or sham EA plus CBT-I for 4 weeks. The real EA group had better sleep, less insomnia, and lower anxiety. More patients in this group achieved meaningful improvement. Sleep tracker data also indicated increases in deeper sleep and REM sleep. No serious adverse effects occurred. These findings suggest that adding EA to CBT-I is a safe and effective option for this population.

Abstract Insomnia and anxiety affect many gynecological cancer patients on chemotherapy, and non-pharmacological options are limited. This randomized trial examined whether adding electroacupuncture (EA) to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) improves both conditions. Seventy-six patients received EA + CBT-I or sham EA + CBT-I for 4 weeks. Outcomes included sleep quality (PSQI), insomnia severity (AIS), anxiety (HAMA), objective sleep parameters, and overall response rate. At Week 4, the EA group showed a greater reduction in PSQI global score (mean difference in change from baseline: −3.11, 95% CI: −4.11 to −2.11, p < 0.001). More patients in the EA group achieved AIS ≤ 6 (71.1% vs. 42.1%, p = 0.010) and HAMA ≤ 14 (92.1% vs. 65.8%, p = 0.005). Deep sleep ( p = 0.001), REM sleep ( p = 0.045), and sleep score ( p = 0.008) also increased more with EA group. The overall response rate was higher with EA (92.1% vs. 71.1%, p = 0.016). No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that adding EA to CBT-I improves sleep and anxiety in this population, with a favorable safety profile.

1. Introduction Insomnia symptoms—difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or early morning awakening—affect 30% to 60% of cancer patients, well above the 10% to 20% observed in the general population [ 1 , 2 ]. These figures come mainly from self-reported symptom scales rather than structured diagnostic interviews, and they cover mixed cancer populations and treatment stages. Among gynecological cancer patients, the risk is even higher. Female sex, hormone changes after surgery, and chemotherapy neurotoxicity all play a role [ 3 ]. Poor sleep in these patients lowers quality of life, weakens immune function, and may reduce treatment adherence and worsen cancer outcomes [ 4 ]. Sleep and immunity also are also closely linked: poor sleep promotes inflammation, which may in turn drive tumor progression and treatment resistance [ 5 ]. Insomnia and anxiety frequently coexist in cancer patients, with comorbidity rates of 30–50%. Patients with both conditions generally have more severe symptoms and poorer treatment responses than those with either condition alone [ 6 ]. Some observational studies have also linked insomnia symptoms to poorer overall survival in cancer patients, although these findings are correlational and cannot establish causality [ 7 ]. Common mechanisms include HPA axis over-activity, GABA and serotonin dysregulation, and chronic low-grade inflammation [ 8 ]. This suggests that insomnia and anxiety reflect a shared underlying dysregulation and should be treated together rather than as separate problems [ 9 ]. Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs, commonly used for insomnia, carry risks of tolerance, dependence, daytime sedation, and interactions with chemotherapies [ 10 ]. These risks, together with many cancer patients’ preference for non-drug options, have driven interest in behavioral and mind–body approaches [ 11 ]. CBT-I is the first-line non-pharmacological treatment and has shown benefit in cancer survivors [ 12 ]. However, many patients do not achieve full remission with CBT-I alone. Its effect on co-occurring anxiety is limited, especially in the short term, and delivering CBT-I requires time and trained staff, which are often in short supply in oncology clinics [ 13 ]. Over the past 20 years, acupuncture has become increasingly integrated into cancer care, with evidence supporting its effects on pain, nausea, and fatigue, and newer data suggesting benefits for sleep and mood problems [ 14 ]. Electroacupuncture (EA) was selected over manual acupuncture for several reasons. EA provides standardized, reproducible stimulation parameters, which reduces variability between practitioners and enhances methodological rigor. A recent Bayesian network meta-analysis of acupuncture therapies for insomnia found that EA ranked favorably for improving sleep efficiency [ 15 ]. EA has also been investigated specifically for insomnia during systemic cancer therapy; a meta-analysis of randomized trials in breast cancer patients showed significant improvements in sleep outcomes [ 16 ]. Furthermore, EA has demonstrated anxiolytic effects in clinical and preclinical studies, potentially through modulation of HPA axis activity, GABAergic transmission, and neuroimmune pathways [ 17 ]. It has also been used safely during chemotherapy without evidence of increased adverse events or interference with chemotherapy efficacy. Key questions remain. Few studies have focused specifically on acupuncture for insomnia–anxiety comorbidity in gynecological cancer patients receiving active chemotherapy [ 18 , 19 ]. Most existing trials have small samples, lack sham controls, or rely only on subjective measures [ 20 ]. It is also unclear whether adding acupuncture to CBT-I provides extra benefit—a question with direct clinical relevance. To address these questions, we designed a randomized, sham-controlled trial based on the “Tiaoshen Ningxin” acupuncture principle. This traditional Chinese medicine framework focuses on regulating the “brain spirit” through Governor Vessel points (Baihui GV20, Shenting GV24) and calming the “heart spirit” through Heart Meridian points (Shenmen HT7), with the addition of Yintang (EX-HN3) and electroacupuncture applied at Baihui and Yintang. We hypothesized that this protocol, combined with CBT-I, would improve insomnia and anxiety more than sham acupuncture plus CBT-I. The primary aim was to assess efficacy and safety; secondary aims included objective sleep measurement with wearable trackers and exploration of possible mechanisms. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Design and Participants This single-center randomized controlled trial was conducted at the Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital of Fudan University (Shanghai, China) between May 2023 and August 2025. The trial was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2300071082) on 4 May 2023 and approved by the hospital’s Ethics Committee (2022-188) on 27 February 2023. All participants provided written informed consent. The trial was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and CONSORT reporting guidelines. Eligible patients were 20 to 70 years of age with histologically confirmed gynecological malignancy (ovarian, cervical, endometrial, vulvar, vaginal, uterine sarcoma, or gestational trophoblastic neoplasia) and comorbid insomnia and anxiety. At enrollment, all patients were receiving active chemotherapy. Randomization and baseline assessments took place during a scheduled chemotherapy cycle, and the 4-week intervention period overlapped with ongoing chemotherapy. Insomnia was diagnosed using the Chinese Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Insomnia in Adults (2017) [ 21 ]. Anxiety was defined as a HAMA score > 14, indicating clinically significant anxiety symptoms [ 22 ]. A formal DSM-5 diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder was not required. Key exclusion criteria were use of sleep medications within 2 weeks before enrollment, severe organ dysfunction or psychiatric disorders unrelated to the primary cancer diagnosis, and concurrent participation in another interventional trial. 2.2. Randomization and Blinding Eligible participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the EA + CBT-I group or the sham EA + CBT-I group. The randomization sequence was computer-generated (SPSS 21.0) by an independent biostatistician and concealed in sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes. The acupuncturists who delivered the treatment could not be masked to group assignment. However, outcome assessors—who administered the PSQI, AIS, and HAMA scales, collected sleep tracker data, and documented adverse events—remained blinded to allocation, as did the statistician who performed the final analysis. 2.3. Intervention Protocol All participants received standard chemotherapy and routine supportive care according to institutional protocols. CBT-I (both groups): Both groups received a 4-week CBT-I program delivered in weekly sessions by trained therapists. The CBT-I program followed the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) definition, comprising sleep hygiene education, stimulus control, sleep restriction therapy, cognitive therapy, and relaxation therapy. Sleep restriction was adjusted based on daily sleep diaries. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 randomized controlled trials ( n = 1803) supports the efficacy of CBT-I in cancer survivors [ 23 ]. EA group: Patients received electroacupuncture three times per week (every other day) for 4 weeks (12 sessions total). Four acupoints were selected based on the “Tiaoshen Ningxin” (regulating the spirit and calming the heart) principle: Baihui (GV20) and Shenting (GV24) on the Governor Vessel, which connects to the brain; Yintang (EX-HN3) to calm the spirit; and Shenmen (HT7), the Yuan-source point of the Heart Meridian, traditionally used for insomnia and anxiety. Acupoint locations followed the GB/T 12346-2021 standard [ 24 ]. Sterile disposable needles (0.25 mm × 25 mm; Suzhou Medical Supplies Factory Co., Ltd., Suzhou, China) were used. Shenmen was needled perpendicularly to a depth of 7–10 mm; the remaining points were inserted at a 15° angle to a depth of 10–20 mm. Manual stimulation was applied to elicit deqi. Electroacupuncture (SDZ-V, Hwato ® , Suzhou, China) was then applied to Baihui and Yintang using a continuous wave at 2 Hz, with intensity adjusted to each patient’s comfort (typically 1–4 mA), for 30 min per session. A similar acupoint combination has been reported to reduce HPA axis activity in patients with chronic insomnia, lowering serum CRH, ACTH, and CORT levels [ 25 ]. Electroacupuncture at Baihui and Yintang also appears to modulate activity in sleep-related brain regions [ 17 , 26 ]. Sham EA group: The control group received sham electroacupuncture on the same schedule and at the same points. We placed blunt-tip placebo needles, identical in appearance to real needles, over the skin through adhesive pads without penetrating it. The needles were connected to an electroacupuncture device via internally disconnected leads; the device appeared active but delivered no current. Patients were told they might not feel the stimulation because it was a “microcurrent”. Co-interventions: Additional sleep medications (including benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, and sedating antihistamines), acupuncture, and psychological therapy were not allowed during the study. We permitted analgesics (including opioids), antidepressants, and anxiolytics if they had been started at least 4 weeks before enrollment and the dose remained stable throughout the study period. We recorded any changes in these medications. Chemotherapy and supportive care medications (e.g., antiemetics, corticosteroids) were allowed as clinically indicated and were recorded. 2.4. Outcome Measures All outcome assessments were carried out at baseline, Week 2, and Week 4 by assessors blinded to group allocation. The primary outcome was change in PSQI global score from baseline to Week 4. The PSQI is a 19-item self-report questionnaire with seven component scores (0–3 each) and a global score (0–21); higher scores indicate poorer sleep quality [ 27 ]. Because sleep medication use was an exclusion criterion at baseline and was not permitted during the study, we excluded the sleep medication component from the global score. The modified global score therefore ranged from 0 to 18. This modification is consistent with prior research that used a modified PSQI in populations with restricted hypnotic use [ 28 ]. Item response theory analyses have shown that the sleep medication component has the lowest discrimination parameter of the seven PSQI components, which supports excluding it when medication use is not relevant [ 29 ]. This avoids inflating the global score due to medication use and ensures that the score reflects sleep quality and disturbance rather than pharmacological treatment. The Cronbach’s α for the modified PSQI (6 components) was 0.72 in this study. Secondary outcomes included: Insomnia severity was measured using the Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS), an 8-item self-report scale with a total score ranging from 0 to 24 [ 30 ]. Scores above 6 indicate insomnia, 4–6 suspected insomnia, and below 4 no insomnia [ 30 , 31 ]. Internal consistency for the AIS was not calculated in this study; however, prior validation studies have reported a Cronbach’s α of approximately 0.90 [ 30 ]. Anxiety was assessed with the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA), a 14-item clinician-rated instrument with a total score ranging from 0 to 56 [ 32 ]. Scores above 14 indicate clinical anxiety, 7–14 suspected anxiety, and below 7 no anxiety [ 33 ]. Internal consistency for the HAMA was not calculated in this study; however, prior validation studies have reported a Cronbach’s α of approximately 0.89 [ 34 ]. The HAMA has also been validated in cancer populations [ 35 ]. Objective sleep parameters were recorded using a HUAWEI Band 8 (Huawei Device Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, China) worn on the non-dominant wrist throughout the study. The device uses the HUAWEI TruSleep 3.0 algorithm to estimate sleep stages and generate a sleep score (0–100), with higher scores indicating better sleep quality. This specific device has not been validated against polysomnography in a clinical population; however, the HUAWEI TruSleep algorithm has been evaluated in other Huawei wearable models, showing acceptable agreement with polysomnography for sleep/wake detection in Chinese clinical populations [ 36 ]. Measurements were obtained at baseline, Week 2, and Week 4. Comprehensive efficacy was graded according to the PSQI reduction rate, calculated as [(baseline total score—post-treatment total score)/baseline total score] × 100%. We classified efficacy as clinically cured (reduction ≥ 75%, nocturnal sleep ≥ 6 h, no disturbing dreams, and refreshed awakening); markedly effective (50% ≤ reduction < 75%, sleep improved with ≥3 h increase); effective (25% ≤ reduction < 50%, symptoms alleviated with <3 h increase); or ineffective (reduction < 25%, no im

title: Context Matters, Doesn't It? The Role of Context in Everyday Emotion Regulation Strategy Use
abstract: A common maxim holds that "context is everything." This perspective transformed the field of emotion regulation, which evolved from understanding  which  regulation strategies people use, to understanding  how  strategy use varies by context (i.e., strategy-situation fit). Theoretical accounts suggest contextual features are crucial in guiding strategy use. However, empirical evidence is isolated in piecemeal studies with inconclusive results. To comprehensively explore context-dependent emotion regulation, we need data on emotion regulation across many contexts, at scale. Combining up to 11 experience-sampling data sets collected from Belgian and Australian samples in an integrative analysis ( N ID  = 500-1,696,  N observations  = 27,023-101,114,  M age  = 25.38 years, 71% women), we examined how regulation-strategy use varies as a function of three theory-derived contextual features- intensity ,  controllability , and  social features  (i.e., the presence and closeness of others). We found limited support that context matters for daily emotion-regulation strategy use. Our study provides a well-powered foundational step to test a theory central to emotion-regulation research and highlights the complexity of capturing strategy-situation fit in daily life.

title: How we see relations: The case of containment and support
abstract: To navigate and act in the environment, it is necessary to recognize objects and the relationships between them. Recognition of objects in visual scenes is rapid and automatic. Are relations between objects in a scene also extracted rapidly and automatically during perception? Here, we considered containment and support, two relations that are fundamental to our understanding of the physical world. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography on human subjects, we measured stimulus-driven neural responses during rapid visual presentation of images (4 Hz), with a periodic oddball structure to isolate the selective response to object pairs presented side-by-side (e.g., a book and a table) versus two objects in support or containment relations (e.g., a book on a table). We found enhanced responses to objects in support/containment relations (vs. objects side-by-side) when a relation was instantiated by different exemplars of the same scene (e.g., a book on a table), but not by different scenes involving distinct object categories (e.g., a book on a table, a lamp on a stand, a laptop on a desk). These findings indicate that, during scene perception, relations are extracted in a format that generalizes within, but not across, types of visual scenes. We propose that, during perception, relations are not represented as discrete, abstract tokens ("in" or "on") but rather as objects' properties, such that changes in the objects entail changes in the relational representation. These results provide new insight into the perceptual foundations of relational processing underlying physical reasoning. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: Investigating how reward retroactively improves memory for associations and items: A registered report
abstract: Given we cannot remember all our experiences, it seems intuitive that we should prioritize events of consequence, like those that lead to a reward. However, rewards have had inconsistent effects on people's memory for preceding neutral experiences in experiments, raising questions as to whether our minds are equipped to remember adaptively. Here, we used online testing in a registered report to investigate whether rewards tend to retroactively enhance certain types of memories. Consistent with prior research and theories involving how dopamine modulates the hippocampus, we hypothesized that reward would retroactively enhance memory in a delay-dependent manner, emerging only after a period of consolidation. Crucially, we further predicted that this long-delay modulation of memory would be stronger for associative memory than for item recognition-a factor not previously considered despite its clear theoretical grounding. Our planned confirmatory analyses did not reveal any evidence for retroactive effects of reward on either associative or item memory. However, in exploratory analyses examining only individuals who were behaviorally sensitive to the reward manipulation, as measured by an independent task, we found evidence that reward retroactively enhanced associative-but not item-memory in a delay-dependent manner. This work sheds light on important open questions about the mechanisms by which reward retroactively enhances memory, elucidating the conditions under which this key aspect of adaptive memory emerges. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: Stronger mnemonic prediction errors can disproportionately impair memory updating in older adults
abstract: Mnemonic prediction errors are discrepancies between memory-based expectations and actual events that can trigger memory updating. However, the conditions under which these prediction errors result in successful memory updating, and whether these effects vary between younger and older adults, remain less understood. In two experiments, the present study investigated how prediction strength affects memory for events that violated memory-based expectations in younger and older adults. Prediction strength was manipulated by first presenting three-word sequences (i.e., trains), each with exemplars from the same category ( Bluejay-Hawk-Eagle ), either once or four times. Predictions based on memory for trains were then confirmed by repeating sequences entirely ( Bluejay-Hawk-Eagle ) or violated by repeating the first two words and changing the ending word ( Bluejay-Hawk-Robin ). Differences in prediction strength, created by varying repetitions, were validated using retrospective judgments (Experiment 1) and prospective predictions of original train endings along with confidence ratings (Experiment 2). Prediction error effects on memory updating were assessed by presenting the first two words of trains as cues for recalling changed ending words. Stronger predictions impaired memory for changed endings disproportionately for older adults, and older adults were less able to recollect that endings had changed when asked directly. Regardless of prediction strength and age, change recollection was consistently associated with better memory for changed ending words. Collectively, these findings suggest that stronger mnemonic predictions exacerbate the negative impact of prediction errors on the resolution of proactive interference, an ability that is often impaired in healthy aging. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: Strength-based organizational approaches facilitate workplace opportunities for people from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds
abstract: The workplace stands as one of the most powerful drivers of societal (in)equality. For employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds, it can represent both a ticket toward upward mobility and a consequential source of stigma. Four studies build on emerging strength-based research to test whether workplaces can challenge this stigma by creating overarching cultures that recognize the beneficial skills employees gain from their otherwise marginalized identities. Study 1 provided foundational insights into these "strength-based organizational approaches" and their implications for key outcomes derived from the State Authenticity as Fit to Environment model. Employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds were especially unlikely to report that their workplaces valued their identities and associated skills, which partially explained subsequent disparities in employees' broad sense of comfort and efficacy at work. Studies 2a and 2b established these patterns experimentally by demonstrating that exposing participants to a workplace that does communicate a strength-based organizational approach facilitated these professionally productive outcomes while increasing participants' likelihood of disclosing their marginalized identities within a job application task. Study 3 extended these findings to consider how the approaches may also indirectly expand employees' equitable access to opportunity through reducing common biases among their supervisors. Randomly assigning workplace supervisors to briefly engage with a company that highlighted the value of employees' lower socioeconomic status backgrounds increased supervisors' positive evaluations and likelihood of promoting these employees by 38% relative to an active control condition. Collectively, these preregistered findings illuminate new opportunities to improve workplace functioning and pinpoint the organizational forces underlying person-context interactions. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: Children can suppress salient distractors
abstract: From a very young age, our perceptual system is particularly sensitive to salient events. When such events are irrelevant, adults can prevent them from capturing attention by suppressing the salient features and by prioritizing task-relevant information. Previous research suggests that both distractor-suppression and target-prioritization mechanisms are not yet fully developed at ages 5-6. However, this work has not clearly disentangled the two mechanisms. Here, we specifically investigated whether children can suppress the salient feature of an irrelevant distractor. Two groups of children (aged 5-6 and 8-9) searched for a shape-defined target among heterogeneously shaped nontargets. All items had the same color throughout the experiment, but on two thirds of the trials, one item (the singleton distractor) had a unique color that changed at the beginning of each block. We expected this distractor to interfere with search performance during the first half of each block (i.e., when its color was novel). The critical question was whether this interference would be reduced during the second block half (i.e., with enough experience with the distractor's color). This finding would indicate that the children suppressed the salient distractor color. We found clear evidence for feature-based suppression, and this effect was similar for the two age groups. These findings indicate that feature-based suppression develops early and may already be established by ages 5-6. More broadly, they are consistent with accounts in which suppression emerges through implicit learning or habituation-like mechanisms that are operational early in development. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: Beliefs about the causal interdependence of virtues and vices
abstract: How do people think different positive and negative moral traits (i.e., virtues and vices) affect one another? For example, do they think that improving one virtue (e.g., honesty) will facilitate improvements in another virtue (e.g., compassion)? Do people believe in "master virtues" that, when improved, have disproportionate positive impacts on other moral virtues? Here, we examine perceived causal interdependence among 15 moral virtues and 13 moral vices. Across four studies, participants indicated their beliefs about how increasing their virtues would impact their other virtues (Study 1; 275 Prolific participants), how increasing their vices would impact their other vices (Study 2; 423 undergraduate students), and how increases in virtues would affect vices (or vice versa; Studies 3 and 4; 337 undergraduate students and 298 Prolific participants). We find people generally believe in facilitation effects, where improving one trait improves other traits and worsening one trait worsens other traits. Specifically, people believe that increasing one virtue tends to increase other virtues (Study 1) and decrease other vices (Studies 3 and 4). Similarly, people believe that increasing one vice tends to increase other vices (Study 2) and decrease other virtues (Studies 3 and 4). Perceived trade-offs were rare and involved laziness and cowardice decreasing or being decreased by other vices. There was little evidence for beliefs in a "master virtue." However, we find some evidence that people think cruelty and greed are disproportionately impactful "master vices." These results enhance our understanding of lay moral concepts by painting a comprehensive picture of people's beliefs about the causal interdependence among moral virtues and vices. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: Time to jump: Exploring the distribution of noise in evidence accumulation as a function of time pressure
abstract: The diffusion model conceptualizes binary decisions as emerging from continuous evidence accumulation with Gaussian noise. The Lévy-flight model (LFM) extends this by allowing accumulation noise to follow a heavier-tailed distribution, enabling sudden, large jumps in evidence accumulation. The heavy-tailedness is governed by the stability parameter α, with smaller α-values indicating more frequent and larger jumps. We demonstrate through simulation that the LFM can generate near-symmetrical response time (RT) distributions typical under strict deadlines. In Study 1, we explored the influence of intense time pressure on α in a letter-number discrimination task, expecting higher time pressure to entail smaller α-values. Participants (N = 341) were assigned to an accuracy (unlimited RT), implicit deadline (feedback discouraging RTs over 500 ms), or explicit deadline condition (timeout at 500 ms). Given the LFM's intractable likelihood, we used BayesFlow, a framework for simulation-based inference with deep learning. Model comparisons consistently favored the LFM over diffusion model variants-even in the accuracy condition. Importantly, α-values decreased with increasing time pressure and were especially low in the explicit deadline condition, where RT distributions also approached symmetry. Estimating both the LFM and a structurally matched diffusion model, with and without timeout modeling, further showed that accounting for timeout-related RT truncation led to substantially lower diffusion model drift rates, whereas LFM drift rates changed only modestly. Study 2 (N = 160) replicated α's sensitivity to time pressure in a brightness discrimination task. Overall, α responded systematically to temporal constraints across both tasks and timeout modeling specifications.

title: Cross-linguistic semantic stability as a driving force of diachronic semantic evolution across lexica
abstract: Word meanings change over time, yet the extent of change varies systematically within each lexicon. Although frequency, age of acquisition, and concreteness have been identified as within-language predictors, a language-general account of why some concepts show greater resistance to diachronic semantic change across languages remains elusive. Here, we propose that cross-linguistic semantic stability - the degree to which a concept's semantic neighborhood is conserved across languages - as a concept-level predictor of diachronic semantic change. We operationalized stability as neighborhood overlap between a target concept's nearest neighbors in English and the back-translated neighbors of its translation equivalents across 10 to 41 languages, and quantified diachronic change as neighborhood turnover in historical embeddings spanning up to 100 years in English, French, German, and Chinese. Higher cross-linguistic stability predicted less diachronic semantic change in each language and in an aggregated analysis of concepts shared across the four languages. This effect dominated all other predictors for shared concepts; remained significant after established psycholinguistic predictors were controlled; was represented as a direct conditional edge in partial-correlation networks; remained robust as the cross-linguistically shared concept set was expanded; and was replicated using historically derived stability estimates. Together, these findings reveal the topological consistency of a concept's semantic neighborhood across languages is a temporally durable, concept-level predictor of resistance to semantic change, linking synchronic cross-linguistic conceptual structure with diachronic lexical evolution across lexica.

title: General versus specific: Investigating the structure of individual differences in post-error slowing across time
abstract: Erroneous actions are typically followed by behavioral slowing, known as post-error slowing (PES), along with other post-error adjustments. These effects emerge on the first trial following an error and can persist across subsequent trials. While PES has been extensively studied experimentally, less attention has been given to inter-individual variability. Evidence suggests that the mechanisms underlying individual differences in PES are largely domain-general, spanning multiple tasks. However, as time elapses from the point of error, task-specific processes may increasingly influence these individual differences. In this study, we applied latent variable modeling to two large samples of participants who completed three canonical inhibitory control paradigms. Our findings indicate that individual differences in PES reflect both domain-general and task-specific abilities, with the influence of the domain-general factor seeming to decrease over time following error commission.

title: Universal patterns in the acquisition of negation and disjunction: Parallels between L1 and L2
abstract: A fundamental question in language acquisition is how learners balance input and prior knowledge to infer meaning. Here, we present novel evidence about the mechanisms guiding adults' second language learning. We examined their interpretation of disjunction ("or") in negative sentences (e.g., "John didn't eat the cucumber or the pepper") as a test case. Languages vary in the assignment of scope to logical operators such as negation and disjunction, depending on their syntactic relationship. When multiple interpretations are possible, how do learners assign meaning? Does the native language of L2 learners influence this process? We report three key findings. First, native speakers of Mandarin and Spanish prefer an interpretation where "or" scopes over negation, meaning "John ate either the cucumber or the pepper, but not both" (the "not both" superset interpretation), whereas L2 learners from both backgrounds favor the opposite, subset (stronger) interpretation, where "John ate neither vegetable" (the "neither" subset interpretation). This pattern resembles child first language acquisition. Second, this preference persists even when the surface order of negation and disjunction does not match the native speaker's preferred interpretation, indicating that learners reconstruct underlying structure during interpretation, rather than rely on surface cues. Third, this tendency is stronger in less proficient learners and shifts with increasing proficiency. These findings suggest that L2 learners employ strategies similar to those of children acquiring their first language, initially favoring the stronger possible interpretation. These results shed new light on universal mechanisms guiding both first and second language acquisition.

title: The emergence of language-specific biases in visual attention in pre-reading toddlers from two cultures
abstract: Skilled adult readers show biases in their visual attention that reflect the direction of their native writing systems (e.g., English readers scan left-to-right while Hebrew readers scan right-to-left), but it not yet clear when these biases develop. We tested the hypothesis that language-specific patterns of behavior precede the ability to read by testing how toddlers (2.5-4 years) exposed to different writing systems allocated their attention in a picture naming task. Across two communities, children tended to name objects in the direction that matched their native language. Hebrew-learning toddlers labeled objects from right-to-left, while English- and Spanish-learning toddlers showed the reverse pattern, and language-specific tendencies strengthened with age. These results demonstrate that children have begun to discover directional regularities associated with their language even before they receive literacy instruction and illustrate how cultural conventions exert a direct influence on children's attention from a very young age.

title: Working- and long-term memory target templates converge to produce coactive guidance of attention during visual search
abstract: Templates that guide attention during visual search can be maintained in visual working memory (VWM) or in long-term memory (LTM). A central challenge for theories of attention is explaining how these sources of bias combine to determine selection. Here, we tested whether they converge on a common priority signal. Specifically, we contrasted a coactive model of guidance, assuming convergence, with three non-coactive alternatives, each holding that guidance from VWM and LTM operate independently. Participants searched for the presence of a target defined by either of two cued colors. One cued color changed on each trial (dynamic, engaging VWM), whereas the other remained constant (static, engaging LTM). The target could match either one of the cued colors (single-target trials) or both (redundant-target trials). Through distributional analysis, we tested for the presence of redundant-target RTs that were faster than could have been generated by the two individual guidance processes operating independently in parallel. Such "violations" of the race model inequality (RMI) are observed only within a coactive system. For single-target trials, searches were substantially more efficient for dynamic-match targets than for static-match targets. Nevertheless, we observed robust violations of the RMI on redundant-target trials. Together, these results demonstrate that target templates can be maintained in qualitatively different states yet ultimately converge to jointly influence a common attentional priority signal.

title: Unpacking the dynamics of cross-situational word learning strategies through trial-by-trial analysis: effects of word frequency distribution and learning context
abstract: Word learning in natural environments often relies on cross-situational word learning (CSWL), whereby learners acquire word meanings from word-referent co-occurrences across different situations. Natural language follows Zipfian distributions where a few words occur very frequently while most occur rarely. However, how Zipfian distributions affect CSWL and how learning mechanisms vary across different contexts remain unclear. We addressed these questions in four CSWL experiments with adults. Experiments 1 (N = 36) and 2 (N = 38) found that Zipfian distributions may promote CSWL performance through prospective mutual exclusivity, whereby established mappings support the incremental disambiguation of new words, suggesting that the effectiveness of mutual exclusivity depends on contextual knowledge. Experiments 3 (N = 32) and 4 (N = 42) used trial-by-trial analyses to examine learning mechanisms under Zipfian and uniform distributions across varying levels of within-trial situational ambiguity, randomization, and contextual diversity. The Zipfian advantage emerged under high within-trial ambiguity, while its facilitative effect on associative learning required high contextual diversity. Moreover, hypothesis testing reduced reliance on associative learning under low within-trial ambiguity but enhanced it under high ambiguity. Together, these findings informed the Contextually Modulated Integrative Model of CSWL, in which the effects of Zipfian distributions and the interplay among learning mechanisms depend on learning context. The present study further advances the integrative model of CSWL and clarifies the sources of the Zipfian advantage.

title: Mentalization as a mechanism for constructing meaning under ambiguity
abstract: Pseudowords lack conventional lexical meanings, but growing evidence suggests that they can nevertheless elicit structured (semantic) interpretations. The present study (N = 103) tested whether individual differences in mentalization are related to how people construct meanings for novel verbal stimuli. Participants generated definitions for real words and pseudowords and completed three mentalization-related measures: the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI), the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET), and the Triangles task. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA), we examined whether participants who were similar in mentalization-related profiles were also similar in their definition profiles. IRI and RMET response-profile similarity showed no evidence of an association with definition similarity, while similarity in open-ended descriptions of Triangles Theory-of-Mind animations predicted similarity in pseudoword definitions, but not real-word definitions. This association remained significant after controlling for similarity in Triangles control Action-clip descriptions, suggesting that it was not reducible to shared verbal-response format or general description style. Additional reconstruction analyses showed that pseudoword-definition embeddings can partially recover the participant-level representational geometry of Theory-of-Mind descriptions. These findings suggest that novel meaning construction is not only a lexical-semantic process but is also aligned with broader interpretive tendencies involved in assigning coherent social meaning to ambiguous experience, with implications for understanding the links between semantic cognition, mentalization, and developmental word learning.

title: Effects of active learning and talker variability on preschoolers' novel word learning
abstract: Words sound different every time they are said, both by the same person and across people. This variability has been found to have mixed effects on learning, sometimes benefitting learning and other times making it more challenging. However, all prior studies investigating effects of talker variability have used passive exposure, presenting participants with predetermined orders or fixed types of variability. Here, we used a novel active learning paradigm wherein 3- and 4-year old preschoolers could choose who to hear words from during word learning. Then, we tested whether participants seek out variability during word learning, how these talker variability choices influence word learning and whether actively making these choices results in different outcomes than passively receiving them. We find that preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers, but that talker variability does not predict word learning. Taken together, our results suggest that preschool aged children do seek out variability, but that word learning outcomes are most predicted by their relative vocabulary sizes and not talker variability choices. These results inform theories on the roles of both talker variability and active learning in language learning.

title: Whole-blood lead-copper association in children with autism spectrum disorder: Implications for toxic-essential metal interactions
abstract: Lead (Pb) is a developmental neurotoxicant that can interfere with essential-metal regulation, whereas copper (Cu) is a tightly regulated redox-active trace element required for normal neurological function. This study investigated whether whole-blood Pb concentrations were associated with whole-blood Cu concentrations in 28 children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), compared with 28 pediatric controls closely matched for age and with the same sex distribution. Mean whole-blood Pb concentration was 70.29 ± 31.34 µg/L in the ASD group and 47.99 ± 13.95 µg/L in controls. Pb concentrations were higher in ASD (geometric mean ratio 1.394, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.146-1.697, p = 0.001). Within the ASD group, Pb was positively associated with Cu (Pearson r = 0.385, 95% CI 0.014-0.663, p = 0.043), with a regression slope of 1.940 µg/L Cu per 1 µg/L Pb (95% CI 0.067-3.813; R² = 0.148). After adjustment for age and sex, the Pb coefficient remained similar in magnitude (β = 1.765, 95% CI - 0.174 to 3.704, p = 0.072). The Pb-Cu correlation was not significant in controls, and there was no evidence that the Pb-Cu association differed between the ASD and control groups. The association remained directionally consistent across additional sensitivity analyses, and adjustment for Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) score did not materially alter the Pb coefficient. The findings are compatible with experimental evidence on Pb-Cu interactions and Cu homeostasis but do not establish causality or ASD-specific Pb-Cu coupling. Replication in larger, prospectively characterized cohorts is required.

title: Longitudinal relationship between sleep and emotional/behavioral problems in autism spectrum disorders: a cross-lagged panel analysis
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Sleep, emotional, and behavioral problems are common comorbidities associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Current longitudinal research on the temporal links between sleep problems and emotional-behavioral problems shows inconsistent results among preschool children with ASD. Hence, this longitudinal study aimed to examine the temporal associations between emotional-behavioral and sleep problems among preschool children with ASD across two time points. Among 124 enrolled preschool children with ASD, 70 completed follow-up and constituted the final analytic sample (mean age 36.7 ± 10.2 months at T1). They were evaluated for developmental quotient using the Griffiths Development Scales-Chinese version (GDS-C), ASD symptoms using Autism Behavior Checklist (ABC) and Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), emotional and behavioral problems using the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL), and sleep problems using the Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ) at time 1 (T1). The evaluations were replicated at a follow-up appointment 18 months after T1 (time 2; T2). The cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) was employed to examine the potential relationship between CBCL and CSHQ scores in the children. The total CBCL score at T1 could predict the CSHQ at T2 (β = 0.348, t = 3.105, p = 0.002), whereas the CSHQ at T1 could not predict the CBCL at T2 (β = 0.117, t = 1.083, p = 0.279). Findings remained robust across five sensitivity subsets after excluding subgroups with distinct rehabilitation exposure, younger age, higher development quotients, girls, or mild ASD symptoms.

CONCLUSION: Emotional-behavioral problems predict sleep problems 18 months later in preschool ASD children. Screening of these symptoms during follow-up supports early sleep-risk monitoring.

WHAT IS KNOWN: • Sleep, emotional, and behavioral problems are common comorbidities associated with ASD. • Thus, researching their temporal correlation over time is necessary.

WHAT IS NEW: • Emotional and behavioral problems indicate a positive temporal correlation at T1, which was also evident for sleep problems at T2, in children with ASD. • Emotional and behavioral problems in preschool children with ASD can forecast sleep problems that develop 18 months later, providing guidance for clinical decision-making.

title: Association of Copy Number Variations in PTEN with Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract:
Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with a strong genetic basis. While copy number variations (CNVs) significantly contribute to ASD risk, the specific role of individual genes within these variants remains unclear. This study investigates the contribution of CNVs in the PTEN gene to ASD pathophysiology by integrating population-level genetic analysis with multi-dimensional biological evidence. Methods: The biological plausibility of PTEN in ASD was first assessed using public multi-omics data, including tissue expression profiles, protein-protein interaction networks, and published cell-type-specific differential-expression data derived from single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Subsequently, a group-matched case-control study was conducted in a Han Chinese population (121 ASD cases and 110 controls) to evaluate the association between PTEN CNVs and ASD susceptibility. One-way ANOVA was performed to compare the differences in ASD clinical phenotype scores among groups with different CNV types of PTEN . Results: Integrative biological analyses revealed that PTEN is enriched in ASD-relevant brain regions (e.g., cerebellum) and exhibits cell-type-specific expression in neurons and glia. Furthermore, protein network analysis confirmed its central position within the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, a critical regulator of neurodevelopment. In the Han Chinese population, no significant association was detected between PTEN CNVs and ASD risks or clinical phenotype scores. Conclusions: PTEN CNVs may not be independently associated with ASD, but may contribute to susceptibility through broader neurodevelopmental networks and molecular pathways.

1. Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is an early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by deficits in social communication and the presence of restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, with a global prevalence of approximately 1% among children [ 1 ]. Family studies consistently demonstrate that ASD exhibits exceptionally high heritability (approximately 80–90%), underscoring the predominant role of genetic factors in its etiology [ 2 ]. Current research is limited by the extreme heterogeneity of ASD, the low individual predictive power of common variants, and the pleiotropic nature of rare variants. Although approximately 10–20% of ASD cases can be attributed to identifiable rare genetic variants, and the heritability of ASD is estimated to be as high as 80%, the high heritability has not yet been effectively translated into clearly actionable clinical findings [ 2 , 3 ]. Therefore, expanding our understanding of ASD-associated genetic variants and their functional implications remains a critical priority for advancing biological insights into this disorder. In recent years, advances in chromosomal microarray analysis and high-throughput sequencing have firmly established CNVs—defined as deletions or duplications of DNA segments larger than 1 kb—as a major source of genetic risk for ASD [ 4 , 5 , 6 ]. Pathogenic CNVs are estimated to account for approximately 5% to 10% of ASD cases, with a notably higher contribution when the affected genes are critical for neurodevelopment or signaling regulation [ 7 ]. Our previous genome-wide CNV analysis in a Northeast Han Chinese population identified multiple rare CNV events and 20 candidate genes associated with ASD risk, including PTEN [ 8 ]. However, CNV regions typically encompass multiple genes [ 9 ]; therefore, the precise contribution of individual genes such as PTEN to ASD pathophysiology cannot be determined from CNV data alone. In addition, common variants in other neurodevelopmental genes, such as RELN , have been associated with ASD in case-control studies, supporting the relevance of single-gene investigations in ASD [ 10 ]. Nevertheless, a substantial body of independent genetic and functional evidence has robustly implicated PTEN in ASD [ 11 ]. The PTEN gene (located at 10q23.3) encodes a tumor suppressor with dual lipid and protein phosphatase activities [ 12 ]. It negatively regulates the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway via dephosphorylation of PIP3 to PIP2, a cascade critically involved in neuronal proliferation, synaptic plasticity, and dendritic development [ 13 ]. Loss of PTEN function results in hyperactivation of this pathway, leading to excessive dendritic growth, aberrant synaptic protein synthesis, and excitatory/inhibitory synaptic imbalance—cellular phenotypes that closely recapitulate the neuropathological hallmarks of ASD [ 14 , 15 ]. Moreover, germline PTEN pathogenic sequence variants are detectable in approximately 0.2–1% of ASD patients, and this proportion reaches up to 17% in those with macrocephaly [ 16 ]. PTEN pathogenic variants are typically sequence-level changes, such as missense, nonsense, frameshift, or splice-site mutations. They directly disrupt PTEN protein function and are well established in ASD. Notably, in patients with germline PTEN pathogenic variants, the presence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic CNVs was significantly more common among those with ASD/developmental delay, suggesting that CNVs may act as genomic modifiers. [ 17 ]. PTEN CNVs are larger genomic deletions or duplications that may alter PTEN dosage but often span multiple genes. Their functional consequences are more complex and may depend on CNV size, breakpoints, and co-deleted or co-duplicated genes. In this study, we therefore focused specifically on PTEN CNVs rather than pathogenic sequence variants. To further delineate the role of PTEN CNVs in ASD, we first integrated publicly available multi-omics data to systematically evaluate its biological plausibility as a candidate gene. Subsequently, we examined the associations between PTEN CNVs and ASD susceptibility and clinical phenotypes in a Han Chinese population. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Tissue-Level Expression Analysis of PTEN To delineate the tissue-level expression landscape of PTEN , we obtained gene expression data from a broad spectrum of human tissues via the GTEx Portal ( https://gtexportal.org/home/ ; accessed on 23 March 2026), a comprehensive resource providing bulk RNA-sequencing-based expression profiles across multiple anatomically distinct brain regions and peripheral organs [ 18 ]. Specifically, tissue-level PTEN expression data were derived from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) Project, Analysis V10 (dbGaP accession: phs000424.v10.p2), using gene-level bulk RNA-seq TPM data. Twelve brain regions were analyzed: the amygdala ( n = 181), anterior cingulate cortex (BA24; n = 233), caudate (basal ganglia; n = 300), cerebellar hemisphere ( n = 277), cerebellum ( n = 266), cortex ( n = 270), frontal cortex (BA9; n = 269), hippocampus ( n = 255), hypothalamus ( n = 257), nucleus accumbens (basal ganglia; n = 285), putamen (basal ganglia; n = 254), and substantia nigra ( n = 183). In addition, the spinal cord (cervical c-1; n = 204) was also included as a central nervous system tissue. 2.2. Cell-Type-Specific Expression Analysis of PTEN To characterize cell-type-specific alterations in PTEN expression in ASD, we used the publicly available differential-expression dataset generated by Wamsley et al. (Science, 2024) [ 19 ]. Specifically, PTEN differential-expression estimates were extracted from Data S1 (“Raw differential gene expression data”), deposited in Dryad ( https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.4b8gthtkr accessed on 23 March 2026). The corresponding cell-type-specific differential-expression data can also be explored through the ASD single-cell browser, the ASD Single-Cell Gene Expression (scGENE) Portal ( http://solo.bmap.ucla.edu/asdscgene/ accessed on 23 March 2026). The underlying snRNA-seq study included frontal cortex samples from Brodmann areas 9 and 4/6 from 33 individuals with ASD and 30 control individuals. Following quality control and doublet removal, 591,043 nuclei were analyzed, representing 306,347 cells from ASD subjects and 284,696 cells from control subjects. In the original study, counts from nuclei belonging to the same sample and cell type were aggregated to generate pseudobulk counts and normalized using a variance-stabilizing transformation. Age, postmortem interval, brain region, sequencing batch, mitochondrial RNA percentage, and the number of detected genes were accounted for before differential-expression analysis using limma-voom. In the present study, the published PTEN differential-expression estimates were extracted and visualized across major cortical cell types. 2.3. PTEN Protein Structure Analysis and Protein–Protein Interactions Protein-protein interaction data for PTEN were obtained from STRING [ 20 ]. UsingSelf-Optimized Prediction Method with Alignment (SOPMA), the secondary structure of the PTEN protein was predicted [ 21 ]. A high-confidence network enriched for ASD-associated genes and PI3K/AKT pathway components was constructed, supplemented by SOPMA protein secondary structure prediction, to define the neurodevelopmental molecular context of PTEN . 2.4. Association of PTEN CNV with ASD Susceptibility and Clinical Phenotypes 2.4.1. Participants Children diagnosed with ASD were recruited from Chun guang Hospital (Jilin Province, China) based on DSM-5 diagnostic criteria. Age and sex-matched controls were selected from the same region. A total of 231 participants were included in the study, comprising 121 children with ASD and 110 controls. Written informed consent was obtained from the guardians of all participants prior to study enrollment. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the School of Public Health, Jilin University (Approval No:2024-08-08). 2.4.2. DNA Extraction Peripheral blood samples were collected from each participant, and genomic DNA was extracted using the EE121-01 Blood Genomic DNA Extraction Kit (Beijing Quanshijin Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Beijing, China.). We quantified extracted DNA with an Epoch Take3 microplate reader (BioTek Instruments, Inc., Winooski, VT, USA.), measured absorbance at 260 and 280 nm, assessed DNA purity by the A260/A280 ratio, and selected samples with a ratio of 1.6–1.8 for genotyping. The extracted DNA were stored at −80 °C until further analysis. 2.4.3. PTEN CNVs Detection Specific primers for the PTEN gene and the reference gene GAPDH were designed for this study, and their sequences are presented in Table 1 . Primers targeting exonic regions of PTEN and the reference gene ( GAPDH ) were co-amplified. Reactions were conducted on a CFX96 Touch Real-Time PCR System (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Inc., Hercules, CA, USA.) using SYBR Green reagents (Tiangen Biotech, Co., Ltd., Beijing, China) in total volumes of 20 μL which contained 10 μL 2 × SuperReal PreMix Plus, 0.6 μL of each primer, and 2 μL of genomic DNA. The qPCR program consisted of an initial denaturation/enzyme activation step at 95 °C for 15 min, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at 95 °C for 10 s and annealing/extension at 60 °C for 32 s. The average of values from genomic DNA of reference DNA samples (G1471, G1521, Promega Corporation, Madison, WI, USA.) was considered the normal reference sample for ΔΔCT calculations. Relative fluorescence intensity was then used to calculate copy number ratios. Samples with copy numbers ≤ 1.2 were classified as deletions, while those ≥ 2.8 were considered duplications [ 22 ]. 2.4.4. Assessment Tools The Autism Behavior Checklist (ABC) is a widely used screening instrument designed to identify behavioral characteristics associated with ASD. It is commonly employed for adjunctive diagnosis and initial screening. The scale was first developed by Krug and colleagues in 1978 and consists of 57 items that describe atypical behavioral manifestations in children with autism across multiple domains. These items are grouped into five core factors: sensory, relating, body and object use, language, and social and self- help [ 23 ]. The Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), developed by Schopler and colleagues in 1980, is a clinical observational instrument used to assist in the diagnosis of ASD and to assess symptom severity. The scale comprises 15 items: relating to people, imitation, emotional response, body use, object use, adaptation to change, visual response, listening response, taste/smell/touch response and use, anxiety reaction, verbal communication, nonverbal communication, activity level, consistency of intellectual response, and general impression. Each item is scored on a 4-point scale ranging from 1 (normal) to 4 (severely abnormal), yielding a total score between 15 and 60 [ 24 ]. 2.4.5. Statistical Analysis Continuous variables were described as mean ± SD or Median ( P 25 , P 75 ), and categorical variables as counts (percentages). Differences in baseline characteristics between groups were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Logistic regression models were used to analyze the association between CNV types and ASD susceptibility, with results reported as odds ratios ( ORs ) and their 95% confidence intervals ( CIs ). One-way ANOVA was performed to compare the differences in ASD clinical phenotype scores among groups with different CNV types of PTEN . All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 24.0 (IBM, Chicago, IL, USA). A two-sided p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. 3. Results 3.1. Tissue-Level Expression Analysis of PTEN Expression of PTEN is broadly distributed across diverse human tissues and is consistently observed in multiple brain regions. These include the cerebellum (cerebellar hemisphere and cerebellar tissue proper), cortical areas (anterior cingulate, frontal, and broader cortical regions), and subcortical structures (amygdala, hippocampus, hypothalamus, caudate, nucleus accumbens, putamen, and substantia nigra). Notably, PTEN transcript levels are relatively higher within central nervous system tissues than in many non-neural counterparts ( Figure 1 ). 3.2. Cell-Type-Specific Expression Analysis of PTEN Published cell-type-specific differential-expression estimates for PTEN were extracted from the Wamsley et al. dataset and summarized across seven major classes of cortical cells, including excitatory neurons (EXT), inhibitory neurons (INT), astrocytes (ASTRO), microglia (MG), oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCS), oligodendrocytes (ODC), and blood-brain barrier (BBB)-associated cells. PTEN showed heterogeneous ASD-versus-control differential-expression patterns across these cortical cell populations, with both the direction and magnitude of the changes varying among individual cell-type clusters ( Figure 2 ). 3.3.
