title: Sex-Related Specificities of Sensory Profiles in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Impact on Clinical Functioning
abstract:
Background and Objectives: Sensory anomalies are a distinctive feature of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) individuals and appear to differ in intensity, frequency, and subtype between male and female subjects. According to the diagnostic framework of the DSM-5-TR, these sensory patterns are key clinical indicators. The objectives of this study were to investigate sensoriality in ASD, to compare sensory profiles in ASD subjects of both sexes and evaluate potential correlations with clinical profiles. Materials and Methods: A total of 94 ASD participants were enrolled at the Children and Adolescents Neuropsychiatry Department of the University of Naples Federico II. The population was assessed through psychometric (cognitive and adaptive levels, and intensity of autism symptoms) and sensory characterization (using the Short Sensory Profile questionnaire). Subsequently, a Mann–Whitney U test was performed to evaluate differences in sensory profiles between males and females. Spearman’s correlation was used to assess significant associations between the sensory profile and cognitive level, adaptive level, and ASD symptom intensity. Subsequently, for the correlations that emerged as significant, an analysis was performed using a General Linear Model (GLM), including age and Intelligence Quotient (IQ) as covariates in the model. Results: No statistically significant differences in the sensory profile emerged between male and female subjects. Sensory anomalies do not appear to be correlated with cognitive level. Although some statistically significant correlations emerged between the sensory profile, the AQ, and the ADOS-2 comparison score, these results were not confirmed after a GLM analysis was performed using the participants’ age and IQ as covariates. Conclusions: The observed results appear partially in line with the existing literature. Following the GLM analysis, it was further observed that variables such as age and IQ play a crucial role in interpreting the functional profile of individuals with ASD. At present, the study has several limitations (the exclusive use of parent-report instruments, an observational design, the lack of a control group) which could affect the robustness of the observed findings. Therefore, further studies are deemed necessary to better define the sex-specific sensory characteristics of ASD individuals.

1. Introduction Atypical sensory profiles are a highly prevalent feature in Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) individuals. In fact, one of the diagnostic criteria currently set forth by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR)—categorized under the B criteria, including repetitive and stereotyped behaviors—describes symptoms as: “Hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment” [ 1 ]. Globally, many studies focused on sensory anomalies in ASD individuals to contribute to a clearer neurobiological and phenotypic definition. Sensory anomalies can affect any sensory channel (sight, hearing, touch, etc.) and may be associated with an individual’s unique behaviors and response thresholds. For instance, referring to the theoretical framework proposed by Dunn W., we can identify four sensory processing patterns (derived from the combination of response thresholds, behavioral self-regulation strategies, and the interaction between these two factors): sensory seeking, sensory avoiding, sensory sensitivity, and low registration [ 2 ]. These aspects impact the functioning of ASD individuals, contributing to the impairment of their ability to adapt to different contexts and exacerbating any concomitant dysfunctional behaviors [ 3 ]. Indeed, it is well known that sensory abnormalities can also affect the social skills of ASD individuals, leading for example to difficulties in integrating social messages provided by other people; such aspects could be underlying by abnormalities in brain circuits that regulate both aspects of sociality as well as sensory processing, such as, for example, the anterior cingulate cortex, the superior temporal cortex, and the insula [ 4 ]. Furthermore, the scientific literature is increasingly exploring differences in symptomatic expression based on sex. Specifically, the ASD phenotype in females may differ both in the intensity of the symptoms expressed and in the potential comorbidities that may develop over time [ 5 ]. In fact, for example, females with ASD tend to present a higher prevalence of internalizing comorbidities (such as depression and anxiety), which often serve as the primary reason for medical consultation and can lead to a missed ASD diagnosis [ 6 ]. For instance, it is well known that ASD women tend to employ camouflage strategies to a greater extent in social contexts; these behaviors result in higher levels of perceived social reciprocity, which can mask the underlying ASD symptomatology [ 7 ]. Sensory processing anomalies are also being studied to evaluate potential differential characteristics based on sex. For instance, Osorio J.M.A. et al. assessed how, in a sample of ASD youth, females exhibit greater differences in the domains of proprioceptive and auditory sensitivity [ 8 ]. Differences in sensory processing are also present from early childhood: Harris H.K. et al. highlighted that, in a sample of ASD preschool-aged children, females tend to exhibit more sensory seeking behaviors compared to their male peers [ 9 ]. In light of the above, the purpose of the present study is to characterize a cohort of ASD individuals and compare sensory profiles between male and female subjects. A secondary objective is to evaluate the potential impact of the sensory profile on the clinical phenotype of both male and female subjects, comparing any observed differences. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Population This observational-retrospective study was conducted at the Interdepartmental Program of Child Neuropsychiatry at the University of Naples Federico II. The study included 94 participants consecutively referred for clinical observation due to suspected ASD or for psychodiagnostic re-evaluation of an existing ASD diagnosis between 2022 and 2024. Inclusion criteria were: an ASD diagnosis consistent with the DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR; age between 3 and 14 years; absence of ongoing psychopharmacological treatment; stability of rehabilitative treatment for at least 4 months; and signed informed consent from a parent or legal guardian. Individuals who did not meet all the aforementioned criteria were excluded. Furthermore, subjects with syndromic ASD (e.g., Fragile X Syndrome) and those with internal medical conditions that could alter the assessed parameters (such as comorbid epilepsy or other neurological disorders) were also excluded. 2.2. Psychometric Evaluation For the enrolled subjects, clinical characterization was performed through cognitive or developmental tests (Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-Fourth Edition, Leiter-3) [ 10 , 11 ], adaptive profile assessment (Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Second Edition) [ 12 ], and the administration of the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition (ADOS-2) to evaluate the intensity of autistic symptom expression [ 13 ]. The Intelligence Quotient (IQ) was extracted as data for our analysis. For the adaptive assessment, instead, the Adaptive Quotient (AQ) was extracted from the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Second Edition interview. Finally, the comparison score, indicating the intensity of the autistic symptomatology, obtained by the ADOS-2 test was extracted. To characterize the sensory profile, the Short Sensory Profile (SSP) questionnaire was administered [ 14 ]. This tool consists of 38 items evaluating different sensory domains and is structured into eight scales: seven subscales divided by sensory channel (‘Tactile Sensitivity’, ‘Taste/Smell Sensitivity’, ‘Movement Sensitivity’, ‘Auditory Filtering’, ‘Low Energy/Weakness’, ‘Visual/Auditory Sensitivity’) and behavioral response type (‘Hypo-responsivity/Sensation Seeking’), plus a total score. The SSP allows for an assessment of how much the sensory profile deviates from typical development, categorized as ‘Typical Performance’, ‘Probable Difference’, or ‘Definite Difference’. This tool is validated for parent/caregiver self-administration for children up to 14 years of age. The data obtained were analyzed to assess potential differences in the sensory profile between males and females in the study sample. 2.3. Statistical Analysis Regarding statistical analysis, a descriptive characterization of the study population was first performed for both demographic and clinical variables. The distribution of study variables was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test, which indicated a non-normal distribution for several variables ( p < 0.05). Subsequently, the sample was divided by sex (male/female): a comparison statistic using the Mann–Whitney U test for independent samples was set up to evaluate significant differences in SSP scores between the two subgroups. Significant correlations were then assessed (via Spearman’s bivariate analysis) between the sensory profile and clinical variables (cognitive and adaptive levels, autistic symptom intensity). Specifically, bivariate correlation analyses were conducted between SSP scores and Intelligence Quotient (IQ), Adaptive Quotient (AQ), and the ADOS-2 comparison score. Results with a p -value < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed anonymously using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) Version 29. 2.4. Ethical Considerations The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethics Committee ‘Campania 3’ (Protocol No. 78/2024, 26 March 2024). For all subjects, informed consent was signed by the parents/caregivers before the start of the diagnostic assessments at our facility. This informed consent also provided availability for the anonymous use of the subjects’ data for research purposes. 3. Results The study sample consisted of 94 subjects, of whom 32 were female and 62 were male (34% F; 66% M). Based on the severity levels estimated according to the criteria of the DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR, the majority of the subjects presented with severity levels 1 and 2. The IQ and AQ parameters were similar between the two groups, as was the comparison score for the ADOS-2 test. The administration of cognitive tests was not possible for subjects aged less than 5 years or due to the limited cooperation provided: this characterization was only possible to perform for 51 subjects. Please refer to Table 1 for a complete and detailed demographic characterization of the sample. The Mann–Whitney U test for independent samples, aimed at evaluating differences in the sensory profile via SSP scores between male and female subjects, yielded no statistically significant results (see Table 2 ). Indeed, the scores obtained by both groups on both the individual subscales and the total scale were comparable. Despite the lack of observed differences, a Chi-square analysis was performed to confirm the data by comparing the distribution of SSP total score categories between males and females; this analysis also yielded no statistically significant results (chi-square 2.01, p 0.366). Bivariate correlation analysis revealed two statistically significant inverse correlations within the female group. These involved the scores of the ‘Auditory Filtering’ subscale (Spearman Rho = −0.542, p = 0.008, 95% CI [−0.785, −0.155]) and the ‘Hyporesponsiveness/Sensation Seeking’ subscale (Spearman Rho = −0.551, p = 0.006, 95% CI [−0.790, −0.168]). Based on the Rho coefficients, both correlations were moderate-to-strong. No statistically significant correlations between SSP scores and the ADOS-2 comparison score were found within the male group. For the 51 subjects (30 M; 21 F) for whom intellectual assessment results were available, a bivariate analysis between SSP and IQ scores was conducted, which revealed no statistically significant results. A statistically significant direct correlation was found between “Tactile Sensitivity” and AQ (Spearman Rho 0.379, p -value 0.017, CI [0.063, 0.626]). A moderate effect is observed for this correlation. In the female group, two statistically significant direct correlations were observed between the AQ score and both the ‘Hyporesponsiveness/Sensation Seeking’ (Spearman Rho = 0.479, p = 0.015, 95% CI [0.091, 0.741]) and ‘Auditory Filtering’ (Spearman Rho = 0.405, p = 0.044, 95% CI [0.010, 0.696]) subscales. In this analysis, age and IQ were entered as covariates to evaluate the impact of these variables on the observed results. Due to the presence of non-normally distributed values, and to ensure the robustness of the analysis, this was integrated with a bootstrap procedure. For the “Tactile Sensitivity” subscale, the GLM applied to the dependent variable AQ showed an excellent overall fit (R 2 = 0.443, F(5, 37) = 5.885, p < 0.001). Among the variables included in the model, IQ was found to be the only highly significant predictor (F(1, 37) = 23.729, p < 0.001), showing a particularly large effect size (partial eta squared = 0.391). Conversely, no significant effects emerged for the age covariate ( p = 0.945), for sex ( p = 0.677), or for the interaction between sex and the “Tactile Sensitivity” subscale ( p = 0.652). title: Emerging Therapeutic Strategies for Child and Adolescent Obesity: A Narrative Review
abstract:
Background/Objectives: Childhood obesity is a chronic, multifactorial disease requiring attention to biological, behavioral, psychological, family, and socioeconomic factors. This narrative review examined the integration of lifestyle, family-based, psychological, and pharmacological approaches, focusing on treatment engagement, eating disorders, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and treatment durability. Methods: A single search interface covering PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science (the University of Turin library discovery platform) was used to identify studies published primarily from 2010 to August 2026. Pediatric trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, guidelines, and public-health reports were prioritized. Results: Intensive family-based, multicomponent behavioral treatment remains the best-supported foundation of care, although psychological outcomes are infrequently assessed. Psychiatric comorbidity is heterogeneous; loss-of-control eating, emotional symptoms, ADHD, and executive-function difficulties may impair engagement in selected patients, and untreated ADHD has been associated with a slower BMI response to weight management. Professionally supervised obesity treatment containing a dietary component did not, on average, worsen eating psychopathology and reduced several related symptoms. Family participation improved outcomes, whereas logistical, socioeconomic, and psychological barriers reduced attendance. Across randomized trials, adding anti-obesity medication to behavioral treatment produced an additional, although on average modest, reduction in BMI. Semaglutide, liraglutide, and phentermine/topiramate produced larger numerical reductions than older agents in separate trials, but heterogeneity and the absence of head-to-head comparisons preclude formal ranking. Gastrointestinal adverse events were frequent with glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists. Pediatric trials and real-world evidence indicate partial weight regain after discontinuation, while prescribing remains limited and unequal. Conclusions: Pediatric obesity care should be phenotype-informed, multidisciplinary, and longitudinal. Pharmacotherapy can enhance BMI reduction but should complement rather than replace behavioral, psychological, and family care. Outcomes should extend beyond BMI to metabolic, psychological, functional, and long-term measures.

1. Introduction Childhood obesity is a widespread global health issue [ 1 ]. When obesity is not secondary to endocrine, monogenic, or syndromic disorders, it can be considered ‘essential’ obesity: a chronic, relapsing, and multifactorial disease arising from interactions among biological susceptibility, eating behavior, environmental exposures, and socioeconomic conditions. In children and adolescents, body mass index (BMI) must be interpreted by age and sex. For individuals aged 5–19 years, the World Health Organization (WHO) defines overweight as BMI-for-age greater than one standard deviation above the reference median and obesity as greater than two standard deviations; comparisons across studies must nevertheless account for differences between WHO and International Obesity Task Force classification systems [ 1 , 2 ]. The global burden has increased sharply. In 2022, more than 390 million people aged 5–19 years were living with overweight, including approximately 160 million with obesity, and the prevalence of overweight in this age group had risen from about 8% in 1990 to 20% in 2022 [ 1 , 3 ]. In the sixth round of the WHO European Childhood Obesity Surveillance Initiative, 25% of children aged 7–9 years were living with overweight, including 11% with obesity [ 4 ]. Italian surveillance similarly indicates that approximately three in ten children aged 8–9 years have excess weight, with higher prevalence in southern regions [ 5 ]. Socioeconomic inequalities are marked: analysis of 53,275 Italian children showed less favorable dietary and activity patterns and higher obesity prevalence among children from families with lower parental education [ 6 ]. Pediatric obesity is associated with hypertension, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and other early or adult complications. It also frequently persists into adulthood and predicts later cardiometabolic morbidity and premature cardiovascular mortality [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ]. Its burden is also psychological and social: weight stigma, bullying, body dissatisfaction, anxiety or depressive symptoms, impaired quality of life, and disordered eating may occur, although these outcomes are heterogeneous and should not be assumed in every child [ 11 , 12 , 13 ]. Neurodevelopmental comorbidity is relevant in selected patients. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with a modest increase in the risk of pediatric overweight and obesity; reward-related behavior may overlap between the two conditions, whereas cognitive-control difficulties appear more specific to ADHD [ 14 , 15 , 16 ]. Given its complex pathogenesis and clinical expression, treatment cannot be reduced to dietary prescription. Contemporary care combines nutrition, physical activity, behavioral strategies, psychological support, and family involvement, while accounting for treatment accessibility and social context [ 10 , 17 ]. Recently, the therapeutic landscape has also expanded: while intensive nutritional, behavioral, and family-based interventions remain foundational, newer drugs such as liraglutide, semaglutide, and other anti-obesity medications can produce rapid and clinically meaningful BMI reductions in selected young people. Their long-term safety, durability after discontinuation, accessibility, and integration with psychological and family care remain incompletely defined [ 18 , 19 , 20 ]. The aim of the present review is to discuss recent evidence on the integration of psychological, family-based, and pharmacological approaches to pediatric obesity, with a focus on treatment engagement, eating psychopathology, and the more limited evidence on the relationship between obesity, ADHD, and stimulant-associated weight trajectories. These domains were selected because each can influence whether a child engages in treatment, how the child responds, and whether the response is maintained: family resources and socioeconomic barriers affect access and attendance; psychopathology, disordered eating, and neurodevelopmental disorders may modulate engagement and response; and pharmacotherapy raises new questions about durability after discontinuation. 2. Materials and Methods This narrative review was supported by a structured literature search designed to identify studies directly relevant to the multidisciplinary management of pediatric obesity, with particular attention to psychological and family-related factors, eating psychopathology, neurodevelopmental comorbidities, treatment engagement, and pharmacological approaches. Searches were conducted between April and August 2026 through the University of Turin library discovery platform, a single search interface that covers PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science; the three databases were therefore not searched separately. The searches were supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking of key publications. The search primarily covered studies published from 2010 to August 2026, with particular emphasis on recent evidence from 2015–2026, while retaining earlier landmark studies when necessary to establish relevant epidemiological, clinical, neurobehavioral, or therapeutic findings. Search terms were used in different combinations and included “pediatric obesity”, “childhood obesity”, “adolescent obesity”, “overweight”, “multidisciplinary treatment”, “lifestyle intervention”, “behavioral intervention”, “family-based treatment”, “psychological intervention”, “cognitive behavioral therapy”, “motivational interviewing”, “emotional regulation”, “treatment adherence”, “attrition”, “socioeconomic factors”, “telehealth”, “depression”, “anxiety”, “weight stigma”, “body dissatisfaction”, “eating disorders”, “binge eating”, “loss-of-control eating”, “ADHD”, “attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder”, “executive function”, “impulsivity”, “inhibitory control”, “delay discounting”, “reward processing”, “neuroimaging”, “stimulant treatment”, “methylphenidate”, “lisdexamfetamine”, “anti-obesity medication”, “GLP-1 receptor agonist”, “liraglutide”, “semaglutide”, “orlistat”, and “phentermine/topiramate”. The main searches combined “obesity” with “childhood”, “treatment”, “pharmacotherapy”, and “incidence”, and were then refined by combining “pediatric obesity” or “childhood obesity” with the other terms listed above. Additional targeted searches were conducted when specific clinical, neurobehavioral, treatment-related, or pharmacological questions emerged during manuscript development. Priority was given to peer-reviewed studies directly examining pediatric obesity and its treatment, including randomized controlled trials, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, large observational and real-world studies, and clinically relevant cross-sectional investigations. Systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and international clinical guidelines were used to characterize the broader evidence base, identify relevant primary studies, and provide context for areas supported by a large or heterogeneous literature. Official reports from recognized public-health institutions, including the World Health Organization and the Italian National Institute of Health, were also considered for epidemiological and surveillance data, and current U.S. prescribing information was consulted during manuscript revision for the indications, contraindications, and safety warnings of anti-obesity medications. Studies involving children and adolescents younger than 18 years were prioritized. Studies including both pediatric and adult participants were retained when pediatric findings were reported separately or when they provided information directly relevant to the aims of the review. Adult-only studies were generally excluded from the main evidence synthesis; however, selected adult studies were retained solely as contextual evidence when controlled pediatric data were unavailable, including studies on binge-eating disorder treated with lisdexamfetamine, post-treatment weight trajectories after semaglutide withdrawal, and family involvement in the treatment of anorexia nervosa. Findings derived from adult populations were interpreted as indirect or hypothesis-generating evidence and were not considered evidence of efficacy or safety in children and adolescents. The limited pediatric observational evidence on stimulant treatment and loss-of-control eating was considered separately and was not treated as evidence supporting routine clinical use. Studies focusing primarily on monogenic or syndromic obesity were not included unless they provided information directly applicable to the broader clinical questions addressed in the review. Duplicate publications, conference abstracts, non-peer-reviewed sources (other than the institutional and regulatory documents described above), and studies without a direct connection to pediatric obesity, its psychological or neurodevelopmental correlates, treatment engagement, or therapeutic management were excluded. Narrative reviews were used mainly to identify relevant concepts and primary studies rather than as the principal source for quantitative estimates whenever original evidence was available. Both authors assessed the relevance and eligibility of the retrieved publications. Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus. 3. Results A total of 57 sources were included in the narrative synthesis: 12 randomized or controlled clinical trials, 15 observational studies, 14 systematic reviews or meta-analyses, 8 narrative reviews or editorials, 1 clinical practice guideline, 3 public-health reports, and 4 drug prescribing information documents. The findings are presented below by thematic area. 3.1. Multicomponent Lifestyle and Behavioral Interventions Intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment combines nutritional counseling, physical activity, reduced sedentary behavior, and behavioral techniques, usually with family participation. The 2023 American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guideline recommends family-based, multicomponent treatment and identifies 26 or more face-to-face contact hours over a 3- to 12-month period as the most effective intensity [ 10 , 21 ]. In the technical evidence review supporting the guideline, Skinner and coworkers included 215 intervention studies; among the 126 randomized trials of lifestyle or dietary interventions, psychosocial outcomes were reported in only about 20% and mental-health outcomes in 5%, confirming that the evidence supporting clinical guidelines remains predominantly weight-centered [ 21 ]. In preschool-aged children, more intensive multidisciplinary interventions appear to improve anthropometric outcomes [ 22 ]. Effective programs commonly use self-monitoring, goal setting, problem solving, environmental restructuring, modeling, and relapse-prevention strategies. A systematic review found that nine obesity-management interventions used a mean of 7.5 behavior-change techniques, but specific psychological components, such as emotion-regulation training and motivational interviewing, were rarely included. Moreover, intervention effectiveness was not explained simply by the total number of behavior-change techniques used, suggesting that their selection, implementation, and adaptation to the child and family may be more important than their quantity alone [ 23 ]. 3.2. Psychological and Family-Based Interventions Evidence from a large randomized clinical trial supports family-based behavioral treatment. In 452 children aged 6–12 years, a primary-care intervention targeting eating, physical activity, and parenting practices produced a greater reduction in percentage above median BMI than usual care at 24 months (between-group difference −6.21 percentage points, 95% confidence interval [CI] −10.14 to −2.29); benefits also extended to participating parents and to untreated siblings with overweight or obesity [ 24 ]. In the smaller two-arm ENTREN/ENTREN-F trial (ENTREN-F, n = 30; ENTREN, n = 40), both intervention protocols included nutritional counseling, support for physical activity, emotional-regulation training, and work on social relationships, using cognitive-behavioral and motivational techniques. Adding parallel sessions for parents was associated with better adherence, greater reductions in BMI z-score and child anxiety, and greater family adaptability, although the sample of 70 children limits definitive conclusions [ 25 ]. title: Three repeated intrathecal injections of allogenic umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stromal cells in autism spectrum disorder: a Phase I clinical trial
abstract:
Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition of etiology, characterized by deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors. Despite its growing prevalence, no treatment has yet demonstrated consistent efficacy across the full spectrum of ASD phenotypes. This Phase I, open-label study investigates the safety and feasibility of three repeated intrathecal injections of allogeneic Umbilical Cord Tissue–Derived Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (UC-MSCs) in children diagnosed with ASD. Methods Five children (aged 3-7) with ASD, confirmed by Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders- Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria and on stable behavioral and pharmacologic regimens for at least two months, received three intrathecal (IT) injections of 20 × 10⁶ UC-MSCs at one-month intervals. Safety was monitored over six months based on Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE). Preliminary behavioral assessments, including the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist (ATEC), and the Behavior Problem Inventory (BPI-S), were conducted at the baseline, one-, two-, four-, and six-month follow-ups. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytokine profiles were measured prior to each injection. Electroencephalography (EEG) and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) were performed at baseline and the final follow-up. Results The treatment was safe and well-tolerated with no serious adverse events (SAEs). All participants experienced at least one mild to moderate, transient adverse event (AEs), most commonly fever (5/5) and nausea (4/5). Exploratory behavioral improvements were observed in CARS in all children, while two participants moved from the mild-to-moderate to the non-autistic ranges, and three shifted from the severe to the mild-to-moderate range. Other measures also improved, though the persistence of these improvements was varied. CSF cytokines showed consistent reduction, particularly in TNF- \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\:\alpha\:$$\end{document} and IL-6 levels across participants, confirming the immunomodulatory impact of UC-MSC administration. The EEG findings revealed that the spectral pattern shifted toward a more typical profile in one participant after treatment. Conclusions This Phase I study showed that three repeated IT injections of UC-MSCs are safe and well-tolerated in children with ASD. Preliminary behavioral and biomarker improvements warrant further study in larger controlled trials. Trial registration Trial Registration ID: IRCT20200217046526N3. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s13287-026-05122-1 .

Introduction Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex and heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by challenges in social interactions, communication difficulties, restricted interests, repetitive behaviors, and atypical sensory processing [ 1 ]. These traits often persist into adolescence and adulthood and are frequently associated with an increased risk of intellectual disability [ 2 ]. Worldwide, about 61.8 million individuals are affected by ASD, estimated at 1 in every 127 people. This prevalence imposes a substantial global health burden, estimated at 147.6 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) per 100,000 population [ 3 ]. The etiology of ASD is multifactorial, involving a complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors. Genetically, ASD has been linked to various pathways regulating brain development and intercellular interactions [ 4 – 6 ], although specific single-gene conditions such as fragile X syndrome and tuberous sclerosis have been directly associated with ASD [ 5 ]. Environmental factors contributing to ASD risk include maternal nutrition and metabolic conditions, prenatal infection, exposure to certain drugs and toxins, such as Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) and antibiotics, during pregnancy [ 6 , 7 ]. Currently, there is no definitive cure for ASD, and treatment strategies primarily focus on managing disruptive symptoms and improving daily functions, including behavioral therapy (e.g., Applied Behavioral Analysis), occupational and speech therapy, biofeedback, neuromodulation, and vocational support [ 4 ]. Pharmacologic treatments are also employed to manage behavioral challenges such as irritability and attention deficit. However, they do not target the underlying pathology [ 8 ]. Emerging evidence suggests that neuroinflammation and immune system dysregulation within the central nervous system (CNS) play a critical role in the pathogenesis of ASD. Studies have identified significant microglial activation and increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interferon (IFN)-γ, interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, and Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF)-α, in both brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Dysregulation of the immune system may disrupt neuronal survival and proliferation, alter neural connectivity and plasticity, and contribute to the production of brain-reactive antibodies, ultimately leading to abnormal brain function [ 9 ]. In light of these findings, immunoregulatory therapies offer a promising approach for ASD treatment [ 10 ]. Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (MSCs) have demonstrated immunomodulatory and neuroprotective properties. Through paracrine signaling and anti-inflammatory mechanisms, MSCs may inhibit microglial activation, suppress oxidative stress, and enhance synaptogenesis and neuronal survival, aiding in the restoration of brain functional pathways [ 11 ]. MSCs can be derived from various tissues, including bone marrow, umbilical cord, adipose tissue, and dental pulp [ 12 ]. Umbilical Cord-derived Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (UC-MSCs) offer several advantages, including high proliferative capacity, ease of isolation, and ethical availability [ 13 ]. Their hypoimmunogenic properties, attributed to the absence of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II expression and low MHC class I level, make them suitable for allogenic applications [ 14 ]. Several cell-based therapies have been investigated in the treatment of ASD, including studies using mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) [ 15 , 16 ], umbilical cord blood [ 17 , 18 ], and human mononuclear cells (MNCs) [ 19 ]. However, the evidence remains insufficient to establish an optimal treatment protocol and reach a consensus on the safety and efficacy of intrathecal (IT) administration of allogenic MSCs in ASD. This open-label, phase I study aims to evaluate the safety, feasibility, and therapeutic potential of three consecutive intrathecal (IT) injections of allogenic UC-MSCs in children (3–7 years) diagnosed with ASD over a six-month follow-up. Methods Study setting This phase I, open-label, single-arm clinical trial was designed to evaluate the safety and feasibility of three consecutive IT administrations of allogenic UC-MSCs at one-month intervals in five children with ASD, followed for six months. The Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of the Academic Center for Education, Culture and Research (ACECR) approved the study protocol (Reference number: IR.ACECR.REC.1398.003). The trial was conducted in accordance with Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines and the latest version of the Helsinki Declaration. The study was registered with the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (Trial registration number: IRCT20200217046526N3). Written informed consents were obtained from the caregivers of the participants after a comprehensive explanation of the procedures and potential risks and benefits by an expert physician. Participation was entirely voluntary. All study-related expenses, including hospitalization, UC-MSC administration, laboratory evaluations, imaging, and clinical assessments, were fully covered by the study sponsor, and no financial compensation was provided for participation. The intervention and data collection were performed in the Children’s Medical Center and the Roozbeh psychiatric hospital, affiliated with Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran. Participants To identify suitable participants, parents of potential candidates completed an online form providing preliminary information, including written informed consent, the child’s medical history, and relevant eligibility details. Following an initial screening, an experienced psychiatrist conducted an interview to confirm the ASD diagnosis and assess its severity based on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders- Fifth Edition (DSM-5). Children who met the inclusion criteria were subsequently enrolled in the study. Five children between the ages of three and seven were enrolled in the study. All had a confirmed diagnosis of Level-II ASD, as determined by clinical evaluation, and met the inclusion criteria without any excluding conditions. The eligibility criteria are detailed in Table 1 . Cell preparation Clinical-grade MSCs were derived from umbilical cord tissue and prepared under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP)-compliant conditions. The full protocol, including donor screening, cell isolation and expansion, quality control measures, and product release criteria, is explained in Additional File A-Supplementary Methods as detailed in our previous publication [ 20 ]. Interventions A fixed dose of 2010 6 clinical-grade GMP-compliant UC-MSCs (Whartocell®) suspended in 2 mL of normal saline with human serum albumin 5% was administered three times intrathecally at one-month intervals. The procedure was carried out in the operating room of the Children’s Medical Center, affiliated with Tehran University of Medical Sciences, located in Tehran Province, Iran. Participants were positioned in the lateral decubitus position [ 21 ]. All participants were kept NPO for at least eight hours and were sedated intravenously with Thiopental Sodium at a dose of 3–5 mg/kg prior to the procedure. Following aseptic preparation, including washing and disinfecting the injection site with povidone-iodine and applying a sterile drape, a lumbar puncture was performed using a 24-gauge spinal needle inserted between the L3/L4 or L4/L5 intervertebral spaces. Three milliliters of CSF were collected: one milliliter was used for CSF analysis and inflammatory biomarker assessment, while the remaining two milliliters were re-infused into the subarachnoid space following the 2-ml cell suspension injection. This re-infusion of CSF prevents entrapment of cells in the dead space of the spinal needle. Participants were closely monitored for four hours following the procedure and were discharged if they were medically stable, alert, able to tolerate oral intake, and reported no complaints. A clinician was available on-call for the first 48 h to manage any potential side effects that might occur after discharge. Outcomes The primary outcomes included any Serious Adverse Events (SAEs) or Adverse Events (AEs), significant laboratory abnormalities, or structural changes on Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), assessed according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE, version 5). The participants were monitored in terms of the occurrence of any AEs over the six-month follow-up. Laboratory and imaging assessments, including complete blood count (CBC), serum chemistry, urine analysis, EEG, and MRI, were performed at the baseline and final visits. Secondary outcomes included changes in the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), the Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist (ATEC), and the Behavior Problem Inventory–Short Form (BPI-S), which was obtained at baseline, one-, two-, four-, and six-month follow-ups. Parents’ quality of life was assessed using the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-28) and the Short Form-36 Health Survey (SF-36). Additional secondary measures included the evaluation of inflammatory biomarkers in CSF at the baseline, one- and two-month visits, as well as findings from EEG and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) at the baseline and final follow-up. The timeline of interventions and follow-up visits is presented in Fig. 1 . The Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) was used to assess autism severity and evaluate changes following the intervention. An expert clinician completed CARS and it consists of 15 items, including relating to people, imitation, emotional response, body use, object use, adaptation to change, visual response, listening response, activity level, taste–smell-touch response and use, fear and nervousness, verbal communication, nonverbal communication, level and consistency of intellectual response, and general impressions. Each item is scored from 1 to 4, with 1 reflecting no impairment and 4 indicating severe impairment. The total score is obtained from the summation of scores, while 15 to 29.5 stands for non-autistic, 30 to 36.5 for mild-to-moderate ASD, and 37 to 60 for severe ASD [ 22 , 23 ]. ATEC is a questionnaire to evaluate the severity of symptoms and track changes in the severity of ASD in response to treatment, and it was completed by parents at each follow-up visit. This questionnaire consists of four subscales: (1) Speech/Language/ Communication, (2) Sociability, (3) Sensory/Cognitive Awareness, and (4) Health/Physical/ Behavior [ 24 ]. The total ATEC score ranges from 0 to 179, with a lower score indicating less severe autism symptoms. A total score below 50 suggests mild ASD, scores between 51 and 103 suggest moderate ASD, and scores above 104 are indicative of severe ASD [ 25 ]. The BPI-S is a 30-item tool to assess maladaptive behavior in intellectual and developmental disabilities, including ASD, completed by participants’ parents. This questionnaire has three main categories: Self-injurious Behavior, Aggressive/Destructive Behavior, and Stereotyped Behavior, whereas each item is rated on a frequency scale and a severity scale. Higher scores indicate greater behavioral dysfunction [ 26 ]. GHQ was administered to assess the parents’ quality of life. It consists of 28 items into four subscales: Somatic Symptoms, Anxiety and Insomnia, Social Dysfunction, and Severe Depression, each containing seven items. The total scores range from 0 to 84, with the higher score indicating a greater probability of mental distress [ 27 ]. The 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36) was used to assess health-related quality of life. SF-36 is a well-known self-report questionnaire evaluating health-related quality of life in 36 items. It has eight domains, which can be summarized in two main components: Physical Component Summary (PCS) and Mental Component Summary (MCS). Each domain score was calculated by transforming raw scores into a 0–100 scale, with higher scores indicating better health status [ 28 , 29 ]

title: Non-Metric Dental Traits, Dental Caries Experience, Parental Perceptions, and Oral Hygiene Status of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder-A Step Towards Sustainable Smiles
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is accompanied by poor oral health outcomes for children with ASD.

AIM: To assess the occurrence of non-metric dental traits (NMDTs), dental caries experience, parents' perception, and oral hygiene status of children with ASD.

METHODOLOGY: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 150 children with ASD and their biological parents. Children with severe sensory or behavioural difficulties who were unable to cooperate for oral examination were excluded. A pre-validated questionnaire was used to assess parental perception. Oral hygiene index-Simplified (OHI-S), Decayed, Missing and Filled Teeth index (DMFT) for permanent and primary dentition was used to assess oral hygiene status and dental caries in children with ASD. Non-metric dental trait (NMDT) was assessed using ASUDAS (Arizona State University Dental Anthropology System). Chi-square test and multiple linear regression analysis were done.

RESULTS: Most parents, 126 (84.0%) had a neutral perception score. The mean OHI(S) score for the children with ASD was 1.86 (SD 0.95). The prevalence of dental caries was 16% in deciduous dentition and 48% in permanent dentition. A statistically significant association was observed between palatogingival groove, cusp of Carabelli, and poorer oral hygiene status. Regression analysis showed that children with ASD whose mothers were employed showed a negative association with oral hygiene status (B = -0.533, p = 0.015). Higher maternal education was associated with lower DMFT scores (DMFT, B = - 1.044, p = 0.040 and for D, B = -1.319, p = 0.003).

CONCLUSION: Parents' perceptions regarding oral health among children with ASD are neutral with both behavioral limitations and oral hygiene practices affecting oral health. This study recommends early NMDTs identification and a multidisciplinary approach involving dental professionals, along with targeted parental education and regular follow-up, that may improve oral health outcomes.

title: Sensory Overstimulation: A Virtual Reality Simulation to Foster Empathy Towards Autistic Youth
abstract: This paper investigates whether a Virtual Reality (VR) simulation of sensory overstimulation in a classroom can increase empathy and understanding toward individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) among students aged 13-15 in Danish elementary schools. The project followed an iterative design process in which an initial prototype was refined through user testing and interviews with autistic adults and a special-needs teacher. The resulting simulation combined auditory overstimulation, environmental distractions, a listening-based classroom task, and hyperfocus mechanics intended to represent selected aspects of Sensory Over-Responsivity (SOR) in school settings. A mixed-methods A/B evaluation compared the VR simulation with a sound-based condition that communicated the same classroom scenario through narration. Fifty-nine participants took part in the evaluation. Broader dispositional empathy showed little change, but target-specific measures indicated short-term increases in empathic concern and personal distress immediately after the intervention. Interview findings suggested that participants gained a stronger understanding of ASD-related classroom challenges, particularly difficulty focusing under layered sensory input. The results suggest that immersive VR may be a useful medium for communicating sensory challenges in classroom environments, while longer-term empathy effects remain uncertain.

title: Measuring Sleep at Home in Adolescents With Autism Using EEG Headbands: Protocol for a Remote Study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep disturbances are prevalent in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) and worsen daytime functioning, yet their neural bases remain poorly understood. This may reflect the challenges of laboratory-based polysomnography for individuals with ASD, including sensory sensitivities and difficulty adapting to changes in routine. The advent of wearable electroencephalography (EEG) devices allows for remote data collection in the home and facilitates large-scale sleep studies.

OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study is to test the hypothesis that thalamocortical circuit dysfunction contributes to poor sleep in ASD by characterizing sleep oscillations that rely on this circuitry. To achieve this goal, we monitored sleep in the home using wearable EEG headbands in adolescents with ASD, including those who are profoundly affected, and their typically developing peers. When necessary, we used a desensitization protocol to gradually acclimate participants to wearing the headband overnight to promote the inclusion of individuals with sensory sensitivities and high support needs.

METHODS: Participants and their families completed assessments and questionnaires and received remote training to use a wearable EEG headband. Those needing time to acclimate followed a personalized 2-week desensitization protocol with a practice headband. Sleep was monitored at home for 3 consecutive nights, the first of which was for adaptation to the headband. Sleep data quality was checked daily, and remote technical support was provided as needed. Using sleep rhythms as physiological biomarkers of thalamocortical circuit function, we will test the hypothesis that abnormal circuit function in ASD is related to worse sleep quality.

RESULTS: This study was funded by the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) and approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board in November 2021. Data were collected between July 2023 and November 2025. A total of 146 participants (ASD: n=77; typically developing [TD]: n=65; profound autism: n=4) completed the study and produced at least 1 night of usable sleep data. Data analysis is underway, and the results will be submitted for publication in November 2026.

CONCLUSIONS: At-home sleep monitoring enables large samples that are needed to characterize the neural underpinnings of sleep disturbances across the autism spectrum. The personalized desensitization protocol promotes inclusion by accommodating individuals often excluded from research due to sensory or behavioral challenges. These methods are adaptable for other conditions and research goals beyond ASD, such as longitudinal studies across development or characterizing sleep in other neurodevelopmental disorders. Desensitization protocols may also increase the tolerability of diagnostic laboratory-based sleep studies and other medical procedures, improving both patient experience and quality of care.

title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Treatment Pattern and Its Associated Outcomes Among Children Referred to Psychiatry and Mental Health Services in Malaysia: Protocol for a Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract:
Abstract Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder associated with significant impairments in academic, social, and daily functioning. Despite the availability of clinical practice guidelines in Malaysia, evidence on real-world treatment patterns and outcomes remains limited. The lack of multicenter data on treatment use and clinical outcomes hinders the evaluation of current ADHD care and opportunities for service improvement. Objective The primary objective of this study is to observe treatment patterns among children with ADHD referred to psychiatry and mental health services in Malaysia after receiving treatment for 18 months. This study will also compare treatment outcomes between children with ADHD who do receive treatment and those who do not receive any ADHD treatment. Methods This multicenter retrospective cohort study will use secondary data from clinical records of children aged 4 to 16 years with a confirmed diagnosis of ADHD. Data on sociodemographic characteristics, clinical features, ADHD subtype and comorbidities, treatment modalities, health care use, treatment trajectories, and clinical outcomes will be extracted using a standardized case report form and will be anonymized prior to analysis. Data collection will be undertaken by trained site investigators and medical officers across participating centers. Statistical analyses will be conducted using R software (R Foundation for Statistical Computing). Descriptive statistics will be used to summarize characteristics, treatment patterns, health care use, and clinical outcomes of children with ADHD. Treatment patterns will be characterized according to pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions, treatment modifications, and service use. Comparative analyses will be performed to examine associations between treatment patterns and clinical outcomes across children with ADHD and clinical subgroups. Results This study will be funded through a Ministry of Health Research Grant obtained in August 2026. It will commence in August 2026 and end in December 2028. Based on the sample size calculation, a minimum of 2771 eligible children with ADHD records will be included in the study. The study will be reported in accordance with the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) guidelines for retrospective cohort studies. The findings will be disseminated through presentations and article publications at the national and international levels. Conclusions This study will address a critical evidence gap in ADHD care by providing comprehensive real-world data on treatment patterns and outcomes among Malaysian children with ADHD. Findings will identify variations in treatment approaches, treatment trajectories, and clinical outcomes across hospitals and regions, assess the alignment of real-world practice with national recommendations, and highlight potential disparities in access to ADHD specialist services. The findings are expected to support evidence-based clinical decision-making, guide strategic health care planning, optimize resource use, and contribute to the development of a more coordinated, efficient, and equitable system of ADHD care across diverse health care settings in Malaysia.

Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is one of the common neurodevelopmental disorders that are typically first diagnosed in childhood. ADHD is defined as persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that may significantly interfere with daily functioning and development. Globally, the prevalence of ADHD among children aged 3 to 12 years and adolescents aged 12 to 18 years is 7.6% and 5.6%, respectively [ 1 ]. In Malaysia, 1.61% of primary school students aged 6 to 12 years are diagnosed with ADHD, with male children observed as having a higher prevalence compared to female children at a ratio of 4:1 [ 2 ]. Additionally, the prevalence of ADHD cases among children has increased from 4.6% in 2015 [ 3 ] to 7.1% in 2023 [ 4 ]. According to the DSM-5 ( Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders [Fifth Edition]), ADHD is divided into 3 subtypes: attention deficit (ADHD-I), impulsive (ADHD-H), and mixed type (ADHD-C) [ 5 ]. Children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD-I often may fail to pay close attention to details or may make careless mistakes [ 6 ], often have difficulty in sustaining attention when completing tasks, do not seem to listen when spoken to directly most of the time, often do not follow instructions, fail to finish tasks, have difficulty organizing tasks and activities, avoid eye contact most of the time, dislike or are reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort, often lose things necessary for tasks or activities, are easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, and are often forgetful during daily activities [ 5 ]. Meanwhile, children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD-H often fidget with or tap their hands or feet [ 6 ] or squirm in their seat [ 7 ], often leave their seat in situations when remaining seated is expected, often run about or climb in situations when it is inappropriate, often are unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly, often are “on the go” [ 8 ], acting as if “driven by a motor,” often talk excessively, often blurt out an answer before a question has been completed, often have difficulty waiting their turn, and often interrupt or intrude on others. To be diagnosed with ADHD, children up to age 16 must exhibit at least 6 symptoms within a specific domain or at least 6 from each domain for the combined presentation, and these symptoms must have emerged prior to age 12. These symptoms must persist for at least 6 months, be present in two or more settings (such as at school and at home), and cause clear evidence of functional impairment [ 5 ]. In addition, these symptoms must not occur exclusively during the course of schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder, and they must not be better explained by another mental disorder [ 5 ]. The occurrence of ADHD in children and adolescents is usually associated with genetic factors. The heritability of ADHD in a family is approximately 74%, and familial aggregation of ADHD increases with genetic relatedness [ 9 , 10 ]. The presence of genetic variants may lead to a risk of ADHD. In fact, in one study, it was found that 33% of children with ADHD had a parent with ADHD, and the child showed more severe ADHD than the parent [ 11 ]. However, the heritability of ADHD cannot be explained by genetic variants alone; it is reported to be due to gene-gene interaction [ 12 ], gene-environment interaction [ 13 ], and gene-environment correlation [ 14 ]. Environmental factors, such as prepregnancy maternal obesity, prenatal factors, and perinatal factors, may also contribute to the development or severity of ADHD among children and adolescents. Studies have shown evidence that maternal smoking during pregnancy, maternal obesity during prepregnancy, and maternal psychosocial stress increased the possibility of the offspring to be diagnosed with ADHD [ 15 - 17 ]. Persistent exposure to environmental stress may interrupt the neurodevelopment of offspring. Additionally, psychosocial factors like traumatic brain injury, the child’s diet, and the amount of screen time may also worsen the condition’s symptoms [ 18 - 20 ]. Globally, the main approaches to ADHD treatment can be categorized into pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions. Nonpharmacological methods include occupational therapy, organizational skills training, and psychological interventions. Although these strategies have demonstrated effectiveness, for example, improving functional outcomes, enhancing sustained attention, reducing distractibility, and decreasing impulsive behaviors, there is evidence that the combination of pharmacological and nonpharmacological treatments yields the most effective results in managing ADHD symptoms and improving overall functioning [ 21 ]. In Malaysia, the number of children aged 5 to 15 years diagnosed with hyperactivity has increased from 4.6% in 2015 [ 3 ] to 7.1% in 2023; this is a worrying issue, as hyperactivity might contribute to ADHD [ 4 ]. A study by Sahril et al [ 22 ] found that younger age, single parents, parents working in the private sector, lower parental education, and parental mental health problems were major factors associated with mental health problems among children in Malaysia [ 4 ]. A clinical practice guideline (CPG) has been established, and several recommendations for the treatment of ADHD in children and adolescents are listed [ 23 ]. The purpose of these treatments is to improve the child’s ADHD clinical symptoms, functioning, academic achievements, medication adherence, and self-worth. Interventions include psychoeducation and pharmacological and nonpharmacological treatments. Nonpharmacological treatments include occupational therapy and psychological interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy and family-based intervention (parent training and behavioral intervention). A previous study showed that cognitive behavioral therapy was effective for adolescents with ADHD who continued to exhibit persistent symptoms despite being prescribed medication [ 23 , 24 ]. The CPG recommends that pharmacological treatment, such as stimulants and nonstimulants, be offered to children aged 6 years or older and to adolescents. Nonstimulants that have Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for use in ADHD are atomoxetine, guanfacine, and clonidine. Other nonstimulants such as bupropion and modafinil have been shown to be superior to the placebo in reducing ADHD core symptoms [ 23 ]. Most children with ADHD who receive treatment show improvement in academic learning, clinical symptoms, and behavior with intervention. In Malaysia, pharmacological treatments such as stimulant medication (methylphenidate) and nonstimulant medication (atomoxetine) have been used to treat ADHD among children [ 25 ]. However, regarding nonpharmacological treatment, including psychoeducation, parent training, and occupational and behavior therapy [ 26 ], there is limited access or these options are unavailable to children in most hospitals in Malaysia due to cost, service, and accessibility constraints [ 3 ]. On a separate note, several treatments used internationally, such as amphetamine, dextroamphetamine, clonidine, digital therapy, school-based interventions, and electroencephalogram neurofeedback (a noninvasive technique that tracks real-time brainwave activity to teach self-regulation of the central nervous system), are currently unavailable in Malaysia. This gap may stem from variations in health systems and local resource availability across different countries [ 27 ], even though the clinical effectiveness of medications such as amphetamine has been widely documented [ 28 ]. Furthermore, there are no reports or data available that provide evidence on which is the most effective treatment for ADHD among children in Malaysia. A previous report stated that the combination of pharmacological and nonpharmacological treatments might be effective [ 3 ]. In short, the limited research on ADHD treatment patterns among children poses a challenge to clinicians, patients, and caregivers. Furthermore, despite existing guidelines for the management of ADHD in Malaysia, currently, no study has specifically observed treatment trends and outcomes in the local context. There are also inconsistent findings on the treatment pattern in ADHD among children globally due to local formulary restrictions, service capacity, and affordability, among other reasons [ 26 ]. On a separate note, there is an increasing number of clinicians practicing in this field, and standardized guidelines may help in guiding clinicians in the management of ADHD. The 2021 CPG on ADHD among children provides valuable but general guidance on management; consequently, this study is necessary to transition from general principles to a standardized, nationwide protocol. By evaluating current clinical practices, this study generates localized, living evidence to drive continuous improvement in care equity and delivery, ensuring that children in all states receive an identical, high standard of evidence-based ADHD management. This study aims to address these gaps by determining ADHD treatment patterns and outcomes among Malaysian children by providing preliminary data to improve diagnosis, management, and interventions. This study will help clinicians and doctors understand real-world practice (actual clinical practice) and compare it to treatment guidelines. Treatment patterns include types of intervention received upon diagnosis of ADHD (pharmacological, nonpharmacological, or both), any changes in treatment over the follow-up period, and reasons for the changes. In addition, treatment outcomes using pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions will evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention based on symptoms before and after the intervention. Findings will also evaluate the outcome based on the number of symptoms, a reduction or decrease in severity (evaluated by a clinician during a clinic session), functionality at home or in a social environment (subjective or objective report from caregiver/parent), and functionality at school (academic results or conduct in school) based on verbal reports from a schoolteacher or school results/formal school reports based on formal reports. All outcomes, such as academic improvement, decrease in symptoms, and functionality at home or in a social environment, will be recorded using the Clinical Global Impression-Improvement (CGI-I) scale. On a separate note, this study will also observe the current treatment trends received and their outcomes among children from the first date of diagnosis. This is important for improving the diagnosis, management, and treatment of ADHD among children. The primary objective of this study is to observe treatment patterns among children with ADHD referred to psychiatry and mental health services in Malaysia after receiving treatment for 18 months. This study will also observe how the academic performance and ADHD symptoms and behaviors in children may improve or not improve at the 18-month follow-up. This study will also compare the treatment outcomes between children with ADHD who receive treatment and those who do not receive any ADHD treatment. Methods Study Design This is a multicenter retrospective study using secondary data. It will be conducted by reviewing the children with ADHD to examine current treatment trends and outcomes among children with ADHD referred to psychiatry and mental health services in Malaysia.
